interaction.content: I'm 28, and right now I have severe depression and moderate anxiety. What should I do? Because there are problems in my relationship, I don’t know what to do. I feel like I’m not in the wrong. If you can’t do what you promised me, then why promise it in the first place? Now he’s avoiding me, he doesn’t take the initiative to message me. If I text him, he still replies, but when I ask him, he just says he doesn’t want to move forward, just wants to keep things as they are now, and that makes me really miserable. How am I supposed to fix this? I don’t know if I just can’t let go of this person, or if I just can’t accept it.

Thanks for reaching out. Reading your story, I can sense that you’re really not in a good place right now, and I understand your confusion about this relationship. First, I want to say that mental health issues can’t be confirmed just through one or two simple tests. For what you described as severe depression and moderate anxiety, we’d need to understand more and look into it further.

Also, you feel you’re not in the wrong because the things you notice are mostly the pieces of evidence that support you. We need to look at the situation more objectively, and also understand that everyone has their own way of seeing things. He might feel that you’re being too aggressive, and that could have led to the current situation. We need to reflect on our own role and mistakes in this relationship, and hope to improve the current situation through learning and growth.

Senior year of high school, social anxiety. I’m thinking about whether I should distract myself a bit to make some friends, or keep my cold/distant vibe. My social anxiety is pretty bad, I don’t like leaving my comfort zone, and talking to unfamiliar classmates takes a lot of courage. Should I just focus on studying and keep to myself, or put some effort into making friends? Even though not having friends saves a lot of trouble, I do feel lonely sometimes.

I hear that you’re torn about whether to make friends or not. In your extra year of high school, you’re probably in a completely new class, while they already have their own friend groups. If you want to make friends, it might take more energy for you to build those connections.

You could think about this: what do you see a friend as? Someone who goes to the cafeteria with you and shares their feelings? Or someone you just chat with about daily life, ask about homework and that kind of thing? Based on your own definition of a friend, do you have to find that kind of friend among your unfamiliar classmates?

If it doesn’t have to be from your current classmates, you could consider looking for friends on some safe online platforms. For example, if you mainly want to vent, you could look for some reliable people online who are willing to listen.

If you really do hope to find friends among your unfamiliar classmates, then what exactly are you worried about when you think of talking to them? If the things you’re worried about actually happened, how much energy would you need to cope with them? How much courage would it take to take that first step toward making friends? How much energy would that courage use up?

How many hours a day are you studying? How much impact do you think having friends would have on your studying? If you had friends, how much extra trouble might that bring, and for you, what does loneliness mean?

After you have a clearer sense of all this, you can then think again about whether you want to make friends. The academic pressure in this extra year must be intense. If you feel you don’t have much energy, then staying in your comfort zone and letting yourself feel comfortable and safe is also totally okay.

If the courage to make friends doesn’t just drain your energy but actually gives you energy, then you can also bravely take a step forward and try to make a friend. I wish you all the best on the college entrance exam!

I really hate him, but I still can’t stop myself from contacting him. Should I get a divorce? My husband and I were high school classmates, we’ve known each other for over ten years. When we were dating as students, I felt like he could endlessly tolerate my bad temper. I’d hit him and yell at him, and he could accept it, so I mistakenly thought he had a really good temper. In the two years we lived together before getting married, he also hit me twice. One time he came home late after drinking, I got mad and slapped him first, then he got angry and slapped me back. The second time, I was in a bad mood and picked a fight, and in front of his friends, he hit me again. But we still got married.

During my postpartum confinement, because I was annoyed that he wasn’t doing anything, I kicked him once, and he slapped me in front of my mom. The day before yesterday, he came home late again and kept lying to me. My parents were helping me take care of the baby. I was afraid of waking them up, so I told him not to drag me back to our room to sleep, that I wanted to sleep with the baby. He wouldn’t listen, so I called his mom. Then he got furious and started kicking the door like crazy. After my parents came out, somehow he and my dad ended up fighting. My dad was hospitalized for two months this year and is still recovering. We called the police, but they didn’t file a case. He was detained for one night and then released, and he still hasn’t come home. I really hate him, but I still can’t stop myself from contacting him. I really, really need someone to comfort me, to hold me.

Hello, I can see that what you’re feeling right now is very complicated. You hate him, but you also can’t stop yourself from reaching out to him. Your marriage has gone through a lot of difficulties and violence, and that leaves you very confused about whether you should get a divorce.

From what you’ve shared, it sounds like your relationship at the beginning was built on you endlessly tolerating his bad temper. But this kind of tolerance hasn’t changed his temper; instead, it’s led to him using violence against you. Before you got married, you had already seen his violent tendencies. During the time you lived together, there were already two incidents of physical fighting, yet you still chose to move into marriage.

Now, becoming a mother has made you more vulnerable. Your urge to contact him might be a kind of dependence and a way of seeking comfort. But at this point, you have to face reality: your husband is not someone who can truly comfort you. His behavior has already gone beyond what is acceptable for a husband. He has used violence against you and your family, and that cannot be tolerated.

Right now, you need a friend or a counselor who can support you, someone who can listen to your anger, loneliness, and sadness, and help you regain your clarity. There are also your parents and others who can offer support; they can stay emotionally connected with you.

At the same time, I hope you can understand that right now you need to grow yourself, and protect yourself and your child. A dangerous relationship is extremely risky for a woman who is in a vulnerable state. Whatever choice you end up making, I hope you can truly become more mature and emotionally stable, because only when you grow yourself can you build a healthy relationship. I’m wishing you the best.
I was sexually assaulted when I was 5. I want to get better. Can you help me analyze and correct my thoughts?

Here I am, someone who’s willing to be a little sun in your life. I’m really glad we could meet here, and here, I want to give you a big hug, okay? I feel deeply for what you’ve been through, and I can understand how you’re feeling. This world has never really treated women fairly. I’ve had similar experiences myself, and I’ve also felt powerless because of them, even had thoughts of wanting it all to just end. But in this world, the way women are treated is always somehow “special.” These are things we can’t foresee, because we can’t know what’s in other people’s hearts, whether good or evil.

One of the reasons we can’t walk out of the shadow is how much we hate these experiences. They’re like a brand burned into our skin, carved into our hearts, constantly reminding us and tying us up inside. It took me a long time to come out of that shadow. I’d like to share how I did it, and I hope it can help you.

Don’t take on other people’s mistakes as your own. You’ve been holding on to what happened when you were five, and when you confronted him face to face, he pushed back and denied it. That must have been a real blow to you. But I can’t give you strong suggestions like having him punished by law, because just like you, I’m a coward too. What I can offer are some ways to heal yourself.

Bringing all this up again is like rubbing salt into the wound. You need to understand that the fault is not yours, it’s that boy’s. Even though you wish you could go back to that time, time can’t be reversed, and that’s why we keep brooding over it. We keep “caring” about it, so we can’t move past it, as if if we had refused back then, it wouldn’t have happened. This endless loop of “what ifs” can overstimulate the brain and leave us unable to feel at peace.

But if we keep fixating on this, do we lose the beautiful parts of life? I used to always look at my past self and see only a stain, so I became more and more insecure. I put other people’s wrongdoing on my own shoulders and couldn’t get out of the shadow, and the people I met just got worse and worse.

To get out of this, we need courage, courage that lets us be unafraid. Don’t be afraid of the bad things that have already happened; you need to strengthen your inner self. Go out more. Make some plans for the weekend—maybe visit a nearby city, and if you have time, travel somewhere a bit farther. By talking with different people, your world will become clearer, and you’ll be more willing to face the vulnerable parts inside you. We know we have our shortcomings, but that doesn’t mean we’re no good.

We don’t have to live up to “the world kisses me with pain, and I sing in return,” but we can still live a richer, more colorful life. Find things you like, and achieve something in the areas you enjoy. That way, even on the bad days, we can still meet better people.

So you don’t have to carry this shadow forever. Just believe in yourself, believe that you have the ability to start over. I’ll be here with you, staying by your side and supporting you.
I’m sixteen this year, and it’s really exhausting getting along with my friends. I’m wondering if I should change to a different group of friends?

When it comes to choosing friends or ending friendships, we all have that freedom. But I want to emphasize first: try not to decide too easily to “change friends,” because that can actually make making friends even harder, and you might end up regretting it and realizing your old friends weren’t that bad.

Everyone has different views. Whether it’s family, friendship, or relationships between people at different levels, getting along with others always needs some adjustment and give-and-take. When people with different personalities are together, conflicts often come up, but that’s when we should try to ease the conflict, not make it worse.

You mentioned your friend often gets mad and stops talking. Do you know why she does that? Is she always like this, or only when she’s angry? If she has a quick temper but then quickly lets things go, maybe you don’t have to coax her every single time. Comfort and care are important, but as friends, when she runs into difficulties or problems, it’s also our responsibility to offer the help and guidance she needs. It can’t just be comforting her when she’s upset and then not caring about her afterward.

If you two used to get along really well, that shows you care about her a lot. I’d suggest you first have an honest talk with her. Tell her how you feel about her always getting angry and not talking. Ask her why she does this and see if she can give you an answer you can accept. If her attitude really doesn’t change, you can gradually create some distance, but try not to do it by just giving her a cold face. After all, you’ve known each other for a long time, and cutting off the relationship might cause a chain reaction.

If this problem only started recently, it’s possible she’s going through something, or she’s hoping for a certain response from you that you didn’t notice, and instead you handled things in a way that made it more complicated.

I hope what I’ve said can be helpful for you.

I’m 26, I have a bachelor’s degree and I’m already married, but I don’t like my current job and feel it’s meaningless. What should I do? The work pressure is too much, especially the psychological pressure, mainly because of the way the system is set up. I work on a railway project and I’m away from home all year round, eating, sleeping, everything is in the same office building. I majored in accounting in college, and after working for three years I changed departments once, from accounting to materials, but I still don’t like it. And I don’t have other skills to make money, and my husband also works in this same organization. I often feel really lost. When I see my college classmates becoming teachers, I feel like their work is free and self-sufficient. How should I face this job of mine that feels meaningless and has such a heavy workload?

From what you’ve described, I’m not sure whether your main stress comes more from the heavy workload itself, or from the pressure of comparing yourself with your friends. About choices, I think there are a few directions you could consider: first, choosing work you love; second, choosing work you’re good at; third, choosing work that society needs; and finally, choosing work that benefits you. You mentioned you’re currently working within the system. I’d like to ask whether you feel somewhat restricted by that, or do you also feel there are some advantages?

Also, you’re seeing the free and self-sufficient side of your friends’ lives. Do you have a sense of what kind of effort and pressure they have to take on in order to pursue that freedom and self-sufficiency? Are there any other options that you could like and that would feel fulfilling for you?

You can think about those four reasons for choosing work and see which kind of choice fits your situation. Generally speaking, the more of those satisfaction points a choice meets, the easier it is for you to succeed and feel happy. Pressure can also become motivation. And you’re still young; you’ll need to take into account possible future pressures around having children and your career. Thinking about the possibilities in your life now is a kind of early preparation, which is actually very good.

You can consider three directions: inward, upward, or outward. Inward means doing your current job as well as you possibly can, learning to love what you do, discovering areas where you can grow within the job, and finding some enjoyment in it. Upward means looking for development in management roles. Outward means expanding into other fields, possibly changing careers or starting a second line of work.

You can research those four dimensions: how much you like it, what abilities it requires, the market potential, and the returns. Any choice involves trade-offs. Based on your current life stage, you can think about things like balancing family and work after having children, and make trade-offs accordingly.

You could also talk in depth with a career planning counselor and hear their suggestions. I hope you can realize your dreams soon.

I’m 26 now, married, and I have a bachelor’s degree, but I’m really unhappy with my current job and feel like it’s meaningless. I’m under huge work pressure, mainly psychological pressure. I work on a railway project and I’m stationed away from home all year round; everything—eating, drinking, using the bathroom—is all done in one office building. I majored in accounting in college and worked in that for three years, then transferred to the materials department, but I still don’t like this job. And I don’t have any other skills I can use to make money, and my husband also works in this same organization. I often feel very confused and I envy my college classmates who became teachers; they have a free and self-sufficient life. How should I face this job that feels completely meaningless and has such a huge workload?

You said you’re “away from home all year round, doing everything in one office building,” and at the same time you long for your college classmates’ “free and self-sufficient” life. I don’t know the exact details of your situation, but generally speaking, your current work and living environment sounds very single-track. You didn’t mention why you changed positions, but I’m guessing this kind of monotony might be the main reason you feel your work is meaningless.

Compared with your long-term field work, being a teacher is indeed more free. If your classmates are teaching in schools rather than in tutoring institutions, that freedom mainly comes from the school setting. Schools usually have weekends off and winter and summer breaks, so it’s very normal to envy them. Even in tutoring institutions, it might still be more flexible than what you’re doing now.

You said, “I moved from accounting to materials and still don’t like it, and I don’t have other ways to earn money.” I’m guessing you’re not only uninterested in the materials department, you might also be dissatisfied with accounting work. Unfortunately, my sense is that what you’re longing for might not really be the profession of teaching itself, but the richer life that teachers tend to have compared with your current job—that is, what we often call freedom.

There’s a saying: “Change industries but not roles, or change roles but not industries.” If the classmates you envy are indeed teaching in schools, then getting into a school would be changing industries, and you’d want to avoid changing roles again on top of that. You have a bachelor’s in accounting and work experience in accounting, so you don’t necessarily need other money-making skills; you could instead change your work environment and life rhythm.

But it’s also possible you don’t like accounting as a profession either. If that’s the case, then it’s a pity, because it sounds like you might not see many options for changing your work environment. If you could get a job as an accountant in a school, your work itself might still not feel satisfying, but at least outside of work you’d have more free time. Of course, that might require you to take some exams.

As for whether you could be self-sufficient, that would depend on the specific situation. If you truly want to go into a school as a teacher, it’s not impossible either—you could take the entrance exam for graduate school. Many vocational colleges in different cities recruit master’s graduates as teachers, so you could do a master’s degree. What major to choose would be up to you. But with the growing number of people applying for graduate school, this is not an easy path.

From what I’ve seen, it’s relatively easier for students to find ways to earn money, so usually the areas around schools have fairly well-developed living and entertainment facilities. Choosing a job also means choosing a way of life. You do have options, but each option comes with a price. If you choose not to change jobs, you don’t have to go through the pain of exams and interviews, but you do have to bear the pain of your current work environment. So you’ll need to weigh the pros and cons yourself, and then make a choice.

I’m 36 this year. I’ve been emotionally manipulated at work and also hurt by a player, and I feel really exhausted and empty. Even though I’ve already made it to middle–upper management in the company, in the past few years there’s been some vicious competition. A really disgusting female boss PUA’d me, spread rumors, smeared me, and sabotaged my relationships, which led to my original position being at risk, and I’m mentally and physically worn out. In my love life I met a guy who doesn’t want marriage and is a total player. It was only a bit over a year, and luckily I managed to end it in time, but I still feel empty inside. I want to go abroad to study and change my situation, but I feel like I just don’t have the strength, because no one around me supports me, and I keep feeling like people my age would look at me strangely. Have I really been drowned out by the social environment?

Reading what you wrote, I can understand the pain and helplessness you’re feeling right now. Your female boss smeared you and squeezed you out—was it because there were conflicts of interest between you, or because she felt threatened by you? As for the player you met, in a way it’s also a bit of a blessing in disguise that after a year together you were able to pull yourself out in time. Whether he’s a player or just a jerk, you need to learn to let it go.

First, the problem has already happened, so you need to learn to face and deal with being smeared. As long as what you do is compliant and legal, what are you afraid of? Are you afraid of losing your job, afraid of losing face in the company, or afraid of the rumors spreading? You need to understand that the schemes of petty people will eventually be exposed. If you haven’t resigned yet, you need to show the confidence you should have and stand up to it. Trust that smart people can see the truth of what’s going on. If that doesn’t work, then try to make peace with your boss. After all, you’re all working in the same company—why keep fighting? With good communication, very few people actually want to be enemies. Keeping things peaceful is the best strategy.

Second, about the player, you can see it as a lesson in misjudging someone. Instead of just feeling unlucky because you met a player, think about why you would meet someone like that and what you need to watch out for next time. Is it that some of your traits attracted a player? Take that as a warning. Start with yourself, keep moving toward the direction you hope for, and if you stick with it, I believe you’ll meet someone who truly understands you and gets you.

Lastly, whether to go abroad to study is completely up to how you see it. Even though 36 is a bit older in terms of age, if you really have the time, energy, and financial support, it might be an option for changing your current situation. Overall, whether you choose to study or not, the key thing is how you would handle it if you run into a situation like your current female boss again. Learn to understand yourself, and also to understand others. There’s no problem that you absolutely can’t get through—the key is how you look at it and how you solve it. Avoiding it is only temporary and doesn’t really solve anything.

I’m 36 this year. I’ve had a lot of time wasted by workplace PUA, and I was also hurt by a total player. I feel really exhausted and empty. As a 36‑year‑old woman, I feel like everything has already lost its meaning, I’ve even had thoughts of wanting to die. Even though I’ve reached a relatively senior position in a company, in the past few years I’ve gone through some vicious competition and was PUA’d by a really terrifying, twisted female boss. She spread rumors and slandered me, ruined my relationships with people, and now my position is hanging by a thread and I’m completely drained, both physically and mentally. In terms of relationships, I also met a player who never wants to get married. Even though it only lasted a bit over a year before we broke up, I still can’t shake this feeling of emptiness. I want to go abroad to study again to change my situation, but I feel like I just don’t have it in me, because there’s no one around me who supports me, and I keep feeling like other people my age will look at me strangely. Do you think I’m someone who’s already been swallowed up by society?

I read your words carefully and really listened to what you shared. I can feel that you’re facing two major themes in your life right now: family and career, or you could say emotions and relationships. I’vesummarized the main things you’re anxious about: you’re 36, you’re a woman, and you feel like you have nothing. Even though you hold a relatively senior position in a company, you ran into a twisted female boss who PUA’d you. She spread rumors and slandered you, damaged your relationships with others, leaving your current position very unstable and you exhausted in body and mind. In terms of relationships, you also met a player who doesn’t want to get married. Luckily you broke up with him in time, but it’s still hard to avoid feeling empty.

You want to go abroad to study and change your situation, but you feel very powerless, because no one around you supports you, and you keep feeling like other people your age will look at you differently. I can understand how painful it is, as a woman, to be PUA’d by a twisted female boss. And the fact that you’ve been able to get back to a mid‑to‑senior level position now shows your ability and value, and that others recognize you. That’s really impressive.

I was once PUA’d by a female department head myself. She tried to control everything about me, but I kept doing what I believed was right and kept developing my professional skills. Now I’m at a level she can’t even reach. Every time I run into her in the hospital courtyard, I still smile and say hello, because I’m a hundred times stronger than she is. I won’t waste my time getting into daily battles with someone who isn’t even on my level.

In terms of relationships, even though you broke up with the player, the fact that you were able to pull yourself out in time is something to be glad about. As for the emptiness you’re feeling now, maybe we can explore what kind of emotional needs you actually have. I believe that someone as outstanding as you will attract someone even more outstanding who loves you, someone who will see you as a treasure and protect you.

As for going abroad to study, that’s just one way to change your situation. Sometimes making adjustments within your current circumstances might actually be more workable. You could join some different circles, get yourself out there more, expand your social network, and improve your environment. Even if you do need further training, I’d suggest not completely giving up your current job. Starting from zero might not be the best fit.

Life needs some planning. To find your emotional home and your career path, you need to start from yourself and understand your own needs. That way, things will gradually get better. I hope what I’ve shared can be helpful for you.
Afraid of not finding a job? And also afraid of working? Confident or insecure?

First, I want to say I really understand what you’re going through, and my heart aches for you. I just want to give you a big hug so you can feel some warmth from the world. Honestly, I really appreciate your open attitude about being 30, that you’re not scared of this stage. After all, 30 is just 30. That popular show this year, “Nothing But Thirty,” already shows how women are getting better and better at being independent. Not being limited by age, not fearing age, breaking your own limits and breaking out of old constraints is one of the main values in our time.

Thank you for your hug and understanding. The problem I’m facing now is that I want to go back into the workplace, but work isn’t going as smoothly as I imagined. Some job postings I don’t even dare to apply for, and for the ones I do apply to, it’s like they just disappear without a trace. I don’t know if it’s because of my age. Friends around me all tell me to have the baby first, since age is a factor, but personally I don’t want kids right now. I’m a bit scared I won’t find a job and will be like a useless person, but I’m also a bit scared of working, repeating the same days over and over. Honestly I don’t even know what I want to do. On one hand I worry that because of my age it’ll just get harder and harder, and on the other hand I don’t know how to change things.

Hearing your confusion, I can understand your anxiety. In the workplace, things are still a bit harsher for women, and there is some age discrimination. But we can’t stop moving forward because of that, because we need to make a living, and we also need to add color to our lives and find our own sense of value and meaning. So work is actually very important for us. But your feelings are conflicted: you feel that working might mean repeating the same thing every day, but if you don’t work, you’re afraid you’ll become a “useless person.” I can understand this kind of anxiety, because once we start working, it is day after day of doing what we need to do. But we can also make every day different—the key is how you look at it. For example, if today you master a new skill, or you look at a problem from a different angle, that’s also a kind of reward that work brings you. But if you don’t work and maybe just stay at home every day as a full-time housewife, your perspective might become narrower. I’m not saying being a full-time housewife is bad—being a full-time wife is actually really hard and exhausting too. It’s just that each path has its own hardships and difficulties; it’s really about how you want to choose between them.

Thank you for your understanding and suggestions. Age really is a workplace issue for women, but we’re still young, we’re not at retirement age, so how could it be that you won’t be able to find a job that suits you? We need to change our mindset. Whatever we do, we should keep that original sense of passion, otherwise nothing we do can last. I’ll try my best to adjust my mindset, cherish each day, and work hard to find a suitable job. Thank you for your encouragement and good wishes. I hope I can be happy.

I’m really worried I won’t be able to find a job, and at the same time I’m afraid that working will make me feel stressed and anxious. I’m almost 30 this year. I’m actually not as scared of this stage as I imagined, but I’ve already been on a break for 8 months now, and it’s been for all kinds of reasons. At the beginning I was very worried, but now I’ve accepted the state I’m in and I’m getting ready to start job hunting again.

But I’m finding that looking for a job isn’t going that smoothly. Sometimes I don’t even dare to send out my resume, and sometimes even if I do, there’s no reply or offer. I don’t know if it’s because I’m too old, or because I just haven’t found a position that really suits me. Friends around me are all telling me to have a child first, but personally I don’t want that right now. I feel really confused and uneasy, and I don’t know what to do.

Job hunting is a very stressful thing, and whether it goes smoothly or not can affect our emotions. But we can’t ignore our own value. Whether we succeed or not, we should still hold on to our confidence and sense of pride.

Not daring to send out your resume might be because you’re afraid of being rejected or ignored, but even if you are rejected, it’s really not that big a deal. Instead, it can help you see where you can improve and build up your abilities. As for having children, you need to first be clear about your own thoughts and plans. If you don’t want to have a child for now, then try not to be swayed by outside pressure.

Being 30 is actually a great age in the workplace. At this stage you can make full use of your experience and skills to look for a job that fits you. I’d suggest you first focus on your interests and strengths, figure out what kind of career direction you want, and then gradually develop and build up your abilities.

What you’re saying makes a lot of sense, but I still feel really lost and don’t know where I should start. My previous jobs weren’t very stable, so it’s hard for me to pin down a clear career direction. At the same time I’m also worried I won’t be able to find a job I actually like, and then I’ll feel even more disappointed and uneasy.

Choosing a career is a process of constant trial and exploration. No one can be sure that their very first job is the one that suits them best. So you need to spend some time getting to know what you enjoy and what you’re good at, and also learn about the characteristics and requirements of different industries and positions.

Try not to worry too much about not finding a job you like. As long as you have a goal and a general direction, and you keep trying and exploring, you’ll be able to find a place that fits you. Even if there are failures or setbacks, don’t give up—these are things everyone has to go through in their career. I believe you can find a career direction that suits you and develop your own career path.

Thank you for your suggestions. I’ll try to explore and look for my own career direction. But I’m still a bit scared—scared that I won’t work hard enough or that my abilities aren’t enough, and I won’t be able to reach my goals. How should I deal with my emotions and this inner anxiety?

In the process of job hunting, you’ll run into a lot of difficulties and setbacks, but these are completely normal. We need to face these issues directly, and at the same time not blame our emotions and inner anxiety entirely on our own ability.

We need to trust our own strengths and potential, and keep learning and growing, continuously improving our skills and our attitude. Besides that, you can also expand your social circle, make full use of resources and opportunities, and look for leads and chances for work. In this process, you’ll discover your own strengths and potential, and become more certain about your goals and direction.

Lastly, no matter what problems you run into, try to believe in yourself. Talk with friends and family, look for support and encouragement, and keep as positive and upward-looking an attitude as you can with your emotions.

There’s this really uncomfortable feeling that stays with me, it’s especially irritating. Today I’m feeling a bit down. My mom came back from outside, she was busy doing things around the house, and just hearing those sounds made me feel really awful, inexplicably annoyed. It reminded me of when I was little. Back then my mom and dad were away, and I stayed with my grandma and my aunt. I never expressed it. Every time I was unhappy, my aunt and grandma would try to help me solve whatever problem I had, but I still wasn’t happy, just really irritated. There was one time I really wanted to ride my bike and ride straight into the big well. This feeling has often been with me, especially during puberty. And there was another period, when I was in eighth grade, I just felt this emptiness inside, like I had no support, it was really painful. I was unhappy all day, just wanted to cry, and I didn’t know why. Now I’ve been diagnosed with bipolar, with emotional and cognitive problems. I feel like it’s related to that time. Actually my grandma and aunt were pretty good to me, they never hit or scolded me. Is there any counselor who can help me figure this out? Thank you.

You’re saying that today you’re feeling low, and that your mom coming home made you feel irritable, right? From a psychoanalytic point of view, your mom’s “voice” is just a trigger that sets off the “shadow” inside you. In your unconscious, there may be a shadow that’s directly or indirectly connected to “your mom’s voice.” When you hear that sound, it’s very likely to activate that unconscious shadow.

In your description, you mentioned that while you were growing up, your parents were often not around, and you stayed with your grandma and your aunt. Every time your aunt and grandpa bought you shoes you didn’t like, you would rub them on the ground, and you’d feel uncomfortable even without a clear reason. You never expressed any of this. Whenever you were unhappy, your aunt and grandma would try to help you solve your problems, but you still felt annoyed. Especially during adolescence, this feeling often stayed with you. There was also a period, when you were in eighth grade, when you felt empty inside, with no support, very distressed, low all the time, wanting to cry but not knowing why.

Now you have bipolar disorder, with emotional and cognitive difficulties, and you feel it’s related to what happened before, even though your grandma and aunt treated you fairly well and never hit or scolded you. Is there any counselor who can help you understand this? Thank you.

Thank you for your reply. It’s true, every time I hear my mom’s voice, I’m reminded of scenes from my childhood. I realize I have a very strong sense of my parents’ absence. I’ve always longed for their love and companionship, but they were always busy with something and didn’t have much time to be with me. I also understand that my grandma and aunt meant well and were good to me, but they couldn’t really fill the gap left by my parents’ love.

I really want to change the way I look at all this, but sometimes it’s very hard. I hope I can find a better way to deal with this emotional distress.

What you’re saying makes a lot of sense. Your sense of your parents’ absence is very strong. You longed for their love and company, but they were often busy and couldn’t meet that need. Your grandma and aunt’s kindness did bring you warmth, but it couldn’t replace the love from your parents.

Changing how you see things is indeed difficult, but it’s not impossible. You can try to shift the way you look at these experiences and examine them in a more neutral, objective way. For example, you might notice that your parents’ busyness is also a reminder not to take other people’s love for granted, and to learn to go with the flow. The past is only one part of your life; it doesn’t have to become a burden.

If you can focus more on and savor the love your grandpa, grandma, and aunt gave you, it might help your mindset gradually shift. I hope these suggestions are helpful for you.

Thank you for your suggestions. I’ll try to change how I see things and to cherish and revisit the love my grandpa, grandma, and aunt gave me. Maybe once I can put down the burden of the past, I’ll be able to move toward a new life. I really do hope I can get out of this distress. Thank you so much for your patient listening and support.

You’re very welcome. I believe you can move past this distress. Remember, the past is just part of your life experience, not a burden you have to carry. When you put that burden down, you’ll be able to welcome a new life.

If you run into any difficulties while you’re making these changes, remember you can reach out to me anytime. I’ll be here to support you. Wishing you all the best!

Hello. Lately I’ve been really troubled. I care too much about what other people think of me, and I always overthink before I do anything. I’m 20, a junior in college. I feel like I put too much weight on other people’s opinions. I always want to leave a good impression on everyone, so before I do anything I think way too much. I’ll imagine, if someone else did this, how would I see them? If I feel there’s even a tiny bit that might look bad, I don’t want to do it. Maybe I’m afraid of leaving a bad impression in front of others.

For example, when competing for some important position, I can clearly see that the people running for it all have a very strong sense of purpose, or you could say they’re pretty utilitarian about it, and I feel kind of turned off by that. So I’m also afraid that if I go for it in that way, others will see me like that, so I don’t want to try. At the same time, I’m also afraid of failing in front of others, kind of holding on to this idea that if I don’t try, I won’t fail.

I’m like this when I interact with people too. I’m afraid they’ll feel I’m approaching them with some agenda. A lot of the time I’m really not proactive, and I overthink everything. My girlfriend says sometimes I’m like a girl, indecisive and thinking too much when I do things. I’m also gradually starting to feel that way about myself, and I really want to change my personality a bit, to become that kind of guy who’s more outgoing and generous, straightforward and decisive.

Hi. From what you’ve said, you feel you care too much about other people’s opinions. When you see others doing things with a clear purpose, you also judge them and see it as being overly utilitarian. But when you yourself want to go after something, you become very hesitant. Deep down, what you really want is to become someone brave, someone who dares to fight for what he wants.

From what you’ve described, I see that as you were growing up, your moods and sense of self-worth were always decided by other people’s evaluations. Maybe because you were well‑behaved, you wanted to hear your parents describe you as satisfactory and excellent. In that process, you gradually faded out your own inner thoughts, expectations, and needs. Inside, it feels like: if I follow my own ideas, expectations, and needs, then that’s bad. Only if I overcome these parts of myself and behave according to everyone else’s (parents’, teachers’, others’) expectations and evaluations, then what I gain is worthwhile, real, and meaningful.

Over time, this inner pattern became fixed. After you became an adult, when everything is supposed to be about living, planning, and working according to your own needs, your inner conflict started to show up. On the one hand, you think this is useful for you, it’s good (even if it’s utilitarian). On the other hand, your old pattern jumps out and says, “How can you just follow your own ideas? What are you ignoring?” At that moment, your subconscious will desperately look for evaluations and standards that are different from your inner needs, to prove that you really do have some “bad” thoughts, that these thoughts are wrong and shouldn’t be there.

And then, as long as other people show even the slightest sign of something, it immediately confirms this for you, making you feel even more that maybe you really “shouldn’t” (for example, being utilitarian). But at the same time, you also know you’re just an ordinary person, and it’s understandable to want these things. The result is inevitably a double conflict.

To change this situation, you already understand the logic; what you need is training. Training yourself to form a new pattern to replace the inner pattern that has been formed over many years of growing up, because the old one wasn’t formed in just a day or a few words. So changing it also won’t happen in a day or with a few sentences. Even if you understand the principle, you can’t get results just by demanding it of yourself. This is a long process.

There are two paths. On the one hand, you need to be able to tolerate this kind of conflict and struggle, and the shame, fear, and sense of crisis that come from going against your long‑standing habits. You need the courage to “burn your bridges,” to be willing to put yourself in a do‑or‑die situation and see what happens if you really try. But the psychological pressure from this process is also huge, no less than the pressure from your current inner conflict. If you’re clear about your reasoning, you’ll need to endure this process yourself and make up your mind to walk this road.

On the other hand, you can find a counselor to walk this road with you. Whether you’re ready and have started to take action to change, or you’re not ready and don’t have the courage yet, in both cases you need someone to safeguard your inner state and each small adjustment and change along the way. No one wants a huge ship in the ocean to change its course and undergo major repairs at the same time, with no safety measures at all. That would obviously be dangerous. And this is exactly why psychologists exist.

Alright, let’s pause here. Think about it for a bit. I hope this lets a ray of light into your world.

Thank you very much for your reply. After hearing your explanation, I really can understand my inner situation now. I know that changing my pattern is a long process that needs patience and determination. I’m also willing to try to overcome my inner conflicts and step out of my comfort zone. But at the same time I feel really scared and under a lot of pressure, afraid I won’t be able to stick with it. Could you give me some suggestions?

Of course. First, be clear that you’re making these changes for your own growth and happiness, not just to meet other people’s expectations. That can help you keep your inner motivation and sense of direction.

Second, try to find a way of practicing this new pattern that really fits you. You can seek help from a counselor; they can give you more specific advice and guidance based on your situation. Also, I suggest you talk with friends or family around you. Let them know you want to make some changes, and ask for their support and understanding, so they can help you keep going.

At the same time, set small goals for yourself and change step by step. Don’t put too much pressure on yourself. The most important thing is to believe in yourself, believe that you have the ability to change, and don’t be afraid of failure. Failing doesn’t mean you’re no good; every failure is a chance to learn and grow. I hope these suggestions can be helpful for you.

What I’m hearing is that every time it’s Spring Festival, Mid-Autumn Festival or other reunion holidays, you feel especially distressed and don’t want to go home. There’s a line from the Tang dynasty poet Wang Wei: “Alone, a stranger in a foreign land, I miss my family all the more on every festive day.” What this poem is expressing is probably that, being away from home, there’s no sense of belonging; on traditional Chinese festivals, when everyone’s family is reunited, you yourself can’t be with them, so you feel especially lonely. I believe you feel something similar. On Mid-Autumn Festival and Spring Festival, when people all over the country are gathering with their families, your longing for home and for your family naturally comes up, but because your family can’t give you warmth and love, you don’t want to go back to them. Reading what you wrote, I really sigh over what you’ve been through and the situation you’re in. Now, let’s explore together what you can do.

Hearing what you’ve shared, I can sense that your external life can basically meet your needs, but in your inner, emotional life you’re severely lacking in love and care, you could even say it’s in a really bad state. It seems like the biggest hurt comes from your mom. On the one hand, you protect yourself from being hurt by keeping your distance from her; on the other hand, you might also try to understand her pain. She may be venting her own inner pain onto you, even though

How can he pull away this fast? Is it being heartless or being rational? We’re long-distance, so why would my boyfriend not reply to my messages from noon all the way through the night, and then when I told him the next day that I was sad and upset, he just said he felt helpless? My heart really aches hearing what you’re going through. It feels like you’re someone who’s very emotionally rich, devoted in love, gentle and kind, while your boyfriend doesn’t seem to put as much effort and importance into the relationship as you do, and is also slowly withdrawing from it. I don’t know what your usual way of getting along is like, but from the two posts you put on your Moments and how he reacted, I get the sense that he might be using a kind of “cold treatment” to force you to be the one to bring up breaking up. Like you said, this hasn’t just been going on for a day or two, and almost every time it ends with you backing down, reaching out first, and barely keeping things going. There’s a line in the song “Red Rose” — the one who’s favored is fearless. Either he’s sure you won’t leave him and uses that to control you, or he wants you to be the one to initiate the breakup and end this relationship. Whichever it is, it’s hard for a relationship like this to last.

So if I say I’m letting go, does he just think there’s nothing at all between us anymore? Whatever I do, whether I’m happy or sad, has nothing to do with him? How can he pull away this fast? Does he really not have any feelings left? Even just as ordinary friends, if you hear the other person cried, you’d at least politely offer a bit of comfort, right?

Every one of those questions is like a knife stuck in your chest — I can really see how much it hurts. Maybe he’s not completely cold and heartless, but he doesn’t want to keep things dragging on and tangled in this relationship. He wants to cut things off cleanly and end it quickly, but he wants you to be the one to say the words, maybe so he can feel less guilty about it. I believe that when people first say “I love you,” they do mean it, and they do hope to grow old together. But life doesn’t stay frozen at that first moment, and most of us aren’t so lucky as to meet the right person from the very beginning. You could try to gather your courage and sit down with your boyfriend for a real talk, to hear what he honestly thinks. Even if the outcome isn’t what you want, it’s still better than being deceived and tormented inside the relationship.

Maybe everyone goes through the pain of a breakup at some point; it can feel like the darkest period of life. I remember when I broke up with my first love, it felt like the world lost its color, the sky and earth went dim, and I couldn’t find any meaning or hope in life. But it was exactly that hard period that gave me more insight into love, helped me grow as a person, and led me to meet someone better. Maybe at the time it was others who hurt us, but they also pushed us to grow and to find better happiness. I also wish for you, girl, that one day you’ll have an even better kind of happiness.

Let me also share how I got through my own breakup: ① Work hard on accepting the reality and stop having expectations of him. ② Let your emotions out: ◆ write about your feelings in a journal ◆ talk to close friends ◆ travel to clear your head ◆ listen to music you like ◆ find a quiet corner to cry or scream ◆ do some cardio exercise. ③ Read and study; learning can calm you and help you become better. ④ Try developing some hobbies to shift your focus. ⑤ Every day, give yourself more affirmation and positive responses, and give yourself confidence and strength. ⑥ Think more about his shortcomings and flaws. ⑦ When you feel really low, you can watch some funny videos — they can bring a lot of laughter!
I was sexually assaulted when I was 5. I want to get better. Can we analyze and correct my thoughts?

Dear, I can see you’re feeling a bit lost about your personal growth. You mentioned that when you were little you were forced and assaulted, and later you realized you actually could have gotten away, but at the time you still went along with it. And when you confronted the other person, they even said you agreed to it and tried to wash their hands of it. After that you started thinking, maybe you did know and agree, so what can you do now? But if you look at how it all started, did you really agree to it? You didn’t. You were forced. If you hadn’t gone along with them, they might have done even more serious harm to you. So in a way, what you did actually protected you to some extent.

Also, before you tried to escape, did you know you could get away? You didn’t. And if you hadn’t escaped, there might have been more assaults afterwards. So in fact, by getting away, you prevented more harm from happening to you in the future.

So you can see that a lot of your reactions and behaviors were actually about protecting yourself from even worse harm. And in that moment it was really hard to think clearly; of course you were terrified and confused. So please don’t blame yourself, dear. This is not your fault. It’s their fault. To put it more strongly, what they did was against the law.

They did break the law, but I keep doubting and feeling guilty about whether I could have broken free. I feel like in that moment I should have made a better choice instead of just letting them control me. I don’t trust myself. I feel like I was just a weak, shameful child back then.

Dear, your strong sense of responsibility is making you judge your own actions in a very negative way. But please remember, in such a terrifying situation, people’s thinking is affected by fear and confusion. You were just a very young child, facing a huge threat and something terrifying you couldn’t even understand. You did your best to escape, and that in itself is an act of courage and an effort to protect yourself. Please stop blaming yourself. You couldn’t possibly have predicted how things would unfold or what the consequences would be. Believe me, you are innocent. This was not your fault.

But whenever I think back to that experience, I always feel extreme fear and pressure, and I just can’t let it go. I don’t know how to get rid of these negative emotions. As for these memories, I want to get rid of their impact on my life as soon as possible.

Dear, what you’re feeling is completely understandable. An experience like that is extremely painful and traumatic for anyone. These negative emotions won’t disappear overnight; healing and recovery take time. I suggest you seek professional psychological support and treatment. A professional counselor can help you work through these memories and ease your stress and fear.

At the same time, I’d also suggest gently shifting some of your attention toward positive things, like taking part in activities you enjoy, talking with friends, and building healthy daily habits. These can help you build more positive emotions and strengthen your inner resilience. You’re not alone in this. We’ll be here supporting you.

Thank you for your suggestions and support. I’ll try to find a suitable counselor and get professional help to deal with these negative emotions and memories. I understand that right now I need to pay attention to my own inner world and feelings, and slowly rebuild my life. At the same time, I’ll also work on developing my hobbies and interests, and staying connected with family and friends. Even though this experience has really troubled me, I believe I can gradually walk out of the shadows and regain a confident and happy life.

Dear, you are very brave and strong. I’m really proud of you. Reaching out to a counselor is a great decision; a professional will be able to offer you more appropriate support and guidance. Remember to give yourself time and space, and don’t rush your healing. Everyone’s healing process is different. Trust that you can come out of the shadows and regain happiness and confidence. Whenever you need, we’ll be here by your side, supporting your choices and your efforts. You’re no longer alone—walking alongside you there is endless love and care.

Even though you feel like you have nothing right now, you’ve already made it to a mid-to-senior level in a company. You have a lot of experience in that area, and that can be turned into something of real value. You’ve gone through some really unfortunate things, but the good thing is you stopped the loss in time and didn’t keep wasting your time and energy. You could also think more about other aspects, like your physical health, the fact that you don’t have to worry about basic needs like food and clothing—aren’t there many things there that are worth feeling grateful for too? A lot of people can’t even find a job and have to worry about food and rent; some people spend their whole life with the wrong person, living every day in resentment and pain. From that angle, even though your current position isn’t secure, you can still find another job, and at least you won’t go hungry. You also got out of a harmful relationship in time, which means you now have more time for yourself and for people who genuinely care about you.

If you keep a grateful mindset and really appreciate what you already have, that will help your mood. You can also look for some hobbies to enrich yourself, to fill your inner world, so that your life doesn’t just depend on work and other people. For example, I personally like to make healthy food, do crafts, paint, and other creative activities. These things make me feel happy, and even if something at work doesn’t go well, I can calm myself down through these hobbies.

Also, you can think about whether other people’s “strange looks” are actually real. Are they really paying as much attention to you as you imagine? Now that you’re focusing on yourself, do you go around paying that much attention to the people around you—constantly worrying about how badly they’re working, how they’re still not married, whispering with coworkers every day about other people’s lives? Not really. Everyone is busy with their own stuff; they don’t have that much time to look at you in a strange way.

So what you need to do is make yourself happy and work hard to live the life you want. Other people won’t take responsibility for you; you are the main character in your own life. If you’re miserable because of other people’s opinions, do you think that’s worth it? So if there’s something you want to do, just go for it. Going abroad to study is also a great option. As long as you’ve weighed the pros and cons and you have enough ability, then don’t worry too much about what others think. Your own life will always be what matters most.
