Now when I see a cross I’ll immediately think of Jesus and also want to curse. Because of this I’ve seen a counselor before, she said God’s way of thinking is different from ours, he won’t punish you, if you want to curse then just curse, it’s fine to curse. But I can’t do it. I’m afraid if I go along with my OCD it’ll just get worse and worse, and I also can’t get over this hurdle in my heart and keep cursing like that. Right now every moment I’m thinking about this problem, controlling myself. From August until now it’s already been half a year… Every day I’m controlling myself. I’ve also read books on Morita therapy, “accept it as it is and do what needs to be done,” but even so, whenever I’m doing things I’ll constantly think of this and try to control it. Do you think I have to live with this kind of pain for the rest of my life? Controlling myself every day? I really feel like I’m being tortured to death… It’s been half a year and I still can’t get out of it, I keep going but I don’t want to die.

With obsessive-compulsive symptoms, there’s often some kind of unmet need inside. In your situation, it might be that you don’t really like directly expressing your anger and your more aggressive side. In a family that believes in Buddhism, the gods and Buddhas may symbolize your family’s hopes and ideals, and at the same time they’re carrying your inner dissatisfaction and aggressive thoughts. You’ve been trying hard to hold back your aggressive impulses, and because that energy hasn’t been released, it can’t find an outlet inside you and turns into anxiety. Your family is very devoted to Buddhism. Even if you yourself might not really believe, you can’t avoid taking in some of their views, like “you must not offend the deities.” Cursing the gods and Buddhas is a bit like challenging your very devout Buddhist family, offending the deities and also offending your elders, so you feel guilty. Whether it’s the gods and Buddhas or Jesus, they’re all spiritual anchors. For you, the gods and Buddhas are your family’s faith, while you’re exploring your own meaning in life and your own beliefs, as if you’re choosing a path that’s different from your family’s. Maybe in your life, you have different opinions about the behavior of some authority figures, you might even feel angry. But because you respect elders and authority, you can’t express your dissatisfaction and anger, or maybe the authority is too overbearing and doesn’t allow you to express it, which leaves you very conflicted inside. As a young person, as you gain more experience, your sense of self is getting stronger, and you’re forming your own judgments and analyses about things. Sometimes we need to break conventions, challenge authority, and establish our own authority. As the saying goes, the waves behind drive the waves ahead; only with inheritance and also breaking through and innovating can each generation become stronger than the last. Try to imagine: if the gods and Buddhas who save all beings, or Jesus who loves others as himself, heard your curses and understood your intention, how do you think they would respond to you?

What you said is very true, I really don’t like directly expressing anger and aggression, especially in my family. I understand that the gods and Buddhas are a very important faith for my family, while inside I feel dissatisfaction and conflict. I know that having thoughts of cursing the gods and Buddhas is offending my family and authority figures, and that’s part of why I feel so guilty. At the same time, I also understand that personal growth means constantly challenging and breaking through, and building my own authority. But this conflict keeps bothering me, and I’m worried it will just get worse because of it. I really don’t want to live in this kind of pain for my whole life, having to control myself every day. It’s been troubling me for half a year, and I still can’t get out of it. Sometimes I even feel really stuck and hopeless.

I can understand your confusion and pain. This kind of inner conflict is really painful for you, and the fact that it’s gone on for so long makes it especially hard. Of course, each of us has our own beliefs and ways of seeing things, and that’s very personal. But I want to remind you that working through this kind of conflict takes patience and time. You could try talking with your family, honestly sharing your inner dissatisfaction and confusion. Maybe they’ll be able to understand how you feel and give you more support and help. Also, you can seek help from a counselor; they can offer professional guidance and support to help you handle this conflict and pain better. Remember, you’re not alone. There are people who are willing to listen to you and help you get out of this painful situation.

Thank you for your understanding and suggestions. You’re right, I really do need patience and time to work through this conflict. I’ll try to talk openly with my family and express how I feel inside, and I hope they can understand and support me. At the same time, I’ll also seek help from a counselor, and I hope I can get professional guidance and support and find better ways to deal with this. Thank you for staying by my side and giving me encouragement and support.
You’re welcome. I’m really glad I can be here with you and offer you support and encouragement. Remember, in this proce

What’s the psychological mechanism behind always going to the bathroom? Some kids like to squat on the toilet and sit there for half an hour at a time, and this happens every day. It’s mainly so they can play on their phones. Has anyone else noticed the same thing?

Hello, let’s work through this step by step. First, we need to look at why the child likes staying in the bathroom. Could you tell me about your child? How old is he, and what is his personality like?
He’s a twelve-year-old boy. He has a very lively personality and likes talking with people. But recently, he keeps wanting to hide in the bathroom, and that really confuses me.

Mm, boys at this age are going through puberty, and they may be more sensitive to their own feelings. So perhaps he needs some time alone right now to think through his own issues. The bathroom gives him a relatively quiet space where he can relax his emotions and step away from reality for a bit.
Then what do you think I should do? Should I let him stay in there for half an hour?

We can communicate with him and ask what he does in the bathroom. Maybe he needs that space to play on his phone, but it’s also possible he’s thinking about some things. If necessary, we can also take him for a physical checkup to see whether there’s any physiological reason causing him to stay in the bathroom for such a long time.
I understand. I’ll try to communicate with him. Thank you for your advice.
You’re welcome. If you have any confusion or concerns, feel free to contact me anytime.

I'm 17, and I've been diagnosed with severe depression. I know my mom is really worried about me, but she can't understand the way I think. The age gap is too big, and we think differently. What should I do?

Your mom not being able to understand your thoughts may lead you to break down, and it can affect her too. This kind of situation is very normal. You hope your mom can support you in carrying out your ideas, right? But because she can't understand you, getting her support becomes difficult. Still, you can try this: when you notice that your mom can't understand you, temporarily let go of trying to get her support, and write down your thoughts. Later, when you have the ability to support yourself, or when someone else can support you, you can put them into action. What feels helpless right now is that you need your mom's support to carry out these ideas, but because she can't understand, you can narrow the scope of your actions and ideas and do the parts she can understand. That way, at least the two of you can get along better. After you go to college, when you have some control over money, you'll have more chances to act according to your own wishes. Sometimes, to avoid conflict, you need to delay meeting some of your own needs. If you need to communicate with others, you can do it through messages or private messages.

I understand your suggestions, but I'm worried I won't be able to keep enduring it. I feel like I've been suppressing things for too long, and now I'm falling apart more and more. I feel hopeless about the future. I really want to find a way to get some relief.

I understand your worries. Suppressing things for too long really can make a person feel hopeless and like they're falling apart. Right now, you need to find a way to get some relief and help yourself. There are some things you can try, such as finding a professional counselor or doctor to help you get through this difficult period. They can give you more specific suggestions and treatment plans based on your situation. In addition, you can also try some self-help methods, such as exercise, journaling, or taking part in social activities. These may help reduce your symptoms and emotions.
Thank you for your suggestions. I'll consider looking for professional help. But I'm still a little worried. If my mom knows I want to see a counselor, she'll be really upset.

I understand your concern. You're worried that your mom may feel upset because you're seeking help from a counselor. You can try communicating with your mom and tell her why you want to see a counselor, and that it's very important for your condition and recovery. Maybe she will gradually understand what you're doing, and feel proud of and supportive of your choice. If she can't accept it for now, you still need to stick with your choice, because what matters most is your recovery and health.

You're right. I'll try to communicate with my mom, and I hope she can understand and support me. At the same time, I'll also look for a professional counselor to help me get through this difficult stage. Thank you for your support and advice.

I'm glad I could help. Remember to keep communicating with your mom, and also look for professional help. You are not alone. There are people who will keep supporting you and stay with you through this difficult time. I hope you can come out of this shadow soon and find a happy and peaceful life again. If you need any more help or want to talk, feel free to come back to me anytime. You are not facing all of this alone.

Should I give up pursuing an absolute sense of safety and let myself focus on work even with risks? I used to live very happily. I felt the world was beautiful, and I was motivated and proactive at work. But a couple of years ago, when things were going really well, I got carried away and made mistakes, and I had commercial sex several times. Afterward, I was terrified of AIDS. I tested negative a few times, and I wasn’t that scared anymore at first. But then, during the COVID pandemic, I started working from home, so I had more time to learn about AIDS. Then I found out it can also be transmitted through wounds. Even though the chance is very small, theoretically it’s still possible! Now I’m getting more and more scared. As long as I have a wound on my hand, I don’t dare go to public places. If I got infected myself, that would be one thing, but what worries me most is, what if I got infected and then passed it to my children? Their lives would be ruined! Now I’m almost unable to work. As soon as I get ready to work, there’s a voice in my head reminding me to check whether I’ve had any wounds on my hands recently, whether I’ve touched public objects or facilities, whether I could get infected, and what I would do if I did. I reflected on it, and I may be wanting an absolute sense of safety, but there probably is no absolute safety in this world. I’m asking for help: how can I give up wanting absolute safety, so I can focus on work even when there is risk?

Seeing that you’re struggling with this, I understand how you feel. I can sense that you care very deeply about your children’s safety and health, and that comes across as very tender and gentle. First, I want to affirm that you are very brave. Being able to face past mistakes and reflect on them is a really good thing.
Thank you for affirming that. But I still can’t get rid of the fear. I really want to focus on work, but these thoughts keep interrupting my thinking.

I know how helpless these kinds of thoughts can make a person feel. I’ve had similar worries before, too. But gradually, I came to see that fear is an emotion that can make people lose rational thinking and magnify problems endlessly. And a sense of safety doesn’t mean pursuing absolute safety; it means taking some actions within a range you can tolerate to reduce risk. You might consider gradually letting yourself go to public places again, while keeping good hygiene habits. This can help you slowly rebuild trust in your surroundings and regain courage. Little by little, you may find that these worries are unfounded, and you can bring your attention and energy back to your work.
Thank you for your suggestions. I’ll try to put these methods into practice. But I’m still worried that I won’t be able to stick with it.

I understand your worry. This process doesn’t happen overnight. It takes effort and adjustment bit by bit, and it also takes a lot of patience and self-affirmation to support yourself. So when you feel a bit irritated or defeated, you might pause, breathe deeply and slowly, and tell yourself that slowing down is so you can keep going better. Give yourself some time and space so you can regain calm and confidence. When you gradually notice that you can do better than before, be sure to reward yourself well.
Okay, thank you for your encouragement. I’ll keep it in mind. Then, when I feel like I need help or support, can I come talk to you?
Of course. I’m always here. Whenever you need me, you’re welcome to come talk with me anytime. It’s also my honor to explore and work through these issues together with you.

I’m feeling really anxious right now. I’m afraid I won’t be able to find a job, but I’m also afraid of working. I’m not sure whether I’m confident or have low self-esteem. Although I’m about to turn 30, I’m not afraid of this stage. But I’ve already been resting for eight months, and now I’m getting ready to return to the workplace. It’s been hard to find a job, and I don’t know if it’s because of my age.
May I ask what kind of work you used to do, and why you paused for eight months?
I worked in financial and administrative management. Because the company had layoffs, I had no choice but to leave. And I rested for this long because of some family reasons.

I understand. Now that you’re stepping back into the workplace, job hunting will definitely come with challenges and difficulties. In this situation, remember to give yourself time and patience. You said you don’t know whether you’re confident or have low self-esteem, and that feeling is very common. Don’t feel discouraged because of your thoughts. During this period, we need to challenge ourselves again and adjust our state and mindset. Would you try sharing with me what your recent thoughts and worries have been? Do you have any specific plans or ideas about work?

In the past few days, I’ve fully accepted this state and I’m ready to return to the workplace. But I’ve found that finding a job isn’t as smooth as I imagined. Some job postings I don’t dare apply to, and for some I’ve applied, there’s been no response at all. I don’t know if it’s because of my age. Friends around me are all advising me to have a baby first. But personally, I don’t want a child right now. I’m a little afraid of not being able to find a job and being like a useless person, but I’m also a little afraid of working, repeating the same day over and over. Honestly, I don’t even know what I want to do. On the one hand, I’m worried things will get harder and harder because of my age; on the other hand, I don’t know how to change.

These thoughts and worries are very normal, but I believe you can definitely find a job you’re satisfied with. Try not to feel pressured by the suggestions of people around you. You need to find work that suits you and make your own choices. Don’t put all your energy into worrying and feeling anxious; instead, spend more time and energy thinking about and planning your future and career development. You can try to identify the type of job you most want, and bring out your strengths and skills in your work. At the same time, you can also learn more about a company’s culture and values in your daily search, and find work that suits you better. You can start by applying to some positions you’re interested in. If you don’t get a response, don’t be discouraged; you can keep looking for other paths.
Thank you for your advice. How can I learn about a company’s culture and values? I also feel like I need some confidence and courage to look for work.

You can start learning about a company’s culture and values in a few ways: first, you can use the company’s official website, job sites, and other channels to learn about the company profile and recruitment information; second, you can look for public comments from employees, or ask people in the same field or friends on social networks; finally, you can get some insight by assessing the company’s core business, philosophy, and goals, so you can find opportunities to bring out your value at work. Most importantly, you need to have confidence and courage, and don’t let failures or setbacks hurt your confidence. As long as you stay confident and prepare and take action in a planned way, you’ll definitely be able to find the job you want.

Studying honestly and grinding away—can studying really bring me the life I want? I’m a junior in college. My grades were always very good in high school, but I messed up on the college entrance exam. Now I’m at a university that isn’t a Double First-Class or 985/211, but it’s actually quite strong. My grades in college are also okay, and I’m planning to apply for a master’s program in the UK. But recently I’ve started feeling lost. I’m in science and engineering, and honestly, if you really study seriously in college, it’s really exhausting, and also very dull. Lately I’ve started envying the lives of a few friends back in my hometown. Their grades weren’t good; some are even in vocational colleges, and some are at first-tier universities but the kind that are Chinese-foreign joint programs—you know what I mean. But it feels like their lives are so rich... They go to bars at night when there’s nothing to do, play mahjong in the afternoon. But they’re not just wasting their days either. They actually meet a lot of people, have a wide social circle, their parents are also fairly well-off, and they all have pretty high emotional intelligence. So I feel like their future development probably won’t be too bad. And I’m the kind of person who just studies honestly, exhausted every day. My life isn’t that colorful, and I don’t meet that many people. I feel like my current state of life is really not what I want. Actually, I already felt this way in high school, but back then I had the belief of getting into my dream university, so I was still very motivated. But now when I think about it, even if I go study in the UK and come back, if my life is still this dull, then it feels meaningless...

First of all, thank you for trusting me and being willing to share what’s been troubling you. I can see that you seem a bit lost right now about your life and future, not knowing where to go from here. It seems like studying hard has also reached a kind of bottleneck. I can feel your exhaustion. You’ve really been working hard—take a rest and catch your breath. You envy your friends back home. Although their grades aren’t as good as yours and their schools may not be as good, they have their own lives—they can go to nightclubs and play mahjong. For someone like you who has studied so hard for so many years, it’s understandable that you would envy that kind of state, because human nature tends toward laziness. Anyone would want to spend every day carefree and happy if they could. Maybe you’re a little better at delaying gratification than your friends, so you chose to suppress that natural side of yourself and work hard for the future.

Yes, I feel lost about my future, and I’ve started to doubt whether the motivation I’ve always had for studying is actually right. Seeing my friends living such colorful lives, I’m starting to feel like I’m wasting my time right now.

Everyone has their own different way of living and their own pursuits. Your friends have chosen the lifestyle they like, and you have chosen to study hard. That is completely a personal decision. Although you may feel stressed and tired right now, please believe that your efforts will not be in vain. Social circles and entertainment can bring a certain amount of happiness, but what can truly shape your future is still your learning and effort.

Sometimes I really feel very tired. When I see how relaxed and free they seem, I start to wonder whether I’ve made the right choice. Also, I’ve started worrying whether my family background will limit my development.

Your feelings are understandable. Life is sometimes like this: we see what others have and overlook what we already have. I want to tell you a story. There was a little girl who kept a black bird. She took very good care of it, and it grew well, with shiny feathers and a beautiful song. One day, she heard that there was a bluebird in the world, and whoever found it could have lifelong happiness, so she decided to set out to look for the bluebird. She traveled to many places and asked many wise people, but no one had ever seen the bluebird. They only said that they had found happiness because the bluebird had flown past their window while they were asleep at night. The little girl became even more curious, until she asked an old woman, who said, “The bluebird you’re looking for is not far from you.” Then that night, the little girl had a dream. In the dream, the black bird she kept was singing beautifully the whole time. The next day, she woke up and suddenly understood. She hurried home, opened the cage, and gently stroked the black bird. It turned out that the bluebird she had been searching so hard for had been right beside her all along. Everyone has their own path. Your efforts have always been with you, and every step you have taken is valuable.

I understand now. Everyone has different paths and experiences. I can’t only look at other people’s lives while ignoring my own efforts and achievements. I should cherish what I have and believe in my own choices.

Exactly! You’re very smart, and you’re able to recognize your own situation and find the right answer. Believe in yourself. You are walking toward the path that belongs to you, and every step matters. After you apply to study in the UK, you may see more beautiful scenery and come into contact with a much wider world. How could that kind of circle compare with a mahjong circle? Hold firmly to your choice. Your future will definitely be full of endless possibilities. You’ve got this!

Just studying honestly and rigidly—can studying really bring me the life I want? I’m a junior in college. My grades were always very good in high school, but I messed up the college entrance exam. Now I’m at a university that isn’t a “Double First-Class” school, though it’s actually quite strong. My grades in college are also okay, and I’m planning to apply for a master’s program in the UK. But lately I’ve started feeling lost. I’m in science and engineering, and to be honest, if you really study seriously in college, it’s honestly pretty exhausting, and also very boring. Lately I’ve started envying the lives of a few friends back in my hometown. Their grades weren’t good; some are even at vocational colleges, and some are at first-tier universities but the kind that are joint Chinese-foreign programs (you get what I mean). But their lives feel so rich… going to bars at night when there’s nothing to do, playing mahjong in the afternoon. But they’re not just wasting their days either. They actually come into contact with a lot of people, have very wide social circles, their parents have decent means, and their emotional intelligence is pretty high. So I feel their future development actually won’t be too bad. And I’m just the kind of person who studies honestly, exhausted every day, and my life isn’t that colorful. I don’t meet that many people either. I feel like my current life is really not what I want. Actually, I already felt this way in high school, but back then I had the belief of getting into my ideal university, so I was still very motivated. But now when I think about it, even if I go study in the UK and come back, if my life is still this boring, then it feels kind of pointless…

When I saw your question, I felt that you’ve begun to think about your own life. You’re also seeing yourself, and seeing is the beginning of change. It happens so quietly, yet like a seed, it has begun to sprout. You ask whether just studying rigidly is useful. If we think about the vast world we open up when we open a book, whether we read in a flexible way or, as you said, in a rigid way, it is definitely, definitely useful. And also, how do you define “studying rigidly”? After ten years of hard study, for students today, there are actually many more choices now. It’s no longer like before, when success seemed to have only one path. Being able to study is, in fact, such a good opportunity.

There are indeed more choices now, but the reason I feel lost is that I think college life is really exhausting, and I’ve started to envy those friends who didn’t have good grades but have rich lives. Sometimes I feel like I’ve always been fighting for grades, and my life doesn’t have that much fun or that many social circles.

Seeing you say that you didn’t do well on the exam back then, I imagine you must have had an ideal university and major in mind at the time. Since you didn’t get to go to your ideal university, I want to encourage you not to lose heart. Life doesn’t only give us one chance to choose. The best time to plant a tree was ten years ago, and the next best time is now. You’re a junior now, and it’s not too late to do anything. Among the friends around me, after starting work, many ended up in jobs unrelated to their majors and chose careers they truly wanted to pursue. Later, because of work needs, some also went on to further study. Our path of growth is very broad. I’ve always followed the idea of learning as long as I live, and I’m also working hard to be someone who keeps growing.
You’re right. I still have the chance now to pursue the life I want. But I still feel envious of my friends’ colorful lives. They seem happier than I am, and they also have more social circles.

When you compare yourself with your classmates and friends, while you’re envying them, they may also be envying you. I saw you say you feel lost and are planning to go to the UK for graduate school. This is another new choice. I’d like to invite you to think carefully: this time, what do you want? What kind of life do you want to live? Through graduate study, how do you want to move closer to your ideal life? You feel your friends’ lives are rich and their circles are wide. Actually, enriching your own life is something that can be a bit easier. For example, I like reading, working out, listening to music, and many other things, and I’m still constantly discovering more. Hobbies and interests can be cultivated. As long as you want to enrich your life, it can become richer; it just takes action.

You’re right. I should cultivate more hobbies and interests, try taking part in some activities, and expand my social circle. I really do need to change my current way of living and make it more colorful.

And with social circles, when you take part in many activities, including volunteer activities, your circle will slowly expand too. Seeing you say your life feels boring, I can also sense the upward strength in you. You want to change; it’s just that when you raised this question, you hadn’t yet found a good point to break through. Maybe when you read the answers, things will suddenly become clear and you’ll find a direction. You’re at the best age right now, and your life is in your own hands. Go ahead and express yourself fully, and paint the picture you want for yourself. The future you will also be very grateful to the you right now. Give it your all and keep moving forward through the challenges. It will all be worth it. Wishing you well, big boy.

I’m full of regret. My friends told me not to think too much—what should I do? Maybe I’m too annoying, so they think maybe I’m not able to do certain things, and then that leaves me full of regret. Then I wanted to check in with them and have my mom help me ease some of my sadness, but they didn’t really tell me anything, just said not to think too much, relax, be happier. What should I do?

I can see that you feel a lot of regret about where you are right now. Sometimes friends’ advice can actually leave you feeling more confused. You said it may be because you’ve been feeling irritable a lot, which led them to think you can’t do certain things. I can understand that feeling, and it also seems quite realistic. Have you thought carefully about what you want to do, and how you might do it? It may help to have a clear direction and plan in your mind, and not spend too much time asking others, but instead look for ways on your own. Asking others is one way, of course, but asking too much may make people feel that you don’t have a clear sense of direction or a plan. Someone with a clear direction usually spends more time thinking about how to do it, rather than asking over and over. Of course, seeking advice appropriately is necessary. The things you want to do shouldn’t depend too much on other people. You can learn to encourage yourself and try to work toward them step by step on your own.

You’re right. I also realize that I may have been relying too much on other people’s replies, while ignoring my own inner thoughts and plans. At the time, I asked my friends for their opinions because I felt uncertain about my own actions, like I had lost my direction and a concrete plan. But I also understand that they didn’t tell me because they care about me and hope I’ll have fewer worries, but that actually limits my ability to try new things. I should practice more on my own and try things myself.

I’m glad you can understand their care. When you mentioned that others didn’t tell you not to think too much, to relax, and to be happy, I get the sense that when you’re doing something, you may have some concerns and worries. Have you had your own thoughts about the way they responded? Why do you think the people around you respond to you in this way? It may be because they feel you think too much, have too many concerns, or that although you want to do something, you don’t have a clear direction or method. Although they didn’t say it clearly, their intention is to hope you won’t be troubled by too many concerns. But this can also affect you when you want to do something but can’t make it happen. So I’d still suggest that you train yourself more and try to complete some things on your own.

I understand now. I realize that I’ve been relying too much on other people’s encouragement and replies, while ignoring my own inner thoughts and abilities. Actually, in the process, I also need to think and try more, instead of getting too caught up in other people’s opinions. Maybe I really do need to train myself more and improve some of my abilities and courage.

I’m glad to see that you’ve come to understand this. Indeed, inner reflection and ability are very important for our growth and development. In the process of trying new things, we need to keep thinking, learning, and training ourselves, so that we can make progress. Believe in yourself and in your abilities. You’ll be able to accomplish the things you want to do.

Thank you for your support and encouragement. I’ll work on improving my ability to think things through, and I’ll try to do some things on my own. Believing in myself is very important, and I’ll keep going.
You’re welcome. I believe you can definitely succeed. Remember to hold on to your beliefs and make full use of your abilities. You’ll be able to achieve your goals. You’ve got this!
I feel really inferior, like I’m not good enough. I always feel like I’ve let my parents down. What should I do?

From what you’ve described, you are very filial and sensible. Because your family’s finances aren’t comfortable, you took the initiative to work and earn money to ease your parents’ burden. Your studies are relatively okay too, and you do have areas you’re good at. When it came to your own decisions, you handed that power over to your parents. You sent all the money you earned from work back home. You’re very selfless and think a lot about your family, barely thinking about yourself at all.

In real life, people who are more sensible often carry more and give more, while the people around them tend to show them less care and attention. Sometimes, real help means first becoming stronger yourself, so you can better help the people who need help. Filial duty also shouldn’t become blind obedience. If you do everything according to your parents’ wishes, then it loses the meaning of being filial. You can do whatever you can for your parents, but you can’t give yourself up completely for them. You think especially much about others and care about their feelings, while not paying much attention to your own feelings. You’re always thinking of meeting other people’s needs first, so it’s easy for you to feel inferior.

I know personality is hard to change, but I still really want to become the kind of guy who seems more outgoing, open, direct, and decisive.

Every kind of personality has its pros and cons. Seeing more of the good sides of your personality can help you better accept your true self. And it’s also possible that if you really did become another kind of personality, you’d find that that personality also has many parts you don’t really like. So accepting yourself is the most important task.
I understand. I think the reason I care too much about other people’s evaluations is that I feel like what others think of me equals the real me.

When we can realize that no matter how others judge us or see us, it doesn’t mean they fully understand us—that it’s only their perspective, filled with a lot of bias and misunderstanding—we can feel less anxiety and pressure about other people’s biases.

Yes, I understand. Maybe some truths take a long, long time to understand, but we slowly come to realize that doing our own things well is what matters most. What other people think really isn’t that important.

I’m very glad you can understand this. I wish you all the best, and I hope you can relax your mindset, be yourself, and no longer care too much about other people’s opinions. You are a wonderful person, and you need to believe in your own abilities and worth. If you need it, I’ll always be here to support you.
Thank you for your encouragement and support. I’ll work on facing my own issues and slowly accepting my true self.

Lately I’ve been really bothered by one thing: after I lose something, I keep dwelling on it, and even when I’m doing other things I keep thinking about it. Today I realized my eye cream was missing, and suddenly remembered that yesterday I helped my roommate throw away a big bag of things, and there was an eye cream in it that looked just like mine. It was very likely mine. The eye cream wasn’t expensive, but losing it really made me unhappy, and I feel very frustrated. Also, before this, somehow my comb disappeared for no clear reason too. Maybe it also fell into that bag, but the bag has already been thrown away now. I know I can’t get it back, but I still can’t help thinking about it. I want to know how I can get out of this feeling.

Accidentally losing something useful to you can definitely feel really upsetting. When you feel upset, what does your inner voice say? Do you blame yourself, thinking that if you had just looked one more time this wouldn’t have happened? Or do you feel like you’re terrible because this isn’t the first time you’ve lost something? Or feel bad about having to buy it again, and so on? These are just examples I’m giving, not necessarily your real thoughts, but you can try to quiet down and listen to what your inner voice is saying. Because it’s these voices that keep making you replay it over and over and keep feeling upset. Once we find these inner voices, we can try to redefine the event: 1) Thankfully, it was only a comb and an eye cream that were lost, not something more valuable. 2) Although the loss came at a cost, it also reminded us to put things away more carefully; this is a valuable experience. 3) The loss of the eye cream brought you a better discovery: curiosity. If something similar happens again in the future, curiosity may help you make a decision that minimizes the loss. These are only my examples. You can find more meanings in this event that are valuable to you, and that may help replace the discomfort caused by the loss. Would you be willing to give it a try?

I understand. I should be calmer about this and not get too stuck on what I lost, but instead try to find some positive meaning and something I can take from it. Thank you for your suggestions. I’ll try to change the way I look at it.

You’re welcome. Being able to notice your emotions and being willing to try changing the way you look at things is already a big step forward. As long as you’re willing, there will be many opportunities for you to learn how to cope with similar things and gradually reduce this uncomfortable feeling. When you encounter a similar situation again, you might try looking at it from a new angle; your mood may feel a bit better that way.

You’re right. I should face these things more positively. When I feel sad or stuck on something again, I’ll try to find the positive side of it and tell myself not to care too much about what I’ve lost. I believe that as long as I keep at it, I’ll definitely be able to overcome this emotional distress.

Very good! Believing in your own ability is very important. You’ve already taken the first step. From here, as long as you maintain a positive attitude and keep going, you can definitely overcome this emotional distress. Remember, don’t put too much pressure on yourself; just do the best you can. If you run into any difficulties or need help, remember that you can seek support from me or from others at any time. We’ll all be here with you.
Thank you for your encouragement and support. I’ll keep it in mind. Knowing that you’re all here supporting me makes me feel very comforted and confident. Thank you again for your help!

You’re very welcome. I’m glad I could help. If you need anything, you can come talk with me anytime, and I’ll keep supporting you. Trust in your ability to adjust and take care of yourself; you can definitely get through this difficulty. I wish you all the best, and keep a positive mindset!
Thank you for your wishes and encouragement. I’ll definitely keep going and maintain a positive mindset. I wish you peace and all the best as well. Thank you again for your companionship and support!
The interview exam is coming up soon, and I’m a little nervous. The pressure feels a bit high?
Don’t worry; this is very normal. Try this: before the interview, take some deep breaths and tell yourself that you’re already prepared. Relax a little—you can do very well.

Thank you for your advice. I’ll try it. But I also have final exams to prepare for, so the pressure has really increased. Every time there’s an exam, I feel a lot of pressure, and I don’t know what to do anymore.

Don’t worry; feeling pressure about final exams is very normal. You can try making a review plan, breaking your study tasks into smaller parts and completing them step by step. This can help reduce your stress and also help you grasp the material better.
That sounds good. I’ll give it a try. And about the teacher qualification interview, I’m really a little scared. I feel like my performance might not be good enough.

Don’t worry; the teacher qualification interview is a valuable experience. You can practice speaking or giving a demo lesson more, and prepare in advance what you want to express. Believe in yourself—you’ll definitely give an excellent performance.
Thank you for the encouragement. I’ll prepare well. But I’m still afraid that when I run into difficulties, I’ll break down, and I won’t know what to do.

If you feel like you can’t control your emotions, you might try some relaxation methods, like exercising or listening to some soothing music. Also, talk with friends or family and share what’s troubling you; they can give you some advice and support.
Okay, I’ll try to relax, talk things out more, and seek more help. Thank you for your advice and support.

You’re welcome. I’ll always support you. Believe in yourself—you can definitely get through this difficult time. Hang in there! If you have any other questions, feel free to come back and talk with me anytime.
Feeling lost after starting senior year, and afraid before the college entrance exam—could you give me some advice?

Reading your question, I get the sense that you’re very anxious. This kind of state can easily come up under the intense pressure of high school. What I want to say is, I can see your determination. That’s something many people don’t have! The most important thing for the college entrance exam isn’t knowledge, it’s mindset. A mindset of believing you will win! All that “just relax” and “take it slow” stuff is easy for others to say—they’re not the ones who’ve already been guaranteed admission. What am I supposed to relax about?! I have my goals. How could I possibly give up? If you have a goal, then things become easier: make a plan! What’s missing is a plan, a review plan with a reasonable allocation of time.

You’re right. I am very anxious, and I really do need to adjust my mindset. I also understand that mindset is very important for the college entrance exam, but how can I truly have that mindset of believing I will win?

First, you need to be clear about your goal. Since you want to get into an undergraduate program, you need to prepare for that. Then, you need to make a reasonable review plan, arranging your study time and content each day based on your own situation. This can help you have better control over the whole review process and reduce your anxiety.
I really don’t have a reasonable review plan. Every day I feel like there isn’t enough time, and I don’t know where to start. Can you give me some advice?

Of course! You can start from the content from your first year of high school and try the “sea of problems” approach. Do more practice questions every day; that can improve your study efficiency. Also, for English, listening more and memorizing more are very important. For math, physics, and chemistry, you can do some classic problems, especially the types that often come up on exams, and practice them repeatedly.
When it comes to difficult problems, I often doubt myself and feel like I can’t learn well. What do you think I should do?

Don’t doubt yourself; that will only add to your psychological burden. If you run into difficult problems, you can be bold and ask your teachers. They’re there to answer your questions. Don’t worry about other people’s expectations. You should believe in your own potential. As long as you study with all your effort, you will definitely gain something.

I’m really grateful for your advice. I’ll do my best to adjust my mindset, make a reasonable review plan, and bravely ask my teachers questions. I believe that as long as I work hard, I’ll definitely be able to reach my goal.
I’m very glad I could help! Remember to keep your confidence and keep working hard. I believe you’ll definitely be able to achieve excellent results. You’ve got this!
I was sexually assaulted when I was 5. I want to get better. Can you help analyze and correct my thoughts?

I first want to acknowledge how you’re slowly opening yourself up. That really takes a lot of courage. After reading your question, I can feel your guilt and self-blame. You blame yourself for not making the “right” choice back then, and for missing the chance to save yourself. Dear, what I want to say is: you were only five years old at the time. Back then, you didn’t know what this meant for you. You only knew that the other person had violated you, and you felt enormous shame. You should never have had to bear any of this. In terms of strength, there was a huge difference between you and a nine-year-old boy. Before you ran away, he used physical violence to threaten you, and you were forced to nod and agree.
Yes, they were five and nine, and I had absolutely no ability to resist.

Yes, you were truly so helpless at that time. When you ran out, you also felt despair, because you felt that it had already happened and there was no way to undo it. The reason you went back was that deep down, you felt too ashamed to face the light. Going back into the darkness could make you feel a little less afraid. That was the desperate choice of a child. From my perspective, you did not make a “wrong” choice. In fact, you were protecting yourself the whole time. He used physical violence against you, and in order to protect yourself, you chose to nod and agree. After you ran out, you realized that walking from the darkness into the light was more painful than staying in the darkness, so you went back into the darkness. All of these were the best choices you could make for yourself at that time.
Thank you for understanding me. But I feel like I gave informed consent, so I feel like I hurt myself together with him, and I’m not qualified to ask him to apologize to me.

The choice you made at that time was made under his threat. It does not mean you truly wanted to do it. He used your helplessness and fear to control you and make you nod and agree. You feel you are not qualified to ask him to apologize, because he is the person who harmed you, but what you need to understand is that you did not genuinely agree to this. You were forced. You made that choice in order to protect yourself from even greater harm.
I understand. But this has been troubling me all along. I feel like I haven’t faced reality, and I don’t have the courage to accept my past self.

I can understand how you feel. An experience like this really can trouble you for a long time. Our greatest pain is that we cannot accept the truth. We very much want to change what cannot be changed, and we wish the past could happen all over again. But any choice a person makes at any moment in their life is the best choice they can make at that time. I believe that a person’s life inherently has this kind of strength. The childhood you was hurt. That terrified, helpless child has been hiding in a corner of your heart for many years. Now we need to use more love to care for her and accompany her, so she can come out of that corner. We are the ones who create history, and we are also the ones who write history. We ourselves are our history. What has passed has already become history, but our life is not over yet. We have the ability to write a new history, don’t we?
I really want to come out of the darkness, but I always feel like I don’t have the courage to face reality. What should I do?

I understand your worry. This is a long-term process, and it takes time and patience. You have already shown a great deal of courage by daring to face your own inner world and the pain from your past. Today, I saw you come out of the darkness and expose your wound to the sunlight. Thank you for your courage, and thank you for your honesty. From you, I can feel the strength of life, and that strength moves me. What is pain? If you can accept this pain, it can be a gift, a gift from life. We will slowly face the shadows of the past together, let them gradually fade, and let light return to your heart again. You are not alone. I will stay by your side and support you. I hope you can soon come out from under the haze and find your own happiness and confidence again. My blessings to you.
I was sexually assaulted when I was 5. I want to get better. Can you analyze and correct my thoughts?

Seeing what you wrote, I feel very sad. There’s a saying: “An unfortunate childhood takes a lifetime to heal.” What happened to you as a child still leaves you unable to let go now, which shows how great the impact has been. Actually, no matter who we are, all kinds of problems can happen in childhood; it’s just that some are small things, while others are the kind of major things that are not easy to let go of at all. For you, it was the latter. Here, I’d like to offer a suggestion, and I hope it can help you a little.

Thank you for your understanding and concern. I often think now, if I hadn’t given in back then and had just stayed in the dark, maybe I wouldn’t be in so much pain. I always feel like it was my own fault. I’ve always felt like I was an accomplice, and that’s why I can’t let it go.

I’m sorry to hear you say that, and I feel very sad. First, I want to tell you that you were not an accomplice. It was their fault. They violated your rights. Whether or not you gave in at the time, they were the ones in the wrong. Don’t blame yourself because of what they said. What happened in the past cannot be changed, but we can learn lessons from it and work to help ourselves become better.

Hearing you say that, I feel like I understand a little. But I still can’t bear the intrusion of these negative memories. Whenever I think about that experience, I feel a lot of pain. How can I let go of all this?

I understand how troubling these emotions are. Painful memories keep replaying in your mind. I suggest you try doing some self-guided emotional processing. When these negative memories come up, you can try shifting your attention and focusing on other things, such as reading, studying, or meditating. Give yourself more positive thoughts, and tell yourself that you will become stronger in the future; this can help strengthen your self-confidence. If you feel especially sad, you can talk to friends. Their support may bring you some comfort.

Hearing you say this, I do think it makes sense. I’ll try to read more books and look for some strength and inspiration in them. I’ll also try meditation and see whether it can help me change my focus and thoughts about this experience.

I’m very glad to hear your response. Reading and meditation are both very good methods, and I hope they can help you gradually let go of the pain from the past. At the same time, you can also try taking part in some psychotherapy or counseling. A professional therapist can provide you with more systematic help and guidance. You don’t have to face all of this alone. More importantly, believe that you can come out from under this psychological shadow and find happiness and confidence again.
Thank you for your suggestions and encouragement. I will try to take your advice and seek more help and support. I believe I can overcome this psychological shadow and embrace a beautiful life again.

You are a strong person. Believe in your own ability, and you will definitely be able to get through this difficult time and find the happiness that belongs to you again. I will always be here to support you. If you need any help or would like to talk again, you can come to me anytime. Wishing you well. Hang in there!
I was sexually assaulted when I was 5. I want to get better. Can you help analyze and correct my thoughts?
I’m very sorry to hear that. I’m willing to listen to your story. Can you tell me more about the details of that experience?

When I was 5, I walked into an abandoned house because we were playing hide-and-seek. They held me down, pulled my clothes open, slapped me, and forced me to nod. I feel like this was very dirty. I’ve always wanted to forget it, but now I realize I need to face it.

That is very brave. We can look at this experience step by step, identify any negative thoughts that came from it, and help you correct them. First, I want you to know that you did nothing wrong at that time. No matter what happened, you should not be responsible for it.
But I nodded at the time. It feels like there was also a bit of willingness in it.

The decision you made at the time does not mean you had any responsibility. In a situation where you were forced to make a choice, you had no real choice; you could only do what you did in that moment. Please don’t blame yourself. The responsibility belongs to the people who did this, not to you.
I know, but I’ve always been blaming myself. I feel like the final choice was terrible, and I’ve always felt I should be responsible for what happened.

First, I really appreciate you sharing this story. This is very important for us, because in this process you may go through many emotions, and that is a normal response. You don’t need to blame yourself, because these thoughts are quite common, especially as you were growing up. We can work through these difficult things together.
I still feel like I’ve always been responsible. Even though I tried my best to escape, I shouldn’t have walked into the house, and I shouldn’t have rushed out at the wrong time.

You don’t have to be responsible for what you did at that time, because you were only a child, and your actions came from curiosity and innocence. Your behavior did not cause any harm to anyone. The fault lies with the people who did this, not with you. Now, I’d like to listen to how you feel about this experience, so that we can better care for your emotions and mental health.

I’m a 29-year-old woman, and lately I’ve been feeling like I’m stupid and always doubting myself. I feel like I’m good for nothing, stupid, unable to learn anything or do anything well. I’m afraid of failing, and I feel really sad. How should I adjust this mindset and believe that I can do it?

Hearing you say you feel stupid, I can understand how you feel. When we spend a long time in an environment that gives us negative feedback, we can start to believe those judgments ourselves. If you believe you’re stupid, it can very likely lead to a lack of confidence in yourself, and then to fear of failure. I’d suggest seeking help from a professional. Based on your current situation, you could explore your innate strengths and learned strengths together, so you can see your potential and continue believing in yourself. This approach may help you understand yourself relatively quickly.

Thank you for your suggestion. It’s true, I don’t have much confidence in myself right now, and I’m always doubting my abilities. Getting support from a professional sounds like a good idea. But I’m really worried that when I face failure again, I’ll feel extremely sad and won’t know how to cope.

I understand your worries. Facing failure is something everyone may experience, but failure doesn’t mean you’re good for nothing. Try to look for your strengths and positive qualities, and consider asking people around you for help. If someone starts criticizing you, you can try saying, “Stop! I need to know my strengths and positive qualities! Thank you!” This can let them know that what you need more right now is positive support.

You’re right. I should try to discover my own strengths and positive qualities. It may not be easy at first, but I’ll work on it. Maybe I can talk with friends or family and see how they view me, to help me find the strengths that belong to me.

I’m really glad you can think this way. Communicating with others is a very good approach; they can give you different perspectives and opinions. Remember, everyone is unique and has their own strengths and positive qualities. No one is good for nothing. As you try to discover your strengths, also be patient with yourself and treat yourself kindly.

Thank you for your encouragement. I’ll try to stay patient and try to change how I see myself. I think I can start now by putting more attention on the things I’m good at, and use that to strengthen my confidence in myself.

That’s wonderful! Focusing on the things you’re good at is a very good strategy. By focusing on your strengths and successful experiences, you can gradually build up your self-confidence. In this process, don’t forget to acknowledge and reward your own efforts and progress. It is possible to believe in yourself, and you can slowly improve your mindset by building confidence over time.

Thank you so much for your support and suggestions. I feel like now I have a clearer direction and strategy for adjusting my mindset. I’ll work on putting it into practice and believe that I can change.

I believe you can do it! You’ve already shown a positive mindset and determination to improve yourself. Remember, change takes time, but as long as you keep going and keep making an effort, you’ll definitely move toward a better version of yourself. I wish you success! If you need more help, feel free to come back and talk with me anytime.

Does showing your feelings on your face put you at a disadvantage? Do we need to control our true emotions? If people around us are always saying, “If your happiness and anger show on your face, you’ll lose out,” how should we change? Should we consciously control it, or just let things happen naturally?

Whether or not to show emotions is indeed something some people think about. Let’s first sort out the issue. In what you described, your main worry comes from other people saying that if your happiness and anger show on your face, you’ll lose out. You’re afraid that doing this might put you at a disadvantage, and that’s what has led to your question. From my perspective, there’s nothing wrong with having your happiness and anger show on your face. The different things we encounter in life can all bring up different emotions, and emotions usually come with facial expressions. Showing joy and anger on your face can reflect a healthy state of mind.

What you said makes a lot of sense, but I’m still a little worried. After all, everyone says that if your happiness and anger show on your face, you’ll lose out. I’m not quite sure how I should change the way I express myself.

I understand your worry. In fact, in everyday life, I believe you may also prefer being friends with people whose expressions are more open, because that way you don’t have to guess what they’re thinking, and it feels easier to get along with them. What’s more, if we suppress our emotions too much, it can create a sense of psychological imbalance. Over time, that may lead to psychological issues. So it’s very important to express yourself and release emotions in a reasonable way. However, with some more intense emotions, if we let them out regardless of the situation, it may lead to awkwardness or cause dissatisfaction in others.
I understand. I need to express my emotions appropriately in the right situations, and manage them. So how can I control my emotions?

That’s a very good question. First, don’t suppress your emotions too much. If the situation really isn’t appropriate, you can release them later in a more suitable place. Second, shift your attention. Especially when anger or sadness comes up, we need to redirect our attention in time, which can reduce the chances of losing control emotionally. Also, self-suggestion is a very good method for emotion management. If used appropriately, it can help us manage our emotions better. Finally, accept the areas where your emotion management is not yet strong. When we recognize that we have some shortcomings in managing our emotions, we need to accept that actively and take the initiative to look for ways to manage them.

That makes a lot of sense. When we can control our emotions well, then whether we choose to show our happiness and anger on our face or not is up to us. Thank you very much for your advice and support.

You’re welcome. I’m very glad I could help you. Emotion management is a long-term process, and I hope you can gradually learn to manage your emotions better and gain better mental health. If you have any other questions, feel free to come back and talk with me anytime.

Thank you very much for your encouragement and support. I’ll definitely work on adjusting the way I express my emotions, and I’ll also pay more attention to my mental health. If I need to, I’ll come back to ask for your guidance again. Thank you.
No problem. You’re welcome to reach out anytime. I hope you can have a better state of mind and a stronger sense of well-being. Wishing you all the best.

I'm a 25-year-old man. I've never been in a relationship and I don't have sexual urges. Am I asexual? I've been single since birth, and with my parents pressuring me into matchmaking dates, I feel extremely anxious.
Hello. It sounds like you're feeling a bit confused about your emotions and sexual orientation.
Yes. I always feel like I'm not quite like other people, like I don't have the feeling of wanting to be in a relationship.

I understand how you feel. At the same time, I think we are all unique individuals, and there's no need to force your emotions or sexual orientation into a certain label. You can explore more of your own preferences and feelings, and find a way of living that belongs to you.
But I feel like I don't have sexual urges, like I'm asexual.

I know a bit about asexuality, but I wouldn't jump to a conclusion about you. If you really want to determine whether you're asexual, I suggest consulting a mental health professional. They can provide you with professional opinions and guidance.
I really want to go too, but my family has been putting a lot of pressure on me, wanting me to hurry up and find a partner.

Your family's expectations and pressure are understandable, but I think you should first respect your own feelings and needs. If you don't want to find a partner right now, you can try communicating more with your family and telling them your thoughts and feelings. Or you could discuss it with them and find a compromise to temporarily ease your anxiety.
Mm, what you're saying makes sense. I'll try to communicate properly with my family, and I'll also consider seeing a mental health professional.
That's good. I believe you will be able to find your own answers and your own way of living. If you need anything in the future, you can always come talk with me.

Could being really obsessed with listening to music have negative effects? I feel like no matter what I’m doing, I can have music on in the background, and I play it really loud. Over time, I’ve started to feel like I can’t adapt to quiet environments anymore. Why is that?

Being appropriately absorbed in something can be very beneficial for our physical and mental health, especially things like music, painting, yoga—activities that can nurture our emotional life or support our physical and mental state, and help us face ourselves and understand ourselves better. These kinds of activities tend to be more popular and can bring us more benefits. But it’s important to remember that everything needs balance. Even something very good can become unhelpful if it goes beyond a certain point. Even drinking too much plain water can cause water intoxication and lower the average level of nutrients in our blood, right?
Mm, I understand. But I’m a little confused—why would I become less and less able to adapt to a quiet environment?

You mentioned that no matter what you’re doing, you can be distracted while listening to music, and that you play it very loudly, so over time you’ve become unable to adapt to quiet environments. What comes to mind is, first, because you can listen to music in the background no matter what you’re doing, even if you feel you’re not focused on the music, the process of wearing headphones or listening at a loud volume can, without you realizing it, lead you to develop a habit of being distracted. Then you may become dependent on having music in order to concentrate when doing things. On top of that, because the volume is high, once your ears get used to that level, your sensitivity to sound can change. A quiet environment may feel harder to adapt to, and you may tend to prefer environments with some sound. Over time, this can not only harm your hearing and your ears, but also affect your psychological habits, making it harder to adapt to quiet environments.
I understand. These things make me a little worried. Is there any way to help me adjust back?

So whether it’s to avoid negative outcomes, return to your previous state, or protect your physical and mental health, I’d suggest that you slightly and appropriately reduce how often you listen to music and how loud it is, and slowly adjust back. You can try planning specific music time—set aside a limited period each day just for listening to music, and during other times, try to keep a quiet environment and build your ability to concentrate. At the same time, you can try other relaxing activities, like reading or taking walks, so you can gradually get used to being in an environment without music. This adjustment process may take time, but I believe you can do it.
Thank you for your suggestions. I’ll try to adjust my habits in the ways you mentioned, and gradually get used to quiet environments. I hope I can return to how I was before.

You’re very welcome. I believe you can succeed! Changing habits takes persistence and patience. Trust in your own ability, and you can gradually return to your previous state. If you have any confusion or need support during the adjustment process, you can reach out to me anytime. I’ll be here to support you!
Thank you so much for your support and encouragement! I’ll keep your words in mind and work hard to adjust my habits. If I have any problems, I’ll reach out to you in time.

You’re very welcome to reach out to me anytime. I will always be here with you! Remember, you’re not facing difficulties alone. I’ll keep supporting you through this adjustment process. You’ve got this!

Academic pressure—I feel awful when I can’t learn it, and all I can do is play games? I’m a computer science major, and it feels like nothing is easy to learn. It’s so hard, too hard. I don’t know how to study. I feel stupid and under huge psychological pressure. My grades are poor, and it feels terrible not being able to learn it, so I can only play games. Computer networks are so hard.

Because your major is computer science, and it feels very difficult to learn, you can’t get the hang of it, so you feel a lot of pressure and don’t want to study. You use gaming to relieve that pressure. I can understand how you feel. We’ve also been students before, and there were things we didn’t know how to do. I also studied some computer-related statistical equations before, and they really were quite difficult. The fact that you’re willing to come to this platform shows that you are someone who wants to improve; you’re just feeling stuck because of the difficulties in front of you right now.

I do feel that the pressure from studying is really heavy. Sometimes I really want to give up, and I don’t know if I can keep going. But gaming is only a short-term relief. Afterward, I still feel like everything is hard.

Yes, gaming is only a short-term relief, and it can’t solve the root problem. We can explore this together: why did you choose computer science as your major? How much do you like computers? Are you willing to spend time working through these difficulties?

I chose computer science because I felt it was a field with good prospects, and I’m very interested in computers. But now it feels really difficult to study, and sometimes I doubt whether I’m suited for this major.

Your choice is a good one. Computer science really is a field with good prospects. Everyone feels that things are difficult when they first come into contact with new knowledge; that’s normal. What matters is your interest in this field and your willingness to put in effort. You can try some ways to overcome the difficulties, such as communicating more with your teachers and discussing study methods with classmates who are doing well. You can also work toward some certificates related to computer science, which will also be very helpful for your future development.

Thank you for your suggestions. I’ll try to communicate more with my teachers and classmates and look for study methods that suit me. But I’m still really worried about my grades and my future, and I’m afraid things will keep getting worse.

Your worries are understandable, but try not to be trapped by them. University is a process of learning and growth; you don’t have to be very good right from the start. You can break your goals down into smaller goals and achieve them step by step. At the same time, you can also think about whether there are other majors that might suit you, or learn some other knowledge and skills related to computer science during university. No matter what, don’t waste time. Keep working forward, and you can definitely achieve better grades and a better future. Hang in there!

Thank you for your encouragement and support. I’ll think it over carefully and try the suggestions you gave me. Although it still feels very difficult right now, I’ll try hard to keep going and not give up on my dream.

I’m very glad to hear your positive attitude. Difficulties are only temporary. As long as you keep working hard and stay persistent, you’ll be able to overcome these difficulties and realize your dream. If you need any help or want to talk again, you can come back here and talk with me anytime. I believe you can do even better. You’ve got this!

Academic pressure. It feels awful when I can’t learn it, so I can only play games? As a computer science major, it feels like nothing is easy to learn. It’s so hard, too hard. I don’t know how to study. I feel stupid and under huge psychological pressure. My grades are bad, and it feels awful that I can’t learn it, so I can only play games. Computer networks are so hard.

Because of setbacks in your studies, you’re feeling that learning is very difficult, and that has brought a lot of pressure. So you’ve chosen to use games to numb yourself and ease the stress. What you’re experiencing is a normal kind of struggle that can happen during student life. The main conflict for you right now is that you can’t complete the learning tasks in front of you, and that makes you feel extremely pressured. Let’s first talk about how to effectively ease the pressure you’re feeling right now.
I do feel that studying is really hard, and I don’t know what to do to reduce the pressure.

Can playing games really relieve stress? We have to admit that it can have some effect. As people often say, playing a little can lift your mood, but playing too much can harm you. A moderate amount of gaming can be good for physical and mental health. But I feel that the way you’re playing games right now is more about relying on them to numb yourself and temporarily escape from the pressure of studying. The pressure hasn’t disappeared; you’ve only set it aside. Then it becomes a vicious cycle: high pressure > playing games > not spending time studying > not finishing the material > even more pressure > wanting to play games... In the end, the pressure can only become greater.
Then what should I do? I really want to get out of this state.

The way to effectively ease your current pressure is to make some progress in your studies and rebuild your confidence, or to change majors and start over. The fact that you chose computer networks shows that you recognize the future of this major, and that you yourself are relatively inclined toward it. So you need to reassess how you truly view this major in your own mind. Whether or not you change majors, you need to be prepared to start over, and have the determination to begin from zero.
You’re right. I should reexamine how I understand the computer networks major. But I’m also really confused about study methods, and I don’t know how to improve my learning efficiency.

Let’s talk about study methods as well. If you want to make a breakthrough in your studies, I think you need to change your study methods. Right now, you haven’t found a method that suits you, which has led to relatively low learning efficiency. So you need to find the key reason why your learning results haven’t been obvious. Is it a memory issue, a comprehension issue, or some other reason? Only by addressing the specific problem can you solve it effectively. You need to rebuild your confidence in learning. You can set a small goal for yourself. Don’t set it too high; keep it within your ability. Each time you achieve a goal, I believe it will have a positive impact on you.
I’ll reassess my study methods and set a small goal to improve my learning results. But when facing the pressure, I still feel a bit helpless.

When facing pressure, the best way is to face it. I hope this can help you! You’ve already taken the first step by becoming aware of your problem and seeking support. Remember, you’re not alone. There are still many people around you who are willing to help. If you need further support and guidance, you can seek help from a counselor or a mentor. They can provide more professional advice and support, and help you cope better with academic pressure. Believe in yourself—you can get through this!

Academic pressure—I feel awful when I can’t learn it. All I can do is play games? As a computer science major, it feels like nothing is easy to learn. It’s so hard, too hard. I don’t know how to study. I feel stupid, and the mental pressure is huge. My grades are bad. It feels awful not being able to learn it, so I can only play games. Computer networks is so hard.

Seeing the words “computer science major” already makes me feel that you’re really capable. At the very least, you got through the college entrance exam and chose a major related to English and logic. I don’t know much about your specific study situation, but I really relate to how you’re feeling right now—that nothing feels easy to learn, that it’s hard, too hard. It reminds me of my sophomore year. Because I was usually busy having fun and didn’t study, when midterms were coming up, I felt extremely stressed and thought I was so stupid, like I didn’t even know the simplest things anymore. I was so scared that I took sick leave and went back to my hometown hundreds of miles away. Because I missed the exam, after I came back I could only settle down and start learning step by step, asking more whenever I didn’t understand. By the end of the term, I passed too. Is your situation similar to mine?
What you said makes me feel like I’m not alone. I always thought I was the only one who found it this hard, and I couldn’t find any direction at all. I don’t know what to do anymore.

Yes, you’re not alone. Many people face all kinds of difficulties and setbacks while studying. But you’re not helpless. I can help you find some ways to cope. First, you could try talking with your classmates or teachers, asking them questions or sharing what you’re struggling with. They may give you some advice or guidance to help you understand the material better. What do you think of this suggestion?
Talking with classmates or teachers really is a good idea, but I’ve always felt like I’m very stupid, and I feel embarrassed to ask them for help. I’m afraid they’ll think I’m foolish.

Don’t worry. Everyone has difficulties with learning, and no one will think you’re foolish because you ask questions. On the contrary, most people are very willing to help others. Also, asking others questions can not only help you clear up confusion, but also encourage communication and cooperation between you and your classmates. Try reaching out to them for help, and you’ll find that they’ll be very happy to help you.

What you’re saying makes sense. I should try asking others questions. But I have another problem. I see that other classmates seem to be able to grasp the computer networks course easily, while I always feel like there are difficulties everywhere. This makes me feel very lacking in confidence.

Don’t compare yourself with others. Everyone’s learning pace and learning style are different. You can only compare yourself with who you were before; as long as you’re making progress, that’s good. Also, studying a course in depth takes time and patience, so don’t put too much pressure on yourself. Try breaking your studying into small steps, working through the difficulties one step at a time, and slowly improving your ability. Trust me, as long as you keep working at it, you will definitely be able to master the computer networks course.

Thank you for your encouragement and advice. I feel much better now. I’ll try to let go of the mental pressure and study step by step, while also asking others more questions. I believe I can overcome the difficulties in studying and become more confident.

I’m very glad to hear that you’re feeling better. Remember, learning is not something that happens all at once. It takes time and effort. But as long as you keep going, you will definitely be able to overcome the difficulties and get good grades. I believe you have the ability to do well in computer science. You’ve got this! If you have any other questions or need more support, feel free to come talk with me anytime. Let’s work hard together and make progress together!
There are problems in my family, and I like a girl, but I’m afraid of “repeating” the pain. What should I do?
Hello, I understand what’s troubling you. First, could you share with me what your specific worries are about your family issues and repeating the pain?

I’m a guy, a freshman in college this year. There’s a girl in my class, and I like her. But I’m worried that because of my past experiences with family problems, I’ll go through the pain again. I feel that what was missing in her upbringing may mean she doesn’t know how to care about other people’s feelings, and may not be good at expressing her own needs either. I suddenly feel scared, worried that I’ll be triggered and experience the pain all over again.

I understand your worries about yourself. Have you ever thought about whether you’re being troubled by the shadow of the past, making it hard to believe that future relationships can get better? In relationships, everyone hopes to be cared for and understood, but it takes time to get to know each other and build trust. Have you tried taking the initiative to communicate with this girl, to understand her inner world and values?

I haven’t taken the initiative to talk to her yet, because I’m worried there are too many differences between us. In the past, I developed a serious and distant way of being, and I’m not very good at chatting with others. But I’m working on changing that. I’ve noticed that when I’m in a normal state, her reactions to me seem more obvious than other people’s, and her footsteps become more unnatural. This makes me feel confused.

It’s great that you’re able to notice your own changes. Compared with who you were in the past, you’re now coming into contact with someone different, and having new feelings and experiences, which is very normal. The patterns we develop can change under the influence of our environment.
