Given your special feelings for her, would you be willing to get to know her more and have more contact with her, so you can truly understand whether there is complementarity and shared interests between you?

I’m willing to try to get to know her, but I still have some doubts about myself. I’m worried that my temperament doesn’t match hers, and I’m afraid this dull atmosphere will get in the way of us getting along. I rarely take the initiative to chat with others, and I need to change this tendency.

Your confusion and doubts about yourself are also very normal. Everyone has their own traits and strengths, and you are someone who reflects and has self-awareness. So, as you get to know her, you can also have confidence and believe in your own value and charm. At the same time, getting along also requires mutual adjustment and understanding. You can slowly change that dull atmosphere around you, and try taking the initiative to chat with her, sharing your interests and thoughts.

I understand now. I should believe in myself, work on changing my dull temperament, and try to start conversations. I’ve noticed that when I think about happy things, my smile is more natural than before. Thank you for your support and encouragement!

You’re welcome. I’m glad I could help you. If you need any further support or communication during this process, you can leave me a message or send me a private message. I hope things go smoothly between you and her!

I'm 17, female, and I'm currently suffering from severe depression. I know my mom wants to care about me, but I still can't control my emotions. I went to the hospital and was diagnosed with severe depression. I know my mom is very worried about me, and I know she sometimes cries in secret. But because she's older, the age gap between us is too big, and she completely can't understand what I'm thinking. I know that once I break down, my mom will break down too, so I can only force myself to hold it in. What should I do?

I understand that this is a very difficult time for you. In some ways, the current situation may also be an opportunity for growth. You might consider letting go of your reliance on your mom and no longer hoping that she can fully understand you. You can try treating yourself like an adult. You can keep some things from your mom, and tell her kind lies to help her feel reassured. At the same time, you can look for support among classmates and friends you trust. Also, you might consider seeing a counselor to get more professional help and support.

Thank you for your understanding and advice. I understand that letting go of my dependence on my mom may be good for me, but I'm still really worried that she will feel hurt and disappointed because of my pretending. I haven't told my mom the truth, and she may feel that I don't trust her. How should I balance this conflict?

Your worry is understandable. After all, there is a deep emotional bond between you and your mom. You can try communicating with her and telling her your thoughts and struggles. Let her know that even though you choose to keep some things to yourself, it doesn't mean you don't trust her; it's to lessen her burden. Help her understand that you still need her support and understanding, but you hope to handle things in a more mature way.

Mm, I think being honest with my mom may be a good thing to try. I don't want her to keep worrying about me, but I also don't want to hide things from her. I'll try to communicate with her with a mature attitude and help her understand that I need her support. Besides my mom, are there other ways I can get emotional support?

Of course. Besides your mom, you can also look for other people close to you to share your emotions and struggles with, such as classmates or friends you trust. They may not be able to fully understand what you're going through, but they can keep you company and listen to your complaints and pain. At the same time, you can also consider looking for a professional counselor. They have a lot of experience and tools that can help you better handle your emotions and difficulties.
Thank you for your advice. I'll try sharing my feelings with my friends and look for their support and understanding. As for counselors, do you have any recommended ways or channels for finding one?

There are many ways to find a counselor. You can go through your school's counseling services, the psychology department at a hospital, or private counseling agencies. You can ask your school or search online for relevant information to find counseling resources in your area. Then you can make an appointment for a session and talk face-to-face with a professional counselor. They will give you more targeted help and guidance based on your specific situation.
I understand. I'll try to look for ways to find a counselor and meet with them. Thank you for your patience and support. This conversation has made me feel comforted and more at ease.

You're welcome. I hope my suggestions are helpful to you. Remember, you're not alone, and there are many channels where you can seek help and support. Trust in your own strength; you can definitely get through this difficult time. If you need to, feel free to come back and talk with me anytime. I hope you can come out of the depression soon and regain your energy.

I want to ask, is it not very realistic to pursue an absolute sense of safety at work? I used to be very happy and had a positive attitude toward work, but lately I’ve become more and more afraid of getting infected with HIV. As soon as I have a wound, I don’t dare go to public places. I’m not even afraid of getting infected myself—the thing I worry about most is, if I do get infected, what if I pass it on to the children?

I’m very glad to be able to help you. I can see the uneasiness inside you, and how much this is troubling your work and life. First, some of your recent experiences have brought up fear inside you; we call this generalization. This generalized fear has already had a big impact on your normal life. But you need to know that this situation can change. And although mistakes may have happened, and we can’t turn back time, we can learn from them and become stronger and braver in facing life. You actually don’t need to pursue an absolute sense of safety. There are no absolutes in this world, including safety. As long as you can let go of the distress from the past and face work and life with a positive mindset, your inner self will become stronger and more confident, and that will also help your work and life develop better.

But I feel like I just can’t let go of the fear and worries from the past. Every time I’m getting ready for work, I think about whether my wound has healed, whether I’ve touched public objects or facilities. When will I really be able to let it go?

I understand what you’re feeling inside, but you need to know that this process of letting go takes time. It doesn’t happen overnight. You can try some ways to relax yourself, such as finding some hobbies, talking more with friends, or choosing some appropriate exercise to relax your body and mind. At the same time, you can also learn some mindfulness methods to calm yourself inside and reduce the impact of some negative thoughts. In your work and life, learn to listen to your inner voice, but don’t let these negative thoughts affect your normal work and life. Try to regulate yourself so your emotions can become more stable.
But I’m still afraid that I’ll get infected with HIV. What should I do about this?

Although we can’t completely prevent this kind of situation, we can take some measures that help protect our safety. For example, you can wear a mask, have regular physical checkups, clean and disinfect the area, and so on. At the same time, we also need to remind ourselves that although the chance of getting infected with HIV is very small, we still need to stay alert and not casually go to any place where there may be risk. Only in this way can we reduce the possibility of infection.
That sounds somewhat doable, but I’m still a little worried. What will happen if I can’t get rid of these concerns and worries?

Don’t worry. These feelings are normal for everyone. You just need to communicate more with friends and family, find some trusted people who can listen to you, and address psychological issues in a timely way. At the same time, you can choose to seek help from a mental health professional, to help you better understand the emotional ups and downs inside you, resolve the distress within you, and feel more relaxed and at ease in both work and life.
That sounds very reasonable. I feel like I now have some ways to give up the idea of absolute safety, and to try to face difficulties and setbacks with a positive and optimistic mindset. Thank you.
You’re welcome. If you have any other thoughts or confusion, please contact me anytime. I’ll be here with you. I wish you all the best in your work and life.

Work pressure, got depression—should I go to work or not? Because of work pressure (working more than ten hours a day), being far from home (200 kilometers), my wife and child are at home (married seven months), low pay (1,900 yuan), and my leader not letting me go home (only two days home each time). Even though it’s a state-owned enterprise, it doesn’t feel like one at all. Because of all this, I’ve developed depression now. I don’t even know if I can ask for leave. Even if I can, my family all hopes I’ll go back, but right now I’m really afraid to go back. I want to avoid it, and I’m also afraid my condition will get worse. My leader keeps pushing me to go back too. Since everyone thinks I should go back, I don’t want to talk to anyone now. What should I do? Should I go back, or take leave and get proper treatment?

Reading your description of your work and family situation, I can sense the pain you’re feeling—wanting to be with your wife and child, while also feeling very dissatisfied with your current job. From what you described, the main pain seems to come from work: “Even though it’s a state-owned enterprise, it doesn’t feel like one at all.” That sentence isn’t very easy to understand, but it may mean it doesn’t match what you expected. At the same time, the pay is low, 1,900 yuan. On top of that, it’s far from home, and your leader won’t let you go home. So working there feels painful for you. Your family isn’t able to understand your pain right now, and thinks you should still go back to work. Have you thought about why your family wants you to go back to work?

I think my family wants me to go back to work maybe because they hope I can earn more money to support the family. I understand what they mean, but right now the work pressure is too much, and it’s had a big negative impact on my physical and mental health. I’m really confused and don’t know how to decide.

From a developmental perspective, you’re now in the newly married stage, you’ve started a family and are building your career. And with a state-owned enterprise, the work pressure should be somewhat less compared with private companies outside, but you feel depressed and uncomfortable, so could there be some difficulties in interpersonal relationships? I think you should first clarify your own goal: do you want to change jobs, do you long for your family’s understanding, or do you need to treat the depressed mood? I suggest having an in-depth conversation with your family, clearly telling them your goal, and then discussing together how to handle it. You can also get a mental health assessment. If it’s only poor social adjustment, then you should still go back to the workplace and build that ability through experience.

You’re right. I do have difficulties. I need to think about my goals now—whether it’s to find a better job, to gain my family’s understanding, or whether I should first treat the depressed mood. I’ll have an in-depth conversation with my family, share my thoughts and goals with them, and then discuss solutions together. I’ll also get a mental health assessment to determine whether it’s a social adjustment issue or whether I need treatment.

I’m glad to hear that you’re willing to have an in-depth conversation with your family and get a mental health assessment. These are all very important steps, and they can help you better sort out your thoughts and goals. Before making a decision, you can also consider your current mental state and whether you’re ready to return to work. Sometimes, appropriate time off and treatment can help us face challenges better. Please remember, your health and happiness are the most important things.

Thank you for your advice. I’ll consider taking appropriate time off and getting treatment, so that I can face work and family in a physically and mentally healthy state. I believe that only by staying in a good state can I better solve problems and deal with challenges. Thank you again for your support and encouragement.

You’re welcome. I’m very glad I could help. You’ve already taken a big step by looking for ways to solve the problem and paying attention to your own health. Remember, in difficult moments, don’t hesitate to seek help from others. You’re not fighting this alone. I hope you find the balance and solutions that suit you soon. Hang in there!

Thank you for your encouragement and good wishes. When I was feeling lost, your words gave me a lot of strength and support. I’ll keep going and look for my own happiness and sense of fulfillment. Thank you, goodbye!

I’m very glad I could help. Your courage and persistence are worthy of appreciation. I wish you well in finding your own happiness and sense of fulfillment, and I hope your situation gets better and better. If you need anything in the future, remember you can always reach out to me for help. Goodbye, and I wish you all the best!
I don’t know right now whether I should give up chasing an absolute sense of safety and let myself focus on work while living with risk.

I understand your confusion and distress. Can I give you a big hug? May you receive warmth from the world; I can only answer your question. In this world, there is no such thing as an absolute sense of safety. Any so-called absolute safety is relative. Just like before the COVID outbreak, China seemed absolutely safe, but in any environment where precautions aren’t in place, we can face all kinds of risks. No matter where we are, as long as there are people, risks will exist.

Yes, I understand that. Right now I’m just worried that I have a wound and then got infected with HIV. I’m also afraid of touching public objects and facilities. I know this kind of worry is overly cautious, but I just can’t control my fear.

Your caution is understandable, but excessive tension and worry can keep us from living normally. Is it worth giving up 99% of your happiness for that 1% danger? What matters most right now is adjusting your mindset. Don’t keep thinking about what happened in the past. After all, when you had commercial sex, you also weren’t infected. That shows the chance of being infected is very low. But this is not teaching you to keep taking risks; it’s giving you a chance to reflect and protect yourself, and not repeat the same mistake. HIV is something you don’t know when it might strike. So as long as you maintain personal hygiene and protection, many things can be avoided. Don’t stay on edge over things that haven’t happened and miss out on the happiness you have now.

You’re right. I need to adjust my mindset. What happened in the past has already happened. I should pay more attention to personal hygiene and protection, instead of just worrying blindly. I understand that I should relax a bit, face the risks directly, and focus on work.

I’m glad to hear you say that. Adjusting your mindset and focusing on work is the right choice. You can make some specific plans to help yourself stay more focused. At the same time, give yourself some time to relax and enjoy life. Don’t let excessive fear and worry affect your work and your quality of life.

That’s true. I need to make some plans and goals to stay focused and motivated. At the same time, I also need to give myself time to rest and relax, and not always sacrifice the joys of life for work.

You’re absolutely right! Work is important, but the happiness in life also shouldn’t be ignored. While pursuing a sense of safety, we also need to learn to enjoy the good and happy moments in life. You can try some ways to relax and relieve stress, such as exercise, meditation, or getting together with friends. Keeping a balance will help you face risks and challenges better.

Thank you for your suggestions! I’ll try using these methods to help myself better balance work and life. I believe that as long as I adjust my mindset, I’ll be able to focus on work amid risk and also have a happy life.

That’s wonderful! Believe in yourself and keep adjusting your mindset. You will definitely be able to overcome difficulties and pursue focus and happiness. If you need any help or would like to share your progress with me, tell me anytime. I’ll always support you! I wish you all the best, and happiness and joy!

I have to go on another matchmaking date. It feels a bit like an interview, and I feel really helpless? This time the person is 4 years older than me. In the past, the biggest age gap was just one year older than me. I’ve started unconsciously imagining things and worrying. He’s almost 40, and he may be very mature. Someone like me would just be like a kid in front of people like that. In terms of how I see myself, my psychological age still isn’t mature enough. Also, I’m thinking that normally I don’t really take care of my appearance, my hair is messy and I look unkempt. This time I probably need to tidy myself up a bit. It completely feels like an interview, caring about other people’s evaluations. It’s like I have to put in this kind of effort. I really don’t like going on matchmaking dates like this. But besides this, I don’t have a choice. When a matchmaking date becomes an interview, what kind of romance is there left? I also know I’m just responsible for showing up. There won’t be any further contact after this. Right now I don’t want anyone else getting involved in my life!!! A one-time meeting is wasting both people’s time and energy… I feel so helpless…

You’re about to go on a matchmaking date, and it feels a bit like going to an interview—somewhat nervous, and also a bit worried. You really dislike this feeling. A matchmaking date is originally something quite simple; it can feel fairly relaxed and pleasant. Even though it’s talking with someone you don’t know, as long as we show our most authentic selves, that’s enough.

I understand that a matchmaking date should be relaxed and pleasant, but the other person is so much older than me. I feel like I’m just a kid in front of people like that, like my psychological age isn’t mature enough.

You’re worried that your maturity level and the age gap might make the matchmaking date difficult. That worry is understandable. But age isn’t the only standard for measuring maturity, and a matchmaking date isn’t a setting where your maturity is being judged. As long as you show your real self, the communication can become natural and relaxed.

I know age isn’t the only standard, but I’m also worried about my appearance. I usually don’t really take care of how I look, and this time I’ll have to tidy myself up a bit. I completely have the feeling of being in an interview, and I really care about what the other person thinks of me.

You’re worried that your appearance might leave a bad impression on the other person, and you really care about their evaluation. This is a common kind of anxiety before a matchmaking date. But a matchmaking date is a process of getting to know each other; it doesn’t require you to present yourself as perfect. As long as you stay confident and authentic, I believe the other person can also understand and accept you as you are.

I really don’t like going on matchmaking dates like this, but besides this, there’s no other choice. I also don’t want anyone else getting involved in my life. After it ends, I won’t have any contact with the other person again.

I understand that you don’t like this way of going on matchmaking dates, and that you don’t want anyone else getting involved in your life. But sometimes, even a one-time meeting might bring you an unexpected encounter. Even if you’re not looking for further contact, you can still enjoy the process of getting to know each other, and there may be an unexpected gain.

I’ll try to relax a bit, not care too much about the other person’s evaluation, and show my real self. Maybe in this process I’ll be able to meet the person I’m meant to meet. Thank you for your support and encouragement!

No problem! You’re doing great. Believe in yourself, relax, and go to the matchmaking date. Try to approach it with the mindset of meeting a new friend. Good luck, and I hope you meet the right person! If you need any more support, remember you can come back and talk with me anytime.

Lately my husband keeps giving me the silent treatment, and it really hurts. I don’t understand why he’s always like this. Every time we argue, it’s over small things. If I’m just a little careless and say the wrong thing, he gets angry. I feel like he has a pretty strong sense of pride, and I don’t know how to handle this situation.

I understand your situation. When men deal with problems, sometimes they can be more reserved and passive, and may choose to use “cold violence” as a way to avoid emotions overflowing. I can sense that you’re feeling very hurt right now, and this feeling may even have been with you for some time. If the two of you can’t understand each other, the relationship may get worse and worse. Each time, in the end, the problem doesn’t really get resolved. So, good communication is very important for your marriage. Have you ever expressed to him, “When you don’t talk to me, I feel very sad. I want to talk with you, and I hope you can understand me”?
Yes, I’ve already told him how I feel. But he doesn’t really understand me, and I don’t know how to communicate with him.

You mentioned that the most recent conflict was caused by unemployment. In modern society, men generally care a lot about whether they can take on the financial burden of the family. So he is under a lot of pressure right now; he just hasn’t expressed it very strongly. At this moment, he may be hoping more for your understanding and support. Try to see his strengths and encourage him more. Use less judging, blaming, or critical language. Remember, people can only change themselves; they can’t change others.
I understand what he’s thinking, but I don’t know how to support him. I feel like he doesn’t care about his appearance, so he doesn’t want to get a haircut.

When you communicate with him, you can express your observations and feelings. For example, when he doesn’t get a haircut, you can say something encouraging about getting one, and tell him it might make him feel refreshed and more energetic. At the same time, express your needs and let him know your expectations. But don’t use judging, blaming, or critical language in the conversation.
I’ll try to do that. But I’ll still care a lot about what he thinks, and his coldness really hurts me.

I can understand how you feel, but you need to know that some men often handle problems this way. Try not to put all the responsibility on him, and your own emotions are also very important. When your emotions are hurt, you can think back to the good times when you first got together. This may help ease some of the negative feelings.
I’ll try to do that. Thank you for your advice.
If you need more help, feel free to contact me anytime. Hang in there!
I'm a first-year college student, and I'm not on the same wavelength as my roommates. How should I get along with them?

This is part of the beginning of a young person stepping into society, so it’s understandable that you’re feeling confused. Don’t blame yourself. Most students haven’t had much experience living in a group. When you enter college and live in a dorm, it’s your first time being part of that kind of group life, so it’s only natural to feel uncomfortable at first.
But I’ve already been in my first year for half a year, and I still feel out of sync with my roommates. Sometimes I feel like I’m being isolated! What should I do?

I understand how you feel. Feeling isolated really doesn’t feel good. But don’t worry—you still have many chances to improve your relationships with your roommates. I’ll offer two suggestions, and I hope they help. First, you can take the initiative to join their activities and interact with them. Don’t keep yourself distant or separate from them, and slowly you may start to fit in with them. Second, if you really can’t accept their activities, you can approach it with a mindset of just watching what’s going on and observe from the side. You don’t have to feel resistant, and there’s even less need to oppose the fact that others are different from you. It’s enough to accept and acknowledge their choices.

I’ll try to take the initiative to join their activities and communicate with them more, and I hope that can improve my relationship with them. But sometimes they often team up to play League of Legends, and when I can’t sleep I get anxious, which affects my classes the next day. Do you have any suggestions?

That’s a very real issue, and your anxiety is understandable. First, you can try communicating with them and tell them that you need good rest for your classes, and that you hope they can be a bit quieter at reasonable hours. Second, you can also try to find your own solutions, such as using earplugs or listening to some gentle, relaxing music to help you fall asleep. The key is to keep a positive attitude and believe that you’ll be able to find a way to solve the problem.

You’re right. I’ll try to communicate with them, and I’ll also look for methods that work for me to help me fall asleep. Thank you so much for your suggestions and support. I’ll work on improving my relationship with my roommates, and I hope I can have a happy college life.

You’re welcome. I believe you can get through this difficult period smoothly. Remember to keep a positive and optimistic mindset, and give yourself some time to adjust to the new living environment. If you run into any problems during this process, you can always come to me to talk or seek help. I hope you have a wonderful college life!

Thank you for your encouragement and support. I’ll keep your words in mind, and I’ll definitely work toward having a wonderful college experience. If I have any problems, I’ll definitely come to you for help. Thank you again for your help!
You’re welcome. I’ll always support you. If you have any difficulties or needs, feel free to come to me anytime. I wish you all the best. You’ve got this!

A 17-year-old orphan online likes me. How should I help her? She’s a friend I met on a voice-chat social app. Because she thinks my voice sounds nice and that I have a good temper, she likes me quite a bit. Before, she would come to my room every day and chat and play with me and my friends.

She has developed feelings for you, and that comes from her liking you and her longing for family affection. It’s important to understand her loneliness and her need to be loved. But for a relationship to develop, both people need to share that understanding and have an emotional foundation. You can choose to keep being her friend and give her emotional support, while also making it clear that the two of you won’t go any further than that.

I used to be really curious why she was always trying to find a partner there. Whenever she got dumped, she would come to me crying. Every time she would say she wanted to leave, that she didn’t want to live anymore. Until last week… she got dumped again and started crying and making a scene again, cutting her wrist with a knife. I really didn’t know what else to do, so I agreed to try being with her for a while.

Her past experiences have brought her a lot of psychological trauma, which has led her to develop negative beliefs about relationships and about herself. Her self-harm is a way of expressing distress and asking for help, but it is not a healthy way to cope. You can understand how hard this is for her, but you also need to tell her clearly that your help can only be temporary. She needs professional psychological support to help her get through this difficult place.

I really only wanted to pull her back from the edge. I don’t have romantic feelings for her. I just didn’t want her to kill herself. So last night I told her, “Do you know, this isn’t going to lead anywhere for us. In the end it will only hurt both of us. I can still be your good friend and keep staying with you and comforting you…” Then she completely broke down. That’s when I found out that three years ago her dad had an affair and had a younger daughter. Her parents got divorced and hid it from her for a year. When they told her, both her father and mother didn’t want her anymore. Now her grandparents and aunt are supporting her through high school in another province.

Your intention was good. You wanted to help her through companionship and comfort. The changes in her family have hit her very hard, making her feel abandoned by love and causing her to lose her sense of safety. Her emotional breakdown is the result of years of buildup, and she needs more care as well as professional psychological intervention. You have already done a lot for her, but you cannot take on everything for her. Deleting you was her own choice, but you can try to contact her in other ways, give her contact information for mental health services, and also report the situation to the social app platform and ask for assistance.

She really has no way out anymore. I really want to help her, but I didn’t think I would hurt her like this. I’m really so scared that she’ll die by suicide. I know that getting out of the darkness is something only she can do for herself, but she needs help! She deleted me, and now I feel especially guilty and especially scared. I don’t know what to do.

I understand your worry and guilt, but her psychological issues need intervention and treatment from professionals. You have already done your best to offer her help. The most important thing now is to try to contact her again, tell her your real concerns, and offer her ways to get help. At the same time, remember that her growth and her way out of this difficult place ultimately still depend on her own efforts.

Thank you for your advice. I’ll try to contact her again, and I hope I can give her some guidance and help her seek professional support. I’ll do whatever I can, and at the same time learn to accept the fact that there are things I can’t control.

I’m glad I could help you. You have already been a very good friend. Remember, you have done your best. What happens next will require her own efforts and the support of professionals. I wish both you and her the best, and I hope she can gradually get through this difficult time.

As a first-year student, I’m not on the same wavelength as my roommates. How should I get along with them? It’s been half a year since I started college, and I feel like I’m not on the same rhythm as my roommates. Sometimes I feel like I’m being isolated! What should I do? My roommates often team up to play LoL, and when I can’t sleep I get anxious, which affects my classes the next day. How can I fit in with my roommates?

It’s been half a year since you started college, but you feel like you’re not on the same rhythm as your roommates. In the dorm, you sometimes feel isolated. Your roommates often stay up late gaming together, and you’re affected by it, feeling anxious and unable to sleep. The insomnia then affects your classes the next day. You’re not sure how to get along with them. With so many worries tangled together, I can sense your sadness, helplessness, and feeling at a loss. And now, after half a year of freshman year, you’ve become aware that you and your roommates aren’t on the same wavelength.

I usually go to class, study on my own every day, and also take part in some club activities. But my roommates all like staying up late and gaming together. I feel like their lifestyle is pretty different from mine, and I don’t know how to fit into their little group.
What do you usually do? Have you observed what your roommates usually do? Do you agree with the things your roommates usually do?

I usually like reading, listening to music, and chatting with friends. I’ve observed my roommates. They like playing games and watching movies. Sometimes I join them, but I always feel like there’s a bit of a gap between us.

Everyone has their own way of thinking and their own goals. If you did the same things as your roommates, would you be able to reach your plans or goals? If you really want to fit into that small group with your roommates, you can also do similar things in moderation, have shared topics, and go to the same places together. You can observe or get to know whether your roommates have any taboos, and avoid stepping on any sensitive areas in daily life or study.

I understand. I can try playing games with them, learn about their interests and hobbies, and communicate more with them. Maybe it will be easier to fit into their little group. I’ll also be careful not to touch on their taboos, and keep things harmonious between us.

You said your roommates team up to play LoL. You could also try it out and experience the fun of it, relax a little, and in that way try to understand why your roommates stay up late gaming together. But there needs to be a limit. Don’t get addicted to it and forget your original intentions. When you feel tired or when it’s time for you to sleep, you can say to your roommates, “No, I’m sleepy. I want to sleep now. Are you guys going to sleep? If you’re going to stay up later, could you keep it down a bit? I’m a little sensitive to noise.”

I’ll try playing games with my roommates, but I’ll also manage my time and not get addicted to it. If it’s time for me to rest, I’ll communicate with them appropriately and hope they can lower the volume so I can get a good rest. Thank you for your advice.

Being kept awake at night by other roommates is truly a painful experience. I’ve been through it too. I even specifically went to talk to a teacher about it. The advice the teacher gave me at the time was to be specific. It’s true that when I was being disturbed back then, what I said was, “Can you all keep it down?” That “you all” was too general. So when you can tell which roommate is being loud, you can be more specific: “XX, could you keep it down a bit? I want to sleep.” But I failed at that back then. Because everyone in the dorm had a good relationship, and I felt too embarrassed to say it. Later, I bought earplugs, set a timer for music, and turned the volume up until I couldn’t hear their voices, or I simply stayed up late with them. Because I already knew that the outside environment isn’t something we can control. When we can’t change the environment around us, if we want to adapt better, we need to go along with the environment. The process of going along with it may take some time, but the feeling of “being isolated” — in your current situation, it probably means seeming a bit out of place — can feel really painful. If you don’t try to adapt to the environment, it may take even longer. Of course, you can also strengthen yourself and be someone who walks your own path, quietly becoming stronger, then turning around and amazing everyone. ———— The above is my view and some of my own personal feelings. I hope it can give you a little inspiration. Please remember, you are not alone.
Lately my husband and I keep giving each other the silent treatment, and I feel really awful. When I want to communicate with him, he just doesn’t want to respond to me. What is going on?

Seeing you facing this kind of issue in your intimate relationship, I can understand how you feel. In what you described, you mentioned that every time there’s a conflict, it’s over small things. And in these small things, your husband’s subjective feelings are quite strong—if you’re even a little careless with one sentence, he gets angry. After all, everyone has self-esteem. And you used to care a lot about face too, so you compromised and went along with the silent treatment. But now you feel this isn’t good, so you want to persuade him to calm down. But he refuses to communicate with you, and you feel at a loss.
Yes, our personalities are pretty different. I care a lot about other people’s feelings, but he always feels like he’s been wronged.

Yes, everyone’s personality is different, and sometimes it really is hard for two people to get along. But to solve a problem, we need to have the “same starting point.” In other words, we need to think about the issue from the other person’s perspective. You hope he can care more about your feelings, and he also hopes you can understand how he feels.
But now he’s unemployed again. I’m doing my best to support him, but when I make even a tiny suggestion, he gets very angry. That makes me feel really hurt.

I understand. During this period, you not only have to take on the main financial responsibility for the family, but also look after his emotions. That really is hard. At times like this, every moment when communication with him doesn’t go smoothly, every time he loses control of his emotions, can leave you feeling discouraged. So I suggest you give him a chance to “work through his emotions,” so he can release some of the negative feelings. At the same time, you also need to learn to speak up for yourself and tell him your thoughts and feelings.
Then how should I say it?

You can try communicating by expressing your needs. For example, “I really care about how you feel, but I also hope you can care about me and listen to my suggestions,” or “We’re both carrying a lot of responsibilities, so let’s try to understand each other.” If he’s having negative emotions because of financial pressure, you can talk with him about ways to find solutions and face the challenges together.
Okay, I’ll try to communicate with him properly. Thank you for your suggestions.
You’re welcome. If you have any other questions, feel free to come and talk with me anytime.
When it comes to pornographic content, how can I firmly say no?

From what you’ve described, you seem like a kind person who really thinks about others. You have a clear sense of right and wrong, and you want to be self-disciplined. I’m curious—what has happened in your life that has made you reject and dislike yourself so much? Even to the point of obvious self-attack?

When I was young and didn’t know better, I got addicted to the online world. Facing all kinds of temptations, I ignored other parts of life and fell into this sticky, daily state that I couldn’t get out of. It also restricted my mom’s freedom, used up my parents’ money, and I became someone who just stays at home.

In fact, when we’re young and inexperienced, it’s easy to do things that make our parents worry. That proves we were young once. If we hadn’t been a bit willful, how would we know what is good and what isn’t?
But I feel like I’ve fallen into a bad cycle. I feel bound by the internet, and every day I can’t pull myself out of it.

Sexual desire is also a basic human instinct. Whether it’s masturbation after viewing sexual content, or masturbation after fantasizing, these are normal behaviors. From what you’ve described, on one hand, you want to become a self-disciplined person; on the other hand, self-discipline seems to be very difficult for you. So anxiety has developed inside, and this anxiety may lead to what you called “indulging your desires.”
Yes, I feel very anxious, and I also feel very disappointed in myself.

Given this, on one hand, you might see whether you can find a professional to help you sort through the causes of your anxiety. On the other hand, you can try learning self-acceptance—allowing yourself to be as you are right now. Then, by expanding your life circle, developing interests and hobbies, broadening your social circle, and exploring your career direction, you can begin to find what kind of person you want to be. Once your life goals become clear, just go do things and try things. This process will help your confidence keep growing.
I understand. I can try to accept myself as I am now, and try to expand my life and find the kind of person I want to be.
Yes. The hardest part may be self-acceptance. In any case, I hope you can give it a try, and give your future more opportunities and choices.

Just studying honestly and rigidly—can studying really bring me the life I want? I’m a junior in college. My grades were always very good in high school, but I messed up on the college entrance exam. Now my university isn’t a Double First-Class or 985/211 school, but it’s actually quite strong. My college grades are also okay, and I’m planning to apply for a master’s program in the UK. But recently I’ve started feeling lost. I’m in science and engineering, and honestly, if you really study seriously in college, it’s really exhausting, and also very dull. Lately I’ve started envying the lives of a few friends back in my hometown. Their grades weren’t good; some are even at vocational colleges, and some are at first-tier universities but the kind that are Sino-foreign joint programs (you know what I mean). But I feel like their lives are so rich… They go to bars at night when they have nothing to do, play mahjong in the afternoon, but it’s not like they’re just wasting their days. They actually get to meet a lot of people and have very wide social circles. Their parents also have a certain level of resources, and they all have pretty high emotional intelligence, so I feel like their future development probably won’t be too bad. And I’m just the kind of person who studies honestly, exhausted every day, and my life isn’t that colorful. I don’t meet that many people either. I feel like my current state of life is pretty unsatisfactory. Actually, I had this feeling in high school too, but at the time I had this belief in getting into my dream university, so I was still very motivated. But now, when I think about it, even if I go study in the UK and come back, if my life is still this dull, then it feels meaningless…

First of all, I understand your situation, and I really feel for you. I want to give you a big hug and let you feel some warmth from the world. Actually, about the way you asked this—can studying really bring you the life you want? Have you asked yourself: what kind of life do you actually want? Later on, you mention feeling that your own life is dull and boring, like it was in high school, but you didn’t specifically describe what the life you want is really like. Instead, you keep envying those classmates and friends of yours, as if they’re all living exciting, rich lives. In reality, everyone has their own life. The side other people show you is the polished side they want you to see. But how would they let you know about the bitterness and hardship behind it?

I understand what you mean, but I really do feel their lives are more interesting, more colorful. They have activities they like every day, while I feel like I’m being crushed by my studies and can barely breathe. And through having such broad social connections, they can get more opportunities and resources. I’m a little envious.

I understand how you feel. When we see other people living rich and colorful lives, it’s natural to feel envious. But you need to remember that everyone’s life path is different. What you’ve chosen right now is to improve yourself through studying seriously, and that’s very worthy of praise. Studying isn’t just about getting high scores; it’s also a way of developing yourself. The knowledge and skills you’re learning will play an important role in the future, and they’re the foundation for you to build the life you want.

I understand the importance of studying, but sometimes it feels really tiring and dull. I also know I should spend more time joining social activities and expanding my network, but I really feel like it’s hard, especially under the pressure of intense coursework.

I completely understand your confusion and the difficulty you’re facing. Under academic pressure, it really is hard to find a balance. But maybe you can start with small steps. For example, set aside one or two times each week to take part in some social activities and get to know new friends. Try not to see socializing as an extra burden, but as a chance to relax and enjoy life. You can choose activities that fit your own interests and hobbies; that way it’ll be easier to get involved and meet friends who share similar interests.

What you’re saying makes a lot of sense, and I do hope I can try some new social activities. But I’m still a bit worried—worried that my studies will be affected. After all, I still have a lot of courses and assignments to finish.

It’s understandable to worry, but we can’t give up trying just because we’re worried. You can make a clear schedule and arrange your studies and social activities in a reasonable way. With good time management, you can both keep up with your coursework and give yourself some space to relax. Remember, social interaction is also part of your growth. It can improve your emotional intelligence and social skills, and it will also be a great help to your future development.

You’re right. I should see social activities as opportunities for self-growth, not as a burden. I’ll try to make a reasonable schedule for studying and socializing so I can balance both. Thank you for your advice and support!

I’m very glad I could help you, and glad to hear your determination to try. I believe that as long as you keep a positive mindset and arrange your time reasonably, you’ll definitely be able to achieve the rich and colorful life you hope for. I’ll always be here supporting you! You’ve got this!

Just studying honestly and grinding away—can studying really give me the life I want? I’m a junior in college. My grades were always really good in high school, but I messed up the college entrance exam. Now I’m at a university that isn’t Double First-Class, though it’s actually pretty strong. My grades in college are also okay, and I’m planning to apply for a master’s program in the UK. But lately I’ve started feeling lost. I’m in science and engineering, and honestly, if you really study seriously in college, it’s exhausting, and also really boring. Recently I’ve started envying the lives of a few friends back in my hometown. Their grades weren’t good; some are even in vocational colleges, and some are at first-tier universities but the Sino-foreign joint kind, you know what I mean. But their lives seem so rich... They go to bars at night when they have nothing to do, play mahjong in the afternoon, but it’s not like they’re just wasting their days. They actually meet a lot of people, have broad social circles, their parents have some resources, and their emotional intelligence is pretty high, so I feel like their future development probably won’t be too bad. And I’m the kind of person who just studies obediently, exhausted every day, and my life isn’t that colorful. I don’t meet that many people either. I feel like my current life is pretty unsatisfying. Actually, I felt this way in high school too, but back then I had the belief of getting into my dream university, so I was still very motivated. But now when I think about it, even if I go study in the UK and come back, if my life is still this boring, then it feels meaningless...

Hello, I can understand your confusion and feeling lost. Hearing you talk just now about your studies and your life, it seems like you don’t feel very confident about your future development. You feel that you’ve always studied honestly and diligently, but your life hasn’t been that rich or colorful, and that has made you start envying those friends whose lives seem less constrained. Is that right?

Yes. I know my life isn’t bad, but I always feel like something is missing. When I look at my friends, they weren’t as good as me in high school, but they seem to have even better lives than I do. It makes me feel like a failure.

You mentioned failure. Actually, everyone defines failure differently. Some people see setbacks as failure, while others see difficulties as part of making progress. I think your direction in life is actually quite clear, especially considering that you’re planning to apply for a master’s program in the UK. That shows you already have a very clear plan for the future. I don’t need to go on about the importance of studying, but what I’d like to remind you is that life is important too. You can try to balance your studies and your life. Over time, you’ll learn how to take charge of your life and make it richer and more colorful.
I have thought about balancing my studies and my life, but I always feel like I can’t do either side well.

I can understand your worry, but actually, not everyone can do both academics and life perfectly. Why not first try to find some balance? You can start with small things, like talking more with classmates, joining more school clubs, or even considering a part-time job. Through these things, you can manage your time more effectively and leave yourself some time to relax and have fun outside of studying.
Thank you for the suggestions, but I’m still worried about a lot of things, like not being able to manage my time well and ending up affecting both my studies and my life.

That’s okay. Worrying is very human. For that, you can try planning and allocating your time, and setting clear goals before each task. Doing this can help you see more clearly which tasks are most important and which ones can be put off a little. It’s also important to make good use of modern technology, such as apps on your phone, which can help you manage your time and tasks better.
I think I’ll try, because I really want to change my current situation.

Good. You’ve already taken the first step. Even if at times you feel helpless, anxious in your personality, or under pressure from school and life, as long as you can find the right support and help, these problems can be overcome. Don’t doubt your abilities. Have confidence in facing the future, because only in this way can you achieve your goals.

I’ve lost a few things recently, like my eye cream and comb. They might have ended up in the bag my roommate used to throw things away. Even though these things aren’t especially expensive, I’m still really unhappy and irritated. I keep wondering how I can get out of this feeling.

I completely understand that feeling of regret and being caught up in it. Do you feel like you just can’t let these things go, and even when you’re doing something else, you’re still thinking about what you lost?
Yes. No matter what I’m doing, I think of those lost things, and it feels really uncomfortable.

That’s quite normal. We all get overly caught up in certain things sometimes. Suppose something you’re working on right now went badly and cost you a lot—you might be able to let go of these small, trivial things.
You’re right. But I keep thinking those things were probably in that bag, and now I can’t get them back. I feel really awful.

First, without evidence, you can’t be sure the eye cream was in that bag. Second, the comb is even more far-fetched. You didn’t see any sign of the comb at all, yet you’ve set up this charge against yourself. Look at where you’re using all these excellent powers of inference.
Yes, I’ve realized I really am imagining things a bit too much. But I don’t know how to let go of this feeling.

People who live in the past can easily become depressed. If you keep getting stuck on the eye cream and the comb, you might as well also think about a lollipop you lost when you were three and a button you lost when you were five, and then try to put these small things outside of your life. That way, you’ll be able to handle all the tasks in front of you better, and you won’t fall behind your peers either.
Mm, what you’re saying makes a lot of sense. What should I do?

Try using emotion regulation skills to help yourself get out of this feeling, such as deep breathing and noticing what you’re feeling. If you still feel sad, you might consider seeking help from a professional to work through these issues.

I don’t know how to handle the problem of not being able to stop myself from raising my voice when my child is studying. Last night I asked her some detailed questions, but she wasn’t willing to think them through, and I couldn’t help yelling again. As a result, around 10:30 p.m., the upstairs neighbor messaged me and told me to watch my emotions because I had already disturbed their rest. I do want to control my emotions, but every time it gets to the evening, I increasingly can’t control myself. I’m always thinking I need to correct my child’s problems. Her biggest problem is that she’s always unwilling to steadily do the basics well, like math calculations and memorizing English words, and she also doesn’t properly review the knowledge points in other subjects. With the same material, she only starts to take it seriously and finally masters it after I’ve yelled many times. But if we do it this way, it’s already midnight, and it’s bound to affect her energy the next day. I know that spending time only doing surface-level studying is the least effective, but because of these things, she has already wasted too much time, and her learning is still getting worse. I don’t know how to get her to truly study steadily and properly. I know she understands the reasoning.

I see several key points in the issue you described that we need to think through together. First, when you ask your child some detailed questions, she isn’t willing to think, which makes it hard for you to control your emotions and eventually leads to yelling. This situation is indeed a bit tricky. Also, the biggest issue is that your child is unwilling to steadily build her basic skills, and the approach you’ve been taking is yelling multiple times. You feel very confused about her study methods and attitude, because you know that only doing surface-level studying is the most harmful thing for her.

Yes, I admit that when I lose control of my emotions, I use yelling to get her to take things seriously. But the result is that she only takes it seriously and really masters the material after I’ve yelled many times. I also know this way of studying isn’t advisable, but every time it’s evening, I’m especially likely to lose control and want to correct her problems.

I understand what you’re thinking. I think we should rethink the effect of “yelling.” From what you described, yelling does have some effect to a certain extent, because she only starts to take things seriously and master the material after you yell. But at the same time, you also mentioned that this way of studying stays on the surface, and the learning results are not good. Instead, it’s affecting her progress.
Yes, you’re absolutely right. I’ve also realized that this approach isn’t a long-term solution, but I just don’t know how to improve it so that she can study steadily and properly.

Then I suggest we start by exploring what causes you to lose control of your emotions. Why is it especially easy for you to lose control at night? Are there other, better ways to respond to the problems of your child being unwilling to think and studying only on the surface? We can take another look at the emotions involved and communicate with your child to understand whether she has encountered difficulties in the learning process and what needs improvement. I also recommended a book, Replicable Leadership, which has some communication methods that may be helpful to you.

Thank you for your suggestions. I think what you said makes a lot of sense. I can try talking with my child to understand the problems and difficulties she’s having in her studies. Maybe through communicating with her, we can find better ways to deal with these challenges.

Exactly. Communication is key to understanding your child’s problems. Through talking with her, we can better understand her learning difficulties and explore solutions together. I believe that as long as we make an effort together, things will gradually get better.
Thank you for your support and encouragement. I hope our efforts can help my child improve her learning situation and help her truly study steadily and properly.
You’re welcome. I believe you will definitely be able to overcome this difficulty. Please remember, patience and understanding are key to solving the problem. Wishing you all the best!

Is it that in a friendship of three people, I’m the one who gets left behind? I have a good friend. We used to be really happy. She told me we were good friends, and I took it seriously. One day she made a new friend, and they were very happy together. I hung out with them too, but I realized that I seemed like I couldn’t really fit in anymore. Because I can’t bring other people happiness the way she can. That time, I realized that so-called good friends really aren’t as good as I had imagined.

You may feel abandoned, but maybe what you want is more attention and care. When she made a new friend, she might spend more time with that new friend, and that may make you feel like she’s paying less attention to you. But people build different kinds of relationships with different people, and at different stages, they have different companions and friends. Just like you will also meet new friends in the future. You can also make friends happily like she does, but the premise is that you first bring happiness to yourself. Only when you’re happy yourself can you attract more friends. Friendship also requires giving, and there is also a certain exchange of value between friends.
But I feel like the friendship between them is more important than mine, and I’m always being left out. How can I bring other people happiness the way they do?

You haven’t been left out; it’s just that your importance to them may not be as high as you think. What matters is that you understand that everyone has their own way of connecting with others and different needs. You can try to discover the value that makes you different from others—the things you’re good at or the things you care about. That can help you get along better with other people. You can also tell them how you feel and try to communicate with them, so they can understand your needs. Maybe that will make the friendship between you deeper.
Sometimes I feel like I’m not confident enough, and I’m afraid of being rejected. I worry that if I express my feelings, they might not understand me, or might even leave me. What should I do?

It’s very normal to worry about being rejected, but it’s also important to understand that only by truly expressing your feelings and needs can others understand you better. Try to believe in yourself and bravely share your feelings with them. Tell them what you need. Sincere communication can make friendship stronger. If they don’t understand you or they leave you, that also shows they may not be people who truly understand and support you. You should also find friends who really understand and support you.
I know what you’re saying is right, but I’m still afraid to face their reactions. How should I overcome this fear?

Overcoming fear takes a little courage and persistence, bit by bit. You can start with small things first, like sharing some topics you’re interested in with them, or doing activities together that you all enjoy. Gradually expand your comfort zone and help yourself get used to facing their reactions. At the same time, remember that friendship is about mutual understanding and acceptance. They should also respect your feelings and needs.
What you’re saying makes sense. I’ll try to overcome my fear and express myself bravely. Thank you for your support and advice.
You’re welcome. I believe you can do it. Taking care of yourself and respecting your own feelings are very important. If you still need my help, feel free to come talk with me anytime. Good luck!
I feel very inferior, like I’m not good enough. I always feel my parents have wronged me. What should I do?

First, I want to say that I understand what you’re going through, and I feel for you. I’d really like to give you a big hug, so you can feel some warmth from the world. Actually, I feel your low self-esteem may have been influenced by your family environment and your parents since you were young, which is why it became this way. Some of it is deeply rooted, and it has stayed with you into adulthood, up to now.
Yes, I was affected by some of my parents’ negative emotions, and I’ve always felt like I’m not good enough.

But from what you’ve described, you’re actually a very good, very kind, and very thoughtful child. At 15, you went out to work for your family and helped share the family’s burden. That’s something many children couldn’t do. And you also had the will to keep going. You wanted to go to school and study, and you weren’t bad at it. You were even the English class representative, and you were good at drawing too. It was only because of limited circumstances that you couldn’t continue your education.
Yes, I wanted to study, but my family’s financial situation was very bad, so I could only choose to go out to work.

But you never gave up on learning. After working, you still continued to learn skills and learn computers. This shows that you’re actually someone with your own plans and direction. You wanted to learn something to make a living, rather than just drift through life. Actually, it can be said that your parents didn’t give you enough love, and that’s why it affected you, making you feel not good enough, very inferior, and very sad. The love your parents gave you was far from enough to help you become better. When you got married and had children, your parents didn’t come to show concern, yet they kept asking you to support your maiden family. That’s actually a kind of unhealthy and mistaken way of guiding you.
Yes, I’m very sad. I feel like I’ve always been giving to them, but I haven’t received the care I should have.

You don’t need to feel inferior, because through your own efforts, you learned techniques and skills. You’re also filial, thoughtful, and you support your maiden family. So you are the best daughter and wife. Your parents’ generation didn’t receive much education, so to a great extent, many of them don’t know how to love their children or how to educate them. So you really don’t need to pay for their mistakes. You only need to learn from the loving, knowledgeable, capable parents around you who treat their children well.
Yes, I need to believe in myself, believe that I’m the best, that I can be a good mother, and that I can educate my child well.

Yes, you really need to believe that you are the best, that you can be a good mother, and that you can educate your child well. Only when you have enough confidence will you be able to become better. Wishing you happiness and joy!
At 22, I always overthink when interacting with girls, and it makes me timid and hesitant?

At 22, being set up on multiple matchmaking dates—to be honest, I don’t quite understand that. From my point of view, at 22, life is only just beginning. You’re always working hard, hoping to become better before meeting someone you like, and you’re always worried about whether, at this stage, you can give the other person a better life. That shows you’re a motivated and responsible young man. You have thoughts and ideas, but you think a lot and act less, right? No matter what thoughts you have right now, first focus on becoming the best version of yourself, and turn those thoughts into reality. You can start by turning down the matchmaking dates your family arranges, and tell them what you want to do and roughly when you might be willing to accept matchmaking dates. Maybe in the process of continuing to improve yourself, you’ll already find the right partner for you. It’s good that, since you don’t have dating experience yourself, you’ve looked at other people’s relationship experiences with a willingness to learn. But relationships are your own, and you can’t just follow a script. You can take in successful experiences. I hope this can help you.

Thank you for your answer. Maybe because I’ve never had any dating experience, I get overly nervous and conflicted about how I would act in a relationship. I always feel like I’m still not able to give the other person enough happiness and stability, and I’m worried I might cause my partner trouble or pain.

I understand your worries. But a relationship is mutual; the responsibility for happiness and stability doesn’t fall on just one person. Trust that the other person has their own thoughts and choices too, and that they can also find their own happiness in being with you. Don’t put all the responsibility on yourself. Try to relax a little, give yourself and the other person some time and space, and trust that there can be a better outcome.

You’re right. I blame myself too much. Sometimes now I hesitate because of these worries, and I don’t know how to build a closer relationship with girls. I’m afraid my uncertainty and timidity will make the other person feel annoyed or disappointed.

Don’t be too hard on yourself. Everyone has moments of hesitation and timidity. Building an intimate relationship takes time and effort, so don’t rush it. Instead of worrying about your uncertainty, try taking one step forward, and actively communicate and express your real feelings. If the other person cares about you, they will understand and support you.

I understand. I should have more confidence and courage in facing difficulties in relationships. But I’m still worried that if I meet someone I like, I won’t know how to express my feelings. I’m afraid I’ll become awkward or say the wrong thing.

That’s a very normal worry. Believe me, when you meet someone you truly like, you’ll find a way that suits you to express your affection. Don’t be overly anxious. Love is a feeling that happens naturally; it isn’t something you need to deliberately chase. Stay genuine and honest, and trust that you’ll make the right choice.
Thank you for your encouragement and support. I’ll do my best to relax and believe that I can handle these confusions and challenges in relationships.

I’m very glad I could help. Remember: relax, believe in yourself, and face the confusions and challenges of relationships with courage. You will grow, and you will find your own happiness. Good luck! If you have any other questions, feel free to come back and talk with me anytime.
I feel really inferior, like I’m not good enough. I always feel like my parents have wronged me. What should I do?

You’ve made a lot of sacrifices for your family, and that’s admirable. Look at what you’ve given: for your family, you interrupted a very good education, and you sent all your wages home. You really are remarkable. But I can understand your feelings of inferiority and of being wronged by your parents. I want to tell you that your sense of inferiority isn’t justified. It’s not that you’re not good enough; you’ve just been limited by your circumstances. Your parents’ attitude is very common in rural areas, but that doesn’t mean you aren’t worthy of love and respect.

Thank you for encouraging me. I’ve always felt I’m not good enough, and that my parents only treat me this way because they want to use me. They’re always asking me to do things for them, but they rarely care about me. I used to work and study really hard, but it seems like no matter what I do, they never praise me or pay attention to me.

I understand how you feel. Feeling valued and appreciated is something everyone longs for. But sometimes, parents’ ways of doing things may not be very appropriate, and they may not realize your emotional needs. You can try to communicate honestly with them about your feelings and needs; they may understand and change their attitude. At the same time, you also need to learn to give yourself some affirmation and praise, and not rely only on other people’s approval to measure your worth.
I want to try communicating with my parents, but I always feel scared and nervous. I’m afraid they won’t understand me, or that they’ll get angry. What should I do?

That nervousness and fear are very normal, but don’t let them stop you from communicating with your parents. You can choose an appropriate time and calmly express your feelings and needs, letting them know you hope to receive more care and support. Remember, this is for improving your family relationships and for your own growth. Don’t treat the conversation as a chance to argue or blame. At the same time, you can also seek outside help, such as finding a counselor or family therapist. They can help you work through your relationship with your parents and provide appropriate guidance and support.

Hearing you say that, I feel like I have a bit more courage to communicate with my parents. But I’m worried that even if they hear me, they still won’t truly understand my needs. They always seem to think their own needs are more important.

I understand your worry. Parents sometimes may have their own expectations and needs, which are different from ours. But that doesn’t mean they won’t understand you or don’t care about you. Through sincere communication, you can help them understand your inner world and your needs. It may take some time for them to adjust and change their attitude. At the same time, you also need to learn to respect and understand their position. Family relationships are mutual, and harmony and understanding require effort from both sides. Keep going, and you’ll gradually discover the power and value of communication.

Thank you for your advice and encouragement. I feel more confident now about communicating with my parents. I’ll try to express my feelings and needs honestly, and I’ll also seek professional help to deal with this issue. I hope I can find happiness and fulfillment of my own.

I’m very glad to hear your determination and confidence. Believe in yourself—you can definitely find happiness and fulfillment of your own. Remember, throughout this process, don’t forget to take care of your own emotions and needs. If you have any confusion or need further support, you can always talk to me. Good luck!
I feel really inferior, like I’m not good enough. I always feel like my parents have let me down. What should I do?
Why do you feel that you’re not good enough? Would you be willing to share some of your experiences with me?

Before I was even 15, I went out to work for my family. I really wanted to go to school. My grades were about average, and I was even the English class representative. I was also very good at drawing. But my family’s financial situation was poor, and I couldn’t bear to see my parents suffer more, so I took the initiative to say I would go work and earn money. I hoped that after earning money for a year or two, I could come back home and maybe go to a vocational school.

It sounds like you are a very responsible and caring person. What you gave and the effort you made played a big role in your family. Taking the initiative to work because of your family’s financial situation was a very remarkable thing to do.
I worked for six years and sent all my wages to my mom. But it wasn’t until the fifth year, when I came back, that my parents said I could go to a training center to learn computers.

Although your parents may not have supported you in going to a training center in time, they may have hoped you could gain better abilities and skills. You created many opportunities for yourself and your family, and that is really remarkable.

When I got married, my parents didn’t come because it was far away. When I had my first child, they didn’t come. When I had my second child, they didn’t come either. But they often ask me now and then to buy things for my parents’ home. Even when they’re occasionally nice to me and call me, they still ask me to buy things for my parents’ home.

It sounds like you felt a lot of disappointment during your marriage and the births of your children, because your parents didn’t come to be part of those moments. Maybe they had their own reasons, but that doesn’t mean your worth or your contribution to the family hasn’t been recognized. Asking you to buy things for your parents’ home may be a way for them to express care, but you can also communicate with them appropriately about your thoughts and what’s troubling you. Your feelings are valid, and you don’t need to place all the blame on yourself.

I feel very inferior, like I’m not good enough, and that’s why my parents treat me this way. I feel inferior in front of my husband too, and I’m very sad. I don’t know whether someone like me can raise my children well.

Actually, you are a very outstanding and capable person, and you have sacrificed a lot for your family. You are judging yourself too harshly. As long as you can accept yourself, value yourself, affirm yourself, praise yourself, and appreciate yourself, you will be able to accept your child, respect your child, affirm, praise, and recognize your child. You can raise him or her well. Raising a child is positively related to the parents’ own growth. The more parents grow in a healthy way, the healthier the child will be physically and mentally. You are a very considerate and sensitive person. What you need now is to give this love back to yourself, to heal what was missing in your childhood, like raising your own child—raise yourself again, and live through a happy “childhood” again with your child. If you can do this, it can greatly reduce your resentment toward your parents. Your parents gave what they were able to give, and they couldn’t give what they didn’t have. What they didn’t manage to do, you can now do for yourself as an adult. In this way, you heal yourself and also give your child the best example through both your words and actions. With your ability, you can definitely get better and better.
I care too much about what other people think of me, and I always overthink before I do anything? I'm 20 this year, a junior male college student.

Hello. I hear that you feel you care quite a bit about other people's opinions and want to leave a good impression on everyone. This is a very common situation, so you don't need to worry too much. You can share your thoughts with me.
Yes. Before I do anything, I always overthink it and worry about what other people will think, and then I end up giving up on doing it.

At times like this, you can try to address the problem at its root. Low self-identity, perfectionism, and a people-pleasing personality—these traits may very likely be related to our childhood experiences. What was the way your parents interacted with you when you were little?
My family treated me pretty well, but when I was little, there were indeed a few pretty bad experiences.

Mm, it's possible that these unpleasant experiences have had some impact on your current psychological state. You can try going back to some specific scenes from the past and looking at how some of your parents' words and actions affected you: What did you feel at the time? What changes did it bring about in you? Why did you have those emotions then? Then reflect on your current situation and see whether there are connections between them.
I remember once when I was little, I failed an exam, and my parents got really angry. After that, I became very afraid of exams and was always especially nervous.

It seems your parents had relatively high expectations for your grades, and that also led you to develop an excessive striving for yourself. But pursuing perfection is an unhealthy mindset, and we need to change it gradually. You need to accept your shortcomings, be clear about your strengths, and try to ease the demands you place on yourself.
I really do often put in a lot for the sake of pursuing perfection, and I feel very tired.

This is very normal. We can all learn to let go of overly high expectations and love ourselves better. Understanding your feelings is very helpful for resolving the issue. I hope you can find a true sense of trust within yourself and believe that you can do better.
What should be done if a left-behind child in the neighborhood is being bullied at school?

I can tell you’re a caring person. There are quite a few cases of school bullying. Whether it’s the person bullying or the person being bullied, both sides have responsibilities. First, for the student being bullied: (1) Tell the teacher right away, or tell the parents of the students doing the bullying and have the teacher communicate with the parents, to stop this behavior as much as possible. (2) When facing bullying, you must be firm. Maybe fighting isn’t good, but if you seem weak, others will definitely think you’re easy to bully!
But I don’t dare tell the teacher or my parents. I’m afraid they won’t believe me, and that the classmates bullying me will treat me even worse.

I understand your worry and fear, but telling a teacher or your parents is the first step toward solving the problem. You can choose the teacher or parent you trust most and describe in detail the bullying you’ve been experiencing, so they understand your situation and what you need. They have a responsibility to protect every student’s safety and to take appropriate action to stop the bullying.
Mm, you’re right. I’ll try to find someone I can talk to and tell them about what I’m going through. But I’m still really afraid they won’t believe me.

I understand your concern. But please trust that teachers and parents will take what you’ve experienced seriously and take appropriate steps to protect your rights and interests. You can prepare some evidence to support what you’re saying, such as writing down the time, place, and people involved when the bullying happens. This can help them trust you more and help you solve the problem.
Okay, I’ll keep records and seek help from others. But I’ve also noticed that the classmates who bully others have their own problems too. Why do they bully people?

That’s a very sharp observation. The students who bully others may also have their own struggles and needs. Sometimes they may be bullied by people who are more powerful, and they bully you to gain a sense of existence. Bullying behavior is often related to the influence of their family environment; they may think bullying is a way to be accepted. Schools and parents should take the main responsibility, address what is missing inside these children, help them understand the problem correctly, and use the right ways to solve problems. So I think both the school and the parents should step in and address this issue.
Thank you for your advice and understanding. I’ll try my best to take your suggestions, and I also hope the school and parents can take this seriously and solve the problem.

You’re very welcome. Your courage and your proactive attitude toward solving the problem are admirable. Please remember, you are not facing this difficult situation alone; you have supporters and people you can rely on.
