Please stay in close communication with your teachers and parents, and seek their help and support. I hope you can be free from the distress of bullying soon!
Whenever it’s a reunion holiday like Spring Festival or Mid-Autumn Festival, I feel especially awful. I don’t want to go home?

Family is supposed to be a warm harbor, but now it has become a place of pain for you, so it’s very normal that you don’t want to go back. Even if you do go back, it probably feels like you have no choice. Right now, there’s no way to prove which one of them had an affair unless they admit it themselves. But for a child, something like this can wound their heart, and no one pays attention to that. Maybe the issue isn’t the affair; perhaps there are other reasons too.

That’s true. I have a lot of confusion. I’m 24 this year. I worked for three years, and now I’m preparing for the graduate school entrance exam. I also have a boyfriend I’ve been with for four years. He plans to apply for a PhD, but he doesn’t want to marry me. Also, I was a left-behind child growing up. My dad left home to work elsewhere when I was in high school, and he didn’t come back to Kunming until I was a junior in college, when he divorced my mom. Both of them say the other one had an affair, but I’m not even sure who actually did, because I spent very little time with them and know very little about them. The day before Spring Festival in 2017, after I had a fight with my mom, I never went back to Kunming for New Year or any other holiday again. Every time I go back, it feels very unpleasant. In my memory, the days with my mom were just scolding and more scolding. So whenever I think about having to go back to Kunming, I feel like I can’t take it inside. I cry for no reason and feel absent-minded. The main reason is that after going back, I don’t have any sense of belonging. My family is very poor. I grew up with my grandmother, but now she’s old and lives with my uncle, and I don’t want to go to my grandmother. My dad doesn’t have a house either. Every time I think of my mom, all I see in my mind are the scenes of her insulting me. I don’t know what to do.

Dear girl, your situation really is very complicated. First, you’re 24 this year. You’ve already worked for three years, and now you’re preparing for the graduate school entrance exam, full of expectations for your future. However, your boyfriend plans to apply for a PhD and doesn’t want to marry you. Being with someone who doesn’t plan to marry you—what is the purpose in your heart? And as a left-behind child, you grew up without your father’s love and company. Your dad left home to work when you were in high school, and didn’t come back to Kunming until you were a junior in college, when he divorced your mom. The marriage problems in your family were clearly very unhappy. Their issue isn’t about the affair, but about other things. Children who are left behind go through a lot inside. No matter what kind of family environment you were born into, we have no way to choose that. You can’t control the previous generation, but you can rely on yourself and become the master of your own life.

Yes, I really did spend very little time with my mom and dad, and I don’t know much about them. The day before Spring Festival in 2017, after I argued with my mom, I never went back to Kunming for New Year or any other holiday again. In my memory, the days with my mom were nothing but arguing, and that made it so that whenever I think about having to go back to Kunming, I can’t take it inside. I cry for no reason and feel absent-minded. Actually, I feel quite sorry for myself now. Spending time with parents should be a normal thing, but for me it feels like a luxury. Behind my mom’s verbal abuse and humiliation toward me is her extreme dissatisfaction with my dad, and it also reflects how twisted she is inside.

Yes, your experiences and feelings make my heart ache for you. For a child, spending time with parents should have been a normal thing, but for you it has become a luxury. All the arguments and separations have been quite painful for you. Your mom’s mental state definitely suggests psychological issues. Under normal circumstances, a mother would not verbally abuse and humiliate her own child like this. Behind her behavior is her extreme dissatisfaction with your dad, and it also reflects how twisted she is inside.

I haven’t gone back to Kunming for New Year or any other holiday for two years now. Every time I go back, I feel very unhappy. Home is supposed to be a place a person misses no matter where they go, but in my heart it has become a symbol of fear and pain. As a left-behind child, I long to reunite with my family, especially during Chinese holidays. But between me and my family, there is the verbal abuse that makes me feel terrified. I really don’t know what to do.

Home is a place a person cares about inside no matter where they go, but in your heart, home has become your fear and pain. As a left-behind child, you long to reunite with your family, especially during Chinese holidays. But between you and your family, there is verbal abuse that makes you feel terrified. This is very unfortunate.

Yes, I cry for no reason and feel like I’m absent-minded. The main reason is that after going back, I have no sense of belonging. My family is very poor. I grew up with my grandmother, but now my grandmother lives with my uncle, who had an affair, and I don’t want to go to my grandmother. My dad doesn’t have a house either. Every time I think of my mom, all I see in my mind are the scenes of her insulting me. I really don’t know what to do.

Girl, why do you cry for no reason? There is a reason behind all pain. All children hope to be loved and to have a sense of belonging, but it seems like you don’t hold out hope for that. Your family members can’t be relied on, so you can only rely on yourself. Your parents both have many problems inside, so they have no way to help you. I suggest you study hard and find a good job in the future,
Why do I always feel like I’m the one being bullied? Am I that easy to push around?

From the fact that you covered the water bill, I can see that you’re actually a very responsible and kind person. I want to give you credit for that. I noticed you mentioned “every time,” which means this isn’t the first time you’ve done this. I think you could first ask the other residents in the community how they handle this kind of situation.

Every time, someone’s home has a water leak, and everyone knows it, but no one admits it. No one is willing to split the extra water bill. I paid the whole water bill upfront, but not a single person has paid me back. Did I make them feel like I’m easy to bully?

I understand how you feel. In this situation, you would feel like you’ve been taken advantage of. There may be a pattern where you kindly paid upfront, and at first people were grateful, but later they got used to it and started to think it was just what you should do. When you do something good and others don’t appreciate it, you’d feel very wronged too. Still, the first thing is to check whether other residents have also paid upfront, whether they received the shared costs, and so on. If everyone has also paid upfront, then you don’t need to think too much about it, because this is a responsibility everyone shares. If others did receive the shared costs, you can ask about the specific approach and learn from it.

Mm, you’re right. I haven’t communicated with the other residents yet. I thought this was something I was responsible for, so I’ve just been quietly paying upfront. But now I realize I also need to communicate with everyone and understand the specific situation. I think I can talk with them first and see whether this problem can be resolved.

I’m really glad to hear you thinking this way. Communicating with others is a key step in solving the problem. But during the communication, remember to stay calm and rational, and express your thoughts and feelings. Also try to understand the other side’s position, and see if you can find a solution that everyone is satisfied with. I hope you can communicate with them smoothly and resolve this issue.

Okay, I’ll try my best to stay calm and rational when I communicate with everyone. I hope this problem can be resolved, and that I won’t keep feeling bullied and wronged. Thank you for your support and encouragement!

You’re welcome. I’m always willing to offer support and encouragement. Remember, you are a kind person. Don’t save your smile for people who don’t know how to be grateful. There must still be many people in life who are worth helping and who know how to be grateful. Whether it’s in resolving this issue or in your life later on, I believe you’ll be able to get through it smoothly. Hang in there! The world and all of us will love you~

Thank you for your blessings and encouragement! Your words make me feel incredibly warm and strong. I will work hard to face the problem, solve it, and stop seeing myself as the one being bullied. I’ll keep a positive and optimistic attitude and make myself stronger. Thank you again for your support!

You’re welcome. I’m very glad I could help you. You have a positive and optimistic attitude, and I believe you’ll definitely be able to solve the problem and get through this difficult situation. If you need help again in the future, remember you can come to me anytime to talk. I hope everything goes smoothly in your life and work. We’ve got this together! The world and all of us will love you~
Why can’t I stop comparing myself to the people closest to me?

I really understand how you feel. From what you’ve described, it seems that you’re quite sensitive about the issue of names being called. But actually, this is very normal and quite common. It may be that, deep down, we feel the other person is better than us and more likely to be recognized by others.
Yes, I always feel like she gets more attention and is liked more than I am.

I understand how you feel. This kind of jealousy is a self-protective mechanism that humans are born with; Freud called it the death instinct. Still, we don’t need to feel ashamed of it or deny it. It’s true that your sister may be better than you in some ways, but you definitely also have your own unique talents and strengths.
Yes, I know everyone has strengths and weaknesses, but I just can’t help comparing myself to her.

I understand how troubling this feels for you. We all have emotions like this, but it’s worth noticing that we can’t tie our own worth to how much attention others give us. Other people’s attention doesn’t represent everything, and they also can’t be with us for our whole lives. What matters most is your own recognition of yourself, rather than relying on other people’s opinions.
I understand. I should focus more on myself, instead of caring too much about how much attention other people give me.

That’s right. You’re being very thoughtful. At the same time, I’d suggest that you seek some professional support from your school’s counseling center. They can help you better adjust your emotions and mindset.
Okay, I’ll try to find a teacher at the school counseling center. Thank you for your support and advice.
You’re welcome. I’m glad I could offer you some help. I hope you can find a solution that works for you, and I wish you all the best. If you need anything, remember you can talk with me anytime.

I’m 26, married, and have a bachelor’s degree. Lately I’ve been feeling very dissatisfied with my current job, and I feel like it has no meaning. The work pressure is intense, especially the psychological pressure. There are also problems with the system in this job. I’m involved in railway projects, and I’m away from home all year round; eating, drinking, and everything else all happen in the same office building. I studied accounting as an undergraduate and worked in this organization for three years. Later I changed departments once, from accounting to materials. But I still don’t like this job, and I don’t have any other skills I can use to make money. My husband also works in this organization, but I often feel very confused. I really long for the lives of my college classmates—some of them became teachers, and they live free and fulfilling lives. How should I cope with this meaningless job that also has such a heavy workload?

It sounds like you’ve been under a lot of pressure recently, and you also don’t like the system of your current workplace, so you feel unhappy in this position. Doing something you like can be enjoyable, while doing something you don’t like can feel like torture. Work is always hard, but only when you’re doing work you like can you still feel happy inside, even if it’s tiring. In contrast, when you’re doing work you don’t like, even if it’s easy, it can still feel mentally exhausting. Since you’re feeling confused right now, the first thing you need is to find a new direction. Understanding yourself is very important, including knowing what you’re good at and where your shortcomings are. At the same time, you also need to be clear about what you like doing and what you dislike doing. Only by understanding your own characteristics can you find work that suits you. Second, combined with your real-life situation, you can consider what kinds of jobs might be suitable for you under your current conditions. If you want to do work you like, you’ll also need to put in the corresponding effort. I wish you good luck!

What you said is very true. Doing something I like would definitely make me happy, and even if it’s hard, it would be worth it. But right now I feel really lost, and I don’t know which direction to move in. I do need to understand myself more deeply, but I feel confused about that too. How do you think I should start getting to know myself?

Getting to know yourself isn’t easy; it takes a process and time. First, you can try looking back on your past and think about what things made you feel fulfilled and happy, and what things made you feel bored and exhausted. You can ask yourself: when you were little, what were you interested in? During college, which courses or club activities were you especially engaged in and enjoyed? At the same time, you can also ask the people around you—family, friends, coworkers—and see how they view your strengths and talents. By gradually understanding your interests, strengths, and talents, you’ll have more clues for finding a work direction that suits you.

Thank you for your suggestions. Looking back on the past and asking people around me really can help me understand myself better. I have another question: if I want to change careers and do work I like, what should I do? I feel like my current qualifications may not really meet the requirements for other jobs.

Changing careers is a big decision, and it requires careful planning and preparation. First, you can start by improving your skills and see whether the skills you currently have can be applied after you change careers. If your current abilities aren’t enough to meet the requirements of other jobs, you can consider taking some relevant courses, or improving your skills through self-study. Also, you can try doing an internship in your current organization or in another related organization to build some practical work experience. At the same time, pay attention to job postings, understand the position requirements and market trends needed for a career change, and put your time and effort into learning and improving. Changing careers may not be easy, but as long as you have determination and put in the effort, you can definitely achieve your goals. Hang in there!

What you said makes a lot of sense. I understand now. I’ll work harder to improve my skills and try to learn and gain experience through practice. Thank you for your support and encouragement! I feel like I have hope again, and I believe I can find work that suits me. Thank you again for your advice!

I’m glad my suggestions were helpful to you. Your positive attitude is really worth encouraging. On the path toward the work you ideally want, you may run into some difficulties and setbacks, but as long as you keep going, you will be able to achieve your goals. Believe in yourself, and believe in the future. I hope you find a job that makes you feel happy and fulfilled. You’ve got this!

Thank you so much for your encouragement and good wishes! I’ll keep working hard, believe in my abilities, and believe in the future. I hope I can find a job that truly makes me happy as soon as possible. Thank you again for your help and support!

You’re very welcome! Your positive attitude and actions make me feel very glad. Believe in yourself and keep working hard, and you will be able to find work you enjoy and feel happy doing. If you have any other questions in the future, remember you can reach out to me anytime. I wish you all the best!

I keep controlling myself so I won’t curse gods or Buddhas. Is this religious obsessive-compulsive disorder? How do I deal with it? I just can’t control myself from wanting to curse gods and Buddhas. My family believes in Buddhism and burns incense every day. One time a thought flashed through my mind, like I wanted to curse gods and Buddhas, and after that I couldn’t stop wanting to curse them. I tried really hard to stop myself. Every day as soon as I open my eyes, I want to fight it, but I’m constantly controlling myself so I won’t curse. Now I can control myself for a whole day without cursing, but inside I’m in so much pain, constantly resisting myself. Now when I see a cross, I’ll think of Jesus and also want to curse. Because of this I went to see a counselor before, and she said God’s thoughts are different from ours and He won’t punish me, that if I curse then I curse, I can curse as much as I want. But I can’t do that. I’m afraid that if I go along with my obsessive-compulsive symptoms, they’ll get worse and worse. I also can’t get past it in my heart, to just keep cursing. Now I’m thinking about this every moment, controlling myself from August until now, already half a year... Every day I’m controlling myself. I’ve also read books on Morita therapy, about accepting things as they are and doing what needs to be done, but even when I’m doing things, I still think of this all the time and try to control it. Are you saying I have to live with this kind of pain for the rest of my life? Control myself every day? I really feel like I’m being tortured to death… It’s been half a year and I keep going on. I don’t want to die.

I can understand how you feel, and thank you for bravely sharing what has been troubling you with me. Everyone has different impulses and thoughts inside, and there can be many different reasons for developing obsessive-compulsive symptoms related to gods or Buddhas. The fact that you were able to control yourself before and not curse gods or Buddhas is a remarkable achievement, but I also understand the difficulty you’re facing now and the pain inside you. You mentioned that your counselor suggested you could curse gods or Buddhas if you wanted to, but you’re worried that doing that would make the obsessive-compulsive symptoms worse. I want to tell you that you don’t have to endure this pain for the rest of your life. We can work together to find a way through it.

Thank you for your understanding and encouragement, but I really can’t accept the suggestion to just casually curse gods and Buddhas. I feel that doing that doesn’t fit with my values, and it’s not the way I want to solve this. I hope I can find a better way to cope with my obsessive-compulsive symptoms so that I can be freed from this.

I really understand your point of view. Everyone has their own standards and bottom lines when it comes to solving problems. So, aside from the suggestion to freely curse gods and Buddhas, are there any other methods in your life that you might be able to try to reduce your pain? You mentioned that you’ve read books on Morita therapy. Did you get any inspiration from them, or have you noticed any effects from putting them into practice?

Reading books on Morita therapy gave me some ideas. It emphasizes letting things take their course and acceptance, but when I’m doing things, I always involuntarily think of this issue and then try to control it. This situation really troubles me. I honestly don’t know what to do.

The fact that you can recognize and try to accept the way of thinking in Morita therapy is already really admirable. But I can understand that when you’re taking action, you’re still troubled by this issue. So when you’re trying to control this problem, have you ever thought about shifting your attention, or trying some methods to relax and ease your anxiety?

I’ve tried shifting my attention before, but the effect hasn’t been very obvious. When I’m anxious, I try deep breathing or some relaxing exercises, but once I return to normal daily life, this issue appears in my thoughts again, and it makes me feel discouraged.

Thank you for bravely trying different methods. Even though the effects haven’t been very obvious, at least you’ve already made some efforts for your mental health. Sometimes solving a problem requires ongoing exploration and trying things out, continually adjusting the approach until you find what works for you. I believe that on the journey ahead, you will find a solution that suits you.

Thank you for your encouragement and support! I’ll keep going and keep trying to find a solution that works for me. Although I feel very confused and discouraged right now, with your company and understanding, I believe I can get through this difficult time.

Your effort and courage truly make me admire you. No matter what stage of life we’re in, we all face all kinds of difficulties and challenges, but as long as we keep searching for solutions without giving up, and have people supporting and encouraging us, we can overcome difficulties and find inner peace and happiness again. Please believe in yourself. I will always be here by your side, supporting you.

I'm a new middle school student, and I’m always having conflicts with my mom, but I can’t really take any action. What should I do? As I’ve gotten older, I always like talking back to my parents. My mom always says I talk back for no good reason, but holding it in makes me feel really upset too. My mom is really worried about my schoolwork. I’m only in seventh grade and she’s already always talking to me about the high school entrance exam. Lately I’ve been addicted to games and secretly taking my phone to play, but I always get caught. My mom and I argue, and maybe during the argument I said some not-so-good things. My mom said, “Has your conscience been eaten by something?” Then she started ignoring me and not caring about me. She said, “Take these twenty yuan yourself. Aren’t you jealous of other people eating instant noodles? Go buy it yourself. After you buy it, figure it out yourself. That way I don’t have to keep coming up with all kinds of meals for you. I work so hard to cook, and then the food I make still gets looked down on.”

After hearing what you described, I can understand that you feel confused in the conflict between you and your mom. It’s true that as we grow up, conflicts with our parents can happen. Your mom may be worried about your schoolwork, which is why she brings up the high school entrance exam. And your being absorbed in games may make her very worried. During the argument, you may have said some things impulsively, but that doesn’t mean you really look down on her. Your mom may have said those things because she was worried about what you eat, but the way she expressed it may have made you feel hurt.

Thank you for understanding. I also know my mom is doing it for my own good, but sometimes it’s still really hard to tolerate the things she says. And she also said I affect her mood, which makes me feel kind of powerless.

Conflicts often come up in the relationship between a mother and child, and that’s very normal. During adolescence, our emotions may be relatively unstable, and a lot of the time we can’t control ourselves either. It’s very understandable that you feel you can’t tolerate what she says, but we can try to shift the perspective a little and think from your mom’s point of view.

You’re right. I need to think from my mom’s point of view. I also understand that emotional ups and downs during adolescence are normal, but sometimes I still feel really frustrated, like I can’t control my emotions.

Yes, the emotional ups and downs of adolescence can indeed feel very troubling. But when you and your mom have a conflict, we can try to separate what matters for your health from what is said verbally, and see which one is more important to you. No matter what happens, our life and health always come first. Maybe, slowly, you’ll stop caring so much about these arguments.
Mm, I’ll try to separate the trade-off between health and words, and remember the importance of life and health. Maybe this way, I’ll be able to handle the conflicts with my mom better.

That’s good. Gradually, you’ll find that you’re better able to cope with and handle the conflicts between you and your mom. At the same time, remember to communicate with your mom and let her know your thoughts and feelings, so she can understand you better too.
Mm, I’ll try to communicate more with my mom and let her understand my thoughts and feelings. I hope we can reduce the conflicts between us through communication.

Your effort and communication are very important. I believe that through the exchanges between you two, the conflicts will gradually decrease, and your relationship will also become better. If you need anything, don’t hesitate to seek help from me. I’ll always be here to support you.
Thank you for your support. I’ll remember that. I believe I can handle the conflicts with my mom well, and our relationship will get better.

I feel like when someone likes me, I start to like them too. What should I do? When I sense that someone is paying attention to me (and it’s real, not something I’m imagining), I start wondering if this person likes me. Then I end up paying way too much attention to him and caring way too much about him, and suddenly, in an instant, my mind is full of him! It becomes like I’m the one who likes him! But I know that’s not liking someone. I’ve never even talked to him, and I don’t know him, just... I really don’t have that feeling of liking him. But if it’s because I’m nervous, then yes, my heart does beat faster (the kind of nervousness that comes from feeling like someone is paying attention to me), but that doesn’t mean I’m attracted to him! Anyway, it’s a really strange feeling. I feel like I’m the kind of person who starts liking someone as soon as they like me. If it were someone else, I’d be like this too. It feels really awful—what should I do? Please help!

I can see that when you feel someone likes you, you may also start to like them, and that this is causing you some distress. People often feel positively toward those who like them, and that’s normal, whether it’s someone of the same sex or the opposite sex. After all, it feels good to be liked, and when someone likes us, we naturally feel happy and may respond by liking them back.

But I feel like I pay too much attention to the other person and care too much about him, to the point where my mind is full of him. This doesn’t seem like normal liking. I don’t truly feel that I like him.

That’s right. As social beings, humans benefit from mutual liking, and we also tend toward reciprocity. According to Baidu Baike: the principle of reciprocity holds that we should try to repay others for what they have done for us in a similar way. In short, one kind of behavior should be returned with a similar kind of behavior. So when someone likes us, of course we may also want to respond with the same kind of liking. Romantic love is exclusive, and you’re also very clear that this is not romantic liking. It’s enough to be clear about that.
But why do I pay too much attention to the other person? How can I control this emotion?

This kind of liking shows up in feelings and behavior, such as paying too much attention to the other person and caring too much about them. You can try allowing yourself to think about the other person; there’s nothing wrong with that. If caring too much about them is affecting your studies, work, or life, you can write down your feelings about them and sort through what you’re feeling. After writing it down, your feelings may become clearer, and maybe once you’ve sorted them out, you won’t care so much.
What’s the point of writing down my feelings? How do I know writing them down can solve the problem?

Writing things down can help you understand your feelings more clearly, and it can also help you better analyze and handle this emotion. After you try writing it down, you can look back at what you wrote and think about why you have these feelings, whether there are any triggers, and so on. This way, you can understand yourself better and find ways to address the problem.
I understand. I’ll try writing it down and see if it can help me solve the problem. Thank you for your advice!

You’re welcome. I hope what I shared above is helpful. Remember, you’re not abnormal. Many people run into similar struggles in relationships and feelings. Take your time trying to understand your feelings and looking for ways that work for you. I believe you’ll gradually move out of this distress. Good luck!
Thank you for your support and good wishes. I’ll do my best!

We didn’t have a fight. Would my girlfriend just have a period of time when she doesn’t want to talk to me or see me? My girlfriend and I didn’t argue, everything was fine, nothing happened, and then suddenly there was a period of time when she didn’t want to talk to me or see me. I don’t know why. Can anyone help me?

You and your girlfriend didn’t have a fight, everything was fine, and nothing happened. Then suddenly, for a while, she didn’t want to talk to you or see you. You feel really confused and don’t know why. How could things be fine, and then she suddenly doesn’t want to talk to you or see you? You must be feeling really sad right now.
Yes. Her sudden coldness has made me feel very frustrated and helpless. I’ve tried hard to think of what her possible reasons might be, but I just can’t figure out what exactly went wrong.

I can understand your confusion and anxiety. After all, this kind of sudden change is hard to predict or understand. Maybe you could try taking the initiative to communicate with her, let her know that you care about her and are willing to listen to her feelings, and see whether you can find a way to work through it.
I’ve also tried reaching out to chat with her, but she always avoids me and even doesn’t reply to my messages. I don’t know what I should do to break this deadlock.

This really is a very difficult situation. She may have become resistant to communicating for certain reasons. You could try giving her some space and not press her too much, but also not give up completely. You can express your care in an appropriate way, while still respecting her wishes.
I understand. I’ll try to give her some time and space. I’m just worried that this period of time will pull us farther apart emotionally. I’m really afraid of losing her.

I understand your worry. Changes in a relationship can definitely feel unsettling. But try to trust that if the feelings between you are real and solid, this difficult period is only temporary. For now, you can try to set aside your own anxiety and focus on growth and communication between you and her.
Okay. I’ll try to adjust my mindset and believe that our relationship can get through this difficult time. Thank you for your advice and support. It makes me feel a little more at ease.

You’re welcome. I’m willing to help you get through this difficult time. Remember to keep a positive mindset, rather than blaming yourself or worrying too much. Trust and patience are key to solving the problem. I believe the two of you can get through this difficult period together. I hope you’re able to repair your relationship with each other and return to harmony.
I was sexually assaulted when I was 5. I want to get better. Can you help analyze and correct my thoughts?

I’m not sure exactly how old you are now, but I’m guessing you must be at least in your teens. So I think it’s important for you to recognize this: a 5-year-old child does not have the capacity to act in the way an adult does. So we can’t look at it from your current perspective and think that a 5-year-old should have acted according to some standard. To put it a bit strongly, even if what happened at age 5 had been initiated by the injured child themselves, it still would not be that 5-year-old child’s fault.
Thank you so much for your reply. I understand your point, but I’ve always believed I was at fault. At the time, I didn’t refuse. I nodded. I feel like I was an accomplice.

And even more so, that 5-year-old child was being treated violently at the time. So the issue you’re facing now is actually how to help yourself realize that the 5-year-old you was not at fault. The reason you have this thought of “even though I was hurt too, I was actually also an accomplice in hurting myself” is that what happened was not properly resolved at the time. On top of that, the attitudes of the people around you had an impact, so some of the aggression that arose from the harmful event itself could not be effectively released. It could only be internalized as an attack on yourself. And some of the later feelings you had, like “I’m so dirty,” are actually the result of that internalized aggression.

You’re right. I’ve had many thoughts of attacking myself all along. I realize these thoughts come from the harm not being handled properly and from the attitudes of the people around me. I want to change this internalized aggression, but I don’t know how.

Under the constant effect of that aggression, in your mind you came to see yourself as “dirty.” This is actually a form of punishing yourself. If you had stayed in the state of internalized aggression we talked about earlier, you probably wouldn’t feel pain. But now you want to come out of it, and that’s why you’re experiencing what you described as “staying in the darkness doesn’t hurt; walking from the darkness into the light is what hurts.” This pain, however, is an unavoidable part of growth. It’s like the pain of childbirth—only after going through that pain can you experience the joy of new life.

You’re right. I understand now. If I want to come out of it, I have to face this pain and accept the suffering that comes with growth. But I’m still afraid to face this kind of pain. Sometimes I feel like I can’t bear it.

This pain is unavoidable, but you need to know that you are not facing it alone. You can seek support and look for a professional counselor to help you work through this pain and help you find a way of growing that suits you. At the same time, you can also share your feelings with people close to you, so they can understand and support you. Although the pain is hard to bear, you are not fighting alone; the strength of love and support will be with you.

Thank you for your suggestions. I’ll consider finding a professional counselor to help me. At the same time, I’ll also try to share my feelings with my family and friends, and I hope they can understand and support me. Although the path of growth will involve pain, there will also be love and support alongside me, and that gives me comfort and courage.

You’re doing really well. Bravely facing what’s inside you, seeking professional help, and sharing your feelings with family and friends are all very good steps. Don’t forget, you’ve already taken the first step. Believe in yourself—you can definitely walk out of that darkness and become a stronger you. I hope my support can be helpful to you. If you need anything, feel free to come back and talk with me anytime.

Thank you so much for your support and encouragement! Your replies have given me a lot of courage and hope. I’ll keep trying, believe in myself, walk out of that darkness, and welcome a better future. If I need to seek help again, I won’t hesitate to come back and talk with you. Thank you again!

I really hate him, but I can’t help contacting him. Should I get divorced? My husband and I were high school classmates, and we’ve known each other for more than ten years. When we were dating as students, I felt like he could put up with my bad temper endlessly. I would hit him and curse at him, and he could accept it, so I mistakenly thought he had a really good temper.

Your living environment is different from when you were students; you and he are also married now. He has to cover expenses for you and your child, so the pressure on him outside must be quite a lot, right? Especially with the pandemic this year. He’s no longer in the environment he was in as a student, when he only had to think about studying and giving in to you. Your sense of him is still stuck in your student days, but he’s no longer the person he was back then. If you still use the same way with him, do you think it will work?
You’re right. I hadn’t realized that what I expect from him has already gone beyond what he can handle. What should I do now?

Your environment has already changed a lot, but you seem not to feel it? You’re already a mother now; you have a child. Your husband can also stand on his own now. Are you still living in your student days? Let’s do a thought exercise, okay? If you keep going in your current state, suppose he brings up “divorce,” or you can’t stand him continuing to be “violent” toward you (his violence, in many cases, is something you lead him into), what are you planning to do? Have you thought about this?

I haven’t thought about this. I should think about the future for myself and my child. If we keep going like this, it may lead to bigger conflicts and hurt. I want to change the way I treat him, but I’m not sure what I should do.

If you don’t want to keep having conflicts with him, you can change the way you treat him. Wouldn’t that solve the problem? In the past, you always treated him in a “violent” way, and now he’s just using a “violent” way to communicate with you. He’s imitating your way of communicating with him, so if you change your way, wouldn’t he also learn from that? If you need to communicate, you can leave a message or send a private message.
What you’re saying makes sense. I should actively change my own behavior and try to use communication instead of violence. Maybe through talking with him, we can find a better way to resolve things.

That’s very well said! Communication is key to solving problems. You can try to find an appropriate time to sit down with him and have a good talk, and honestly express your feelings and needs. At the same time, you also need to listen to his thoughts and opinions. Through mutual respect and understanding, you can find a solution together.
Thank you for your advice. I’ll communicate with him as soon as I can. I feel much better now. I really needed someone to comfort me and hold me.

Of course. I understand how you feel. Although I can’t give you a hug in person, you can imagine that I’m here with you, supporting you. If you need any help or want to talk again, you can come to me anytime. You won’t be alone in this process. Believe in yourself; everything will get better.
Thank you for your support and encouragement. I’m really grateful. I’ll work hard to change and solve the problems, and I hope our marriage will get better.
There’s this really uncomfortable feeling that stays with me, and it’s especially irritating?
I can understand how you’re feeling right now. This kind of distress must be making things really hard for you.
Yes. I’ve been feeling a bit down today. My mom came back from outside, and she’s been busy with things, but her voice makes me feel really uncomfortable. I feel irritated for no clear reason.
It sounds like that voice may have triggered this discomfort in you. When you hear that voice, does it bring back experiences from when you were little?

Yes, hearing that voice makes me think back to scenes from my childhood. Back then, my parents worked away from home, and I lived with my grandma and my aunt. Every time my aunt bought me shoes, or my grandpa bought me shoes, I didn’t like them, so I would rub them hard against the ground to let out my emotions, even though I felt really bad inside too. I never expressed those feelings to anyone.

It seems like, since you were little, you never found a suitable way to express your dissatisfaction and distress. Every time you were unhappy, your aunt and grandma would try to help you solve the problem, but you still felt unhappy and irritated. Was there ever a time when you really wanted to escape, like riding your bike into a big well?
Yes, there was one time when I really wanted to do that. This kind of emotion has often stayed with me, especially during adolescence, when it became even more obvious.

Adolescence really can be a stage that makes people feel helpless and confused. There was also a period when I was in the second year of middle school when I felt empty inside, couldn’t find anyone to support me, and felt really awful. I felt low all day, and even wanted to cry. I can understand that the bipolar disorder and cognitive difficulties you’re experiencing now are related to that period. Although your grandma and aunt were still very good to you and never hit or scolded you, the love you felt wasn’t the kind you truly needed. For example, you didn’t like the shoes and clothes they bought you, but you forced yourself to wear them, and you couldn’t express the dissatisfaction inside. For a long time, you kept enduring things you didn’t like, feeling helpless and confused. At that time, you may have wondered, where is Mom? If she were by your side, maybe you could get the things you liked. So you also have some resentment toward your mom—why couldn’t she be there with you?

You’re right. Right now I really do have a lot of conflicting emotions. I don’t want to keep going on like this, because deep down I think my mom left me when I was little and didn’t love me enough. When I needed her, she wasn’t there, and she didn’t give me the support and strength of love. But now that she’s back, I feel like I don’t really need her that much. Still, sometimes when she’s not around, I occasionally miss her. I feel very conflicted myself.

Conflicting feelings are always distressing. First, to change these conflicting emotions, you need to build a better connection with your mom, to understand her and also let her understand you. At the same time, learn to accept your current life situation, and understand that your mom not being by your side doesn’t mean she doesn’t love you. In this highly competitive social environment, your mom had no choice but to go out to work, possibly so that you could have a better life. She must have been very reluctant to leave you too, but she had no other way. Also, you need to learn to communicate with your family. It’s okay to tell your mom what you need. As long as it’s within a reasonable range, she will definitely support you. Don’t wrong yourself or go against your true needs inside. I hope you can learn to communicate better with your family, and I hope you can spend each day happily.

Thank you for your suggestions and support. I’ll try to change my attitude. I hope I can build a better relationship with my mom, and also learn to express my true needs better. Thank you again for your help!

What should be done if a left-behind child in the neighborhood is being bullied at school? A left-behind child nearby is being bullied by classmates, and the parents aren’t home because they’re working away from home. The child also doesn’t dare tell the teacher, because if they do, the bullies will get even worse. What should be done?

You’ve been through a lot, and hearing what you’re facing makes me feel very sad for you. As a left-behind child, you’re already facing a lack of care and support from your parents, and now you’re also experiencing school bullying. That is really painful and heartbreaking. I understand that inside, you may be filled with sadness, helplessness, grievance, and hurt. In this situation, I hope you can find someone who can understand how you feel inside and notice all the difficulties you’re carrying, and talk to them about your feelings. That process itself can give you strength.
Thank you for your encouragement and support. I think having someone listen to what I’m feeling inside would probably make me feel comforted and able to let some of it out.

That’s right. When you’re able to express your inner feelings to others, you can feel eased and released. After you find someone who can listen to you, and after you have gained a little strength inside, you can work with them to look for appropriate ways to respond to being bullied by classmates. Of course, this is not an easy thing. It requires you to actively build up courage and strength, and gradually find small victories through setbacks. It’s important to remember that classmates who bully others are often also bullied by others, and they use the same kind of behavior to hide their own helplessness. They also have a vulnerable side. Understanding this may be helpful to you.

I understand. Knowing that other classmates also have a vulnerable side might give me a bit more confidence. But as a left-behind child, I’ve gone through a lot of pain, and I can only work hard to face it on my own. How can I turn the suffering I’ve experienced into resources, abilities, and meaning in life?

I really admire your strength. Whether someone is a left-behind child or not, everyone goes through their own difficulties. When we face pain, trying to turn it into resources and abilities is a positive approach. You can try to look for the positive impact these experiences may have had on your growth and development. Doing this can not only help you understand yourself better, but also give you confidence to face future challenges. Remember, you are not fighting alone. We will all support you through this process.

Thank you for your understanding and encouragement. I will do my best to face difficulties positively and turn suffering into opportunities for growth. I hope I can become stronger and more confident.

You’ve already taken the first step by reaching out to others for help. Your strong determination will help create a better future for you. I believe you will become stronger and stronger, and bravely face all kinds of challenges in life. You are not alone; there have always been people supporting you. Please remember, you deserve a happy and joyful life. If you have any confusion or need further support, feel free to come back and talk with me anytime.

Thank you very much for your encouragement and support. When I needed it most, your companionship and guidance helped me a lot. I will always remember your support, and I will face the challenges in life more positively.

You’re very welcome. Helping you is my responsibility and mission. Seeing that you can face difficulties positively also makes me feel very comforted. If you need further help, don’t hesitate—come talk to me anytime. Believe in yourself. You will definitely be able to get through all the difficulties and move toward a brighter future. My best wishes to you.
Thank you again for your support and encouragement. I will keep your words in mind, keep working hard and moving forward, and create a happy and beautiful tomorrow for myself.

I feel like I care too much about what other people think of me, and I always overthink things before I do them. I’m 20 this year, a male junior in college. I feel like I care a bit too much about other people’s opinions. I always want to leave a good impression on everyone, so before I do anything, I tend to think way too much. I’ll imagine that if someone else did this, how would I see him? If I feel even a little bit bad about it, then I don’t want to do it. Maybe I’m afraid of leaving a bad impression on others. For example, when competing for some important positions, I can actually clearly see that the people running for them all go in with a very strong purpose, or you could say a very utilitarian mindset. I feel pretty resistant to that inside, so I’m also afraid that if I did that, other people would see me that way, so I don’t want to go for it. At the same time, I’m also afraid of failing and having others see it, kind of holding onto the mindset that if I don’t try, I won’t fail. It’s the same when I interact with people. I’m afraid others will feel like I’m approaching them with an agenda. A lot of the time I’m especially not proactive, and I overthink a lot. My girlfriend says that sometimes I’m like a girl, indecisive when doing things and thinking too much. Now I’m gradually starting to feel that way too. I hope my response can bring you even a little bit of help. At 20, such a youthful age, because you don’t yet have very rich social experience and your understanding of yourself isn’t yet very deep, everyone, at this stage, tends to care a lot about other people’s evaluations. We also tend to have some internal standards of judgment, thinking that doing this is right and doing that is wrong. I went through that stage too, and once had the same confusion and uncertainty as you. There’s no need to blame yourself, and no need to be afraid. Go experience things, go explore, and step by step, as you grow, you’ll find your own answers.

Thank you for your understanding and advice. Maybe it really is because I don’t understand myself deeply enough that I care too much about other people’s evaluations. I feel like I’m always suppressing my own inner needs in order to satisfy others. Do you have any specific suggestions?

Here are a few suggestions for you: First, accept yourself, get to know yourself, and keep exploring who you are. You are someone who really likes to think, and you’re willing to put yourself in other people’s shoes and feel what they feel. You also take care of other people’s feelings, and you’re very considerate. It’s true that being considerate helps us have good interpersonal relationships, but if, while being considerate, we suppress our own inner needs, it can turn into people-pleasing. We not only need to consider things from other people’s perspectives, but also take care of our own feelings at the same time. Communication is not about getting the other person to approve of you, and it’s not about making you approve of the other person. It’s about, through sincere exchange, sharing each other’s thoughts, allowing both people’s needs to be seen by the other, and finally finding a suitable solution. I suggest that you keep noticing your own needs, keep getting to know yourself, see your strengths and weaknesses, and accept all of who you are. When you understand yourself very well, you won’t care so much about other people’s evaluations.

That’s true, I understand. I usually pay too much attention to what other people think and ignore my own needs and feelings. I’ll try to pay more attention to and understand myself, and accept my strengths and weaknesses. I won’t let other people’s evaluations control my behavior anymore.

Good, you’re understanding this very quickly. Next, there’s one more point, which is to treat other people’s evaluations in the right way. Actually, everyone’s understanding has its limits. Some people may think that those who participate in competitions have a very strong purpose, and yes, there will be people who think that. But there will also be people who think that those who participate in competitions are brave, that they dare to take on challenges. Others may think they have a strong sense of curiosity and are willing to join competitions to explore the unknown… In short, different people will have different views about the same thing. So we don’t need to care so much about other people’s evaluations. Those are things we can’t control. What we can control is doing the things we want to do. If you want to do something, you need to encourage yourself to do it, because the things that attract you must be connected to your interests, and they can also meet your inner needs. If you keep delaying action, your needs won’t be met, your interest will naturally decrease, and you may end up with some regret and disappointment. But as for what’s already in the past, let’s not dwell on it for now. What you need to do now is focus on what’s in front of you, listen to your inner voice, and bravely try. Believe that you can do it. You’ve got this.

Thank you for your encouragement and advice. I understand now. I should trust my own choices more and not pay too much attention to other people’s evaluations. I need to take action more actively and bravely try the things I want to do, instead of being afraid of failure and regret.

Good, your mindset is shifting very quickly. That’s really great! Lastly, there’s the issue of personality. Maybe you’re a relatively introverted boy, but from your description, you said you want to become an outgoing person. Actually, whether someone’s personality is more extroverted or introverted is something they’re born with, and there’s no need to deliberately change it. Personality also isn’t a matter of good or bad. Introversion has its strengths, and extroversion has its strengths. See the strengths in your own personality, accept yourself, and find work where you can make use of your strengths. You can shine just the same.

I understand. I don’t need to force myself to become a completely outgoing person. I’ll accept my own personality, see the strengths of being introverted, and find a direction for development that suits me. Thank you for your patience and advice. This conversation has helped me become clearer about the direction I need to change in.

Believe in yourself, and believe that you can find a way that suits you and become more confident and fulfilled. If you have any other questions or confusion, feel free to come back and talk with me anytime. I’m rooting for you!

At the same time, remember to stay positively connected with the people around you, and take part in more things that help you feel recognized and valued. Also, learn to accept failure and difficult situations, and believe that you can get through this hard time.

I understand. I'll try to look for inner value and a sense of fulfillment, and also keep up positive communication and connection. This kind of emotional dependence is actually a common psychological response, and many people have similar feelings. We can work on changing this by strengthening your self-confidence and independence. Developing your own interests and hobbies, improving your skills and knowledge, and building healthier interpersonal relationships are all effective ways. Okay, I'll try to strengthen my self-confidence and independence, and I'll also think about the possibility of seeking professional help. First, try not to focus too much on other people's lives or compare yourself with others. Everyone's life experiences and opportunities are different, and they can't be used as the standard for judging yourself. What's important is to focus on your own growth and progress, and keep working toward your own goals. At the same time, you can look for some positive sources of motivation in life, such as joining interest groups, reading uplifting books, or taking part in volunteer activities. These can all help you find joy and meaning in life.

Thank you for your suggestions. I'll try not to pay too much attention to other people's lives anymore, and instead focus on my own growth and progress. I'll also try taking part in some positive activities and look for joy and meaning in life. Thank you for your support and encouragement. I feel a little more relieved.

I understand. In your communication with your mom, you haven’t had much experience of receiving care and comfort, and that leaves you feeling disappointed and lonely. Those feelings are very normal; we all need care and support from others. I understand your pain and confusion.

If you return to the old pattern again, know that this is normal, and that you have the ability to find a pattern that suits you again.

Thank you for your suggestions. I’ll try using other ways of relating, observe other people’s behavior, and gradually change my own pattern. I understand that change takes time, but I believe I can do it.

That’s great! Believing in yourself is very important, and you’ve already taken the first step. I hope you find a pattern you like and let that pattern become your habit. If you run into difficulties along the way, remember you can come back anytime to talk and seek support.
Thank you for your support and encouragement! I’ll work on changing, and if I need to, I’ll come talk with you again.

Her personality is just way too slow. Should I keep this friendship going? In college I only have one friend I’m pretty close with, but her personality is really too slow, and she drags things out. She talks slowly too, and she’s very soft, very weak, has no opinions of her own, and has no patience. Lately we’ve had a lot of conflicts, because I feel like she can never do anything well, and she usually likes to complain. Every time I hear her voice, it’s slow and full of negative energy, and it gives me such a headache. But if I leave her, I’ll be on my own. I can hang out with my roommates, but everyone has their own fixed little group. I can spend time with them, but I can’t really fit in. I’m so torn. Lately, honestly, every second I spend with her feels painful.

After reading what you described, it sounds like you’ve had some differences come up in your friendship. Given that you’ve had depression before, I can really understand that you may be in a vulnerable state right now. From what you’ve described, it’s hard for you to accept your friend’s personality as it is now, and you feel she isn’t positive enough. It’s true that most people see friendship as being about sharing and companionship, and those positive factors are what motivate us to make friends. Personally, I think that apart from friendships connected by shared interests and shared goals, most friendships are actually quite fragile. Because most people are self-centered, and that’s normal.

Yes, I also understand that friends need to support each other, but now I’m gradually feeling like this friendship makes me feel really frustrated and in pain. I tried to change her personality, to make her more positive, but I realized I’m only torturing myself, and that makes me feel really conflicted inside.

Trying to change someone’s personality is very difficult, and she also has her own personality and way of doing things. Perhaps you could try to accept the parts of her that fall short, while also looking for other friends who are more positive. That way, you can have multiple friend circles and won’t have to rely on just her.
Actually, I’ve also thought about making other friends, but in college, everyone already has their own little groups. I’m afraid it’ll be really hard for me to fit into other people’s circles.

I understand your concern. But in college life, new friends often enter our circles, and there are also activities and clubs you can join. These can be good opportunities to make new friends. You can take the initiative to participate in some activities and share interests and hobbies with like-minded people, and gradually you’ll be able to fit into new circles.
I’ll try. But right now I’m really in pain because of this friendship. I’ve even had thoughts of suicide, and my mood is really terrible. What should I do?

I’m really concerned to hear that you’re having thoughts like this. Suicide is not a way to solve the problem. First, you need to know that this pain will not last forever; everyone has low points in life. Second, you can actively seek some psychological support, such as talking with a teacher or a counselor. They can offer more specific help and suggestions for what you’re going through.
I didn’t expect my problem to make me feel this much pain. I’ll try to learn to seek help. Thank you for your advice.
You’re welcome. You can come talk with me anytime. Remember to keep a positive mindset, and believe that you can overcome these difficulties and find your own happiness and joy.

Thank you for your support and encouragement. I’ll do my best to face this difficulty. It’s true, we can’t trap ourselves in an unhappy relationship. I’ll work on finding friendships that are more suitable for me.
That’s right. Trust in your courage and wisdom—you will definitely be able to find your own happiness and joy. Hang in there!
There’s this really uncomfortable feeling that stays with me, and I feel especially irritated?
Reading your question, I get the sense that when you were little, you actually weren’t very happy. Even though your aunt and grandmother were very good to you, you still couldn’t feel happy.
Yes. When I was little, I always had this depressed feeling. When my aunt and grandmother bought me shoes I didn’t like, I would scrape them on the ground, even though doing that felt awful too.

I understand. This feeling may be an expression of anger. Sometimes you feel irritated, especially when you hear the sound of your mom coming back, and it reminds you of how it felt to be separated from your mom and dad when you were little, right?

Yes. I feel like I have emotions toward my parents, because they were always working away from home, and I could only live with my grandmother and aunt. Even though they were very good to me, I wanted even more to be with my parents.

I see. You longed for your parents’ company and love, but you also understood that they went away to work for your family’s livelihood. You may have been suppressing that emotional need all along, which led to feelings of irritation and loneliness.
Yes. I’ve always felt I was very sensible and didn’t want to cause trouble for my grandmother and aunt, but inside I still felt very irritated. Can I try expressing my feelings to my parents?

Of course you can. You can tell your parents that when they weren’t by your side when you were little, you weren’t happy, and that you hoped they could be there with you. You can also express your resentment toward them, as well as your feelings of loneliness and helplessness, and that you hope to receive their support and help.
I understand. I’ll try to express my true feelings to my parents. Also, sometimes I criticize myself and think, my aunt and grandmother treated me so well, so why do I still feel irritated?

These are very normal emotions. Try not to be too hard on yourself. When you were little, you had many inner needs that weren’t met, and because you didn’t express them, the aggression turned inward toward yourself. When you feel depressed, it’s also because that aggression has turned inward. Accept your true state, and see the unmet needs inside you. This will help you face yourself better.
Thank you for your understanding and advice. I’ll try my best to accept my feelings and express my true feelings to my parents. This is a kind of healing for me.
You’re welcome. I hope my response can be helpful to you. I wish you peace and healing inside. If you need more help, feel free to come back and talk with me anytime.
My mother has a mental illness, and it’s affecting my life. What should I do?

Oh—after reading your description, because your mother isn’t cooperating with treatment, her uncontrolled behavior has affected your normal life, and you’re feeling very troubled. I can really understand how you feel. Based on what you described, first of all, you don’t know how to persuade your mother to actively accept treatment. Actually, this is something that needs to be handled by a professional doctor. I suggest you take her to a reputable tertiary hospital for treatment.

I really don’t know how to convince her to get treatment. She always thinks there’s nothing wrong with her and that she doesn’t need to take medication. I can’t do anything about it either. I feel like I’m trapped again.

I understand how helpless you feel. Some patients may have psychological resistance and be unwilling to accept treatment, and that really can be distressing. You can try having a deeper conversation with her, gently telling her about your worries and care, and try to help her open up so that she may be willing to accept treatment.
But I’ve already tried. Every time, she flatly refuses. I even feel powerless and frustrated, and I don’t know if I can still help her.

I understand how you’re feeling right now, but please don’t give up hope. Sometimes this takes time and patience. You can consider seeking help from a professional doctor, and let professionals face this problem together with you. Maybe they’ll have better ways to persuade your mother.
Mm, maybe I really do need help from professionals. But I’m still really worried that she’ll go and say all kinds of nonsense to my coworkers. I’m afraid my coworkers will become biased against me.

I understand your concern. In a situation like this, you can choose to be honest with your coworkers and tell them the real situation with your mother, so they can understand what you’re dealing with and where you feel caught in the middle. If your coworkers are genuine friends, they should be able to understand and support you. And as for those who become biased against you because of this, perhaps we don’t need to care too much about what they think.
I understand. I should face this problem bravely and not care too much about other people’s prejudice. Thank you for your support and advice.

You’re welcome. I’m very willing to offer you support and help. No matter what problems you run into, you can always come to me and talk. I hope your mother can accept treatment smoothly, and that your lives can gradually return to normal. Hang in there!
Thank you for your encouragement. I’ll work hard to face and solve this problem. I’m really grateful to have a supporter like you.

You’re welcome. I believe you can handle this problem that’s been troubling you. Remember, you’re not alone; I’m here by your side supporting you. I wish you and your family strength in getting through this difficult time.

Will showing my feelings on my face make me lose out? Do we need to control our real emotions? If people around us are always saying, “If your happiness and anger show on your face, you’ll lose out,” then how should we change? Should we consciously control it, or just let it happen naturally?
I saw your question. I’ll share some of my thoughts with you, and I hope they can be helpful. Should we show our emotions? That depends on the situation and what’s needed.
I understand. So we don’t necessarily have to completely control our emotions, right?

That’s right. Completely controlling your emotions may not be healthy, but it’s not necessarily about letting them out however you want either. If you want others to see your emotions, to notice that you’re unhappy and so on, then wearing your emotions on your face is, I think, okay.
So in what situations should I control my emotions?

Most of the time, it’s better not to suppress our emotions, like pretending to be very happy when you’re unhappy—how exhausting that is. But in the workplace, in some more specific situations, like when you’re in a work meeting, if you lose your temper “however you feel like it” or look obviously unhappy, that’s not so good. In moments like that, you do need to manage yourself well.
I feel like sometimes it’s hard to control my emotions. What should I do?

Yes, controlling emotions is definitely a challenge. But remember, you can learn skills for managing emotions. For example, deep breathing can help you calm down, or you can try shifting your attention to something that helps you feel calmer, such as listening to music or taking a walk.
Then if I have some emotions I need to express, but I don’t want them to be too obvious, what should I do?

Emotions do need to be expressed and communicated. For example, when you’re feeling emotional, if you show it on your face and wait for others to notice, they may not notice at all, and even if they do, it can be hard for them to guess what you’re thinking. Then your emotions may get even worse. It might be better to tell the other person directly: because of such-and-such, I’m feeling this way right now, and I need you to comfort me, help me talk it through, keep me company, and so on.
I understand. Thank you for your advice. I’ll try to better understand and express my emotions.

I’m very glad I could help. Remember not to be too hard on yourself. Expressing emotions takes time and practice. If you need any further help or someone to talk to, I’ll be here to support you. You’ve got this!

What should I do if I want to find the people in my memories to talk to, but I can’t accept Gestalt therapy? Hello teachers. After going through counseling for a while, I feel that the people in my memories are so precious. But most of them have already gone separate ways from me, or moved on with their own lives. I can no longer find them and say the things I want to say in my heart. But I can’t really accept Gestalt therapy (as I understand it, Gestalt therapy is talking to myself about my feelings?). What can I do?

It sounds like you’re someone who takes a lot of responsibility for your emotions and also really values relationships and loyalty. Looking at other people’s answers, I imagine you already have some understanding of the letter-writing approach.
Yes, I understand the letter-writing approach, but I’m hoping for more real-time communication and sharing.
I’d like to introduce another form of psychotherapy here that is still relatively niche. Some people call it drama therapy, some call it psychodrama, and in English it’s called Playback.
Drama therapy? Psychodrama? Could you explain more specifically how this method works?

Of course! Drama therapy is a way of addressing psychological issues through performance. The client tells a story from their own experience, a memory that is hard to let go of, or simply chooses an emotion that is troubling them, and the actors immediately reflect parts of the story back to the client through performance.
It sounds a bit like acting, but is it effective for working through my memories and emotions?

In a larger group, the client can also choose actors who fit their memories or feelings to perform the scenes. When we re-observe, feel, and experience memories that have been stored in our minds from the perspective of an audience member, or when the actors are able to capture, with precise empathy, details that even we ourselves hadn’t noticed, the feeling of being seen and heard can be very healing and also very powerful.
It sounds like a very special kind of experience. Through drama therapy, can I look at my memories and emotions from a new perspective?

Yes. Through drama therapy, you can try to observe and experience your memories and emotions from different angles, which can help you better understand and work through them. At the same time, when we’re able to separate ourselves from past relationships or memories, we can also say goodbye to them more fully.
It sounds like drama therapy could be very helpful for dealing with my past relationships and memories. I’ll consider trying this method. Thank you for your suggestion!

You’re welcome! I hope what I shared can be helpful to you. Lastly, when you asked this question, you were already on the path of preparing to say goodbye to the past. If you have any other questions, feel free to ask me anytime!

What is the psychological mechanism behind always going to the bathroom? Some kids like to squat on the toilet and sit there for half an hour at a time, and this happens every day, mainly so they can play on their phones. Has anyone else noticed the same thing?

Hello, I can understand your confusion. I’ve come across a similar situation before. When my nephew was in high school, he was like this too—every time he went to the bathroom, he would stay there for a long time, mainly because he liked playing on his phone. There may be a few reasons for this. First, children may usually be restricted from using their phones, but when they go to the bathroom, they can conveniently play for a while, so it feels a bit more justified. Parents may also not realize that the child is spending too long in the bathroom. Second, the phone itself is a form of entertainment for children, and time passes very quickly, so they end up staying there for a long time without realizing it. Third, the child may feel a lot of pressure from schoolwork, and going to the bathroom becomes a way to avoid that pressure; playing on the phone helps them relax. You can talk with the child about this, find out what they’re looking at on their phone, and listen to their thoughts, while making sure the communication is based on respect for the child. If the child is younger, appropriate guidance is needed. If the child is in adolescence, you need to be more mindful of your approach, so as not to trigger rebellious feelings. Overall, this issue itself is not serious, and parents don’t need to be overly nervous. You can offer moderate guidance. My nephew is in college now, and his family no longer interferes too much with his phone use, so this issue has not appeared again. I hope my thoughts are helpful to you. If you find them useful, please click “Helpful.” Thank you for your question.

Thank you very much for your answer. I have indeed noticed that the children at home spend a long time in the bathroom, sometimes even more than an hour. I understand now that this may be because they want to take the chance to play on their phones without being disturbed. I’ll try to talk with the children about this, understand their feelings and thoughts, and give appropriate guidance at the same time. Thank you for your advice and support.

You’re welcome. I’m glad I could help you. Communicating with the children is very important, and understanding their inner world can help you support them better. I hope you can build good communication and understanding with them and give them appropriate guidance. If you need further support or have other questions, feel free to ask me anytime. I wish you and the children at home all the best!

Thank you for your kind wishes! I’ll do my best to communicate with the children and guide them appropriately. If I have other questions, I’ll ask you again. Thank you again for your help and support! I wish you all the best!

You’re very welcome. I’ll always be here to help. If you have any questions or need further support, feel free to consult me anytime. I hope you and the children have a pleasant time together. Wishing you all the best!
Okay, I’ll remember that. If I need anything, I’ll reach out to you for help. Thank you again for your support and encouragement! Wishing you all the best!
Thank you very much for your kindness. I’ll always be here to support you. I wish you and your family all the best, and you can consult me anytime. Wishing you all the best!

Thank you very much for your care and your answer! Your advice is very helpful to me. I’ll try to communicate with the children, understand their feelings, and give appropriate guidance. Thank you again for your help! I wish you all the best!

You’re welcome. I’m just helping as much as I can. I hope the children can listen to what you say and work with you to find a solution. If you have other questions, feel free to consult me anytime. I wish you and your family all the best!

Thank you very much for your understanding and advice! I’ll do as you said and do my best to communicate with the children and give them appropriate guidance. If I have other questions, I’ll definitely ask you again. Thank you again for your help and support! Wishing you all the best!

I’m very glad I could help you! Remember, everything will get better as long as you work on it together. If any new issues come up or you need help, you can consult me anytime. I wish you and your family health, happiness, and all the best!

Hello, teachers. After a period of counseling, I feel that the people in my memories are so precious, but most of them have already gone their separate ways from me, or moved on with their own paths. I can no longer find them and say the things I want to say in my heart. But I can’t really accept Gestalt therapy (as I understand it, Gestalt therapy means talking to yourself about your feelings?). What can I do?

Gestalt therapy, as I personally understand it, simply put, is about doing what you want to do and accepting your original, true self. If you want to find those precious people in your memories and tell them what you want to say, then from the perspective of Gestalt therapy, that would mean going and doing that. I’m not sure what you mean here by “can no longer”—what specific aspects are you referring to?

Specifically, they have already lost contact with me, they don’t accept my contact information, or our relationship has already become distant, so I can’t find them, and I have no way to tell them my thoughts and feelings.

I understand the difficulty you’re facing. Although they can’t directly hear your voice, you can still try other ways of communicating with them. For example, you could choose to write letters to express what’s in your heart. Letter writing is an old yet warm way of communicating. It can help you express your emotions and build a connection with the people in your memories.
Writing letters sounds good, but I don’t know how to start. How should I write so that they can feel my sincerity and understand what I want to say?

Writing a letter doesn’t need to be too complicated. What matters more is your sincerity and emotional expression. You can first set aside a specific time for writing, so you can focus and let your thoughts and feelings flow onto the page. You don’t need to worry about grammar or vocabulary; just write freely. This process itself is a form of self-expression and emotional release.
Writing letters sounds a bit scary, because I’m not sure whether they’ll receive my letter, or whether they’ll write back. I’m afraid I’ll be disappointed.

I understand your concerns. The purpose of writing a letter is not entirely to get a response from the other person, but to release the emotions inside you by expressing your longing and feelings. Whether or not you receive a reply, the act of writing the letter itself can already become a form of emotional release and healing. You can also choose to send the letter to them. If you can’t get in touch with them, you can choose to keep the letter as a memento, or burn it, as a symbol of saying goodbye to the people in your memories.
I understand. Maybe this approach can help me release the emotions inside. But I’m still afraid of facing my own emotions and memories, and I don’t know how to handle them.

Facing your own emotions and memories is a journey that takes courage, but it is also an opportunity for self-growth and learning to accept yourself. In this process, you can seek help from a professional counselor. They can provide appropriate support and guidance to help you get through the difficult stages.
