Everyone has their own personality traits. Some people are good at being with others, and that makes them feel happy. But some people are more introverted and prefer thinking on their own. If you prefer being alone, I believe you can find your own strengths and make friends with people who also like being alone. Having two or three close friends who truly care about each other is already enough.
I don’t trust anyone. I’m extremely guarded, and I don’t want others to know me deeply. I feel like I automatically switch into a people-pleasing mode with no boundaries.

When interacting with others, everyone chooses different ways to show their value. However, being your true self is the best way. That way, you won’t feel exhausted, and the people who spend time with you won’t feel exhausted either. You don’t need to always consider other people’s feelings while ignoring your own. After all, the time we spend with many people is brief, and in each person’s own little world, everyone may end up in very different places.
Every time I show even a little emotion, like complaining or getting angry, I start to hate myself and blame myself. Then I begin to sink into feeling down about myself.

We are all human, and no one is perfect. Things have two sides, and our emotions are changeable too; it’s impossible to always stay in a high-spirited state. Only by accepting the imperfect side of yourself can you truly enjoy a fulfilling life. Life is dynamic. Allow your emotions to change, and keep a positive attitude inside. Even if your emotions shift a bit, it won’t affect your overall emotional state.
I want to know how to like myself a bit more, and how to feel more at ease when I’m with other people.

First, you need to understand yourself, know your personality traits, and not go against them. Second, when you’re with others, show your true self and allow yourself to be imperfect. Other people all have their own imperfections too, so why can’t you? Finally, lower your expectations of yourself. No one is perfect. I believe you can allow yourself to have emotional ups and downs and flaws. That way, you can become more whole and feel more at ease with yourself and with others. Hang in there!
I was very reluctant to marry my current husband. How can I move past the resentment?

You’re unhappy with your marriage now, and resentment keeps coming up. Even though you’ve been together for so many years, you still feel dissatisfied with your partner. Back when you married him, you were already a bit reluctant. I wonder, why did you choose him at that time?

I married him because he accepts everything about me, but I still feel very dissatisfied. He isn’t capable, and he’s short. He can’t provide me with support to fall back on. After all these years, I still just can’t get used to him.

I want to say that since you chose him at the time, there must have been something about him that attracted you, something that made you choose him even though you knew so many of his shortcomings and felt dissatisfied with him. But as the two of you have been together longer and longer, I wonder whether that quality that attracted you is still there. What I can sense now is only your reluctance about this marriage and your dissatisfaction with him.
That’s true. I now focus more on his shortcomings and ignore his strengths. Maybe I should take another look at why I chose him back then.

Exactly. You can think more about his strengths. Sometimes we keep focusing on what we didn’t get, and end up overlooking what we already have. From another angle, if we had chosen someone else back then, would we all necessarily be living better than we are now?
Maybe you’re right. I should cherish my current marriage and look at his strengths and good qualities more from a positive perspective.

Marriage also needs to be worked on. You can look at what you can do for your current life, and what you might be able to change. If there really is no way to change it, then you can consider whether this marriage still needs to exist.

I understand. I need to rethink and adjust my understanding of marriage and my attitude toward it. Maybe I can try to improve my quality of life, strengthen my ability to be independent, and face my current marriage with a more positive mindset.
Good. Your thinking is very positive. By improving your own abilities and quality of life, you can change how you see your marriage and manage this relationship better. I wish you good luck!
Thank you for your advice and encouragement. I’ll try to adjust my mindset and put more effort into the marriage. I wish you all the best!
You’re welcome. I believe you can overcome the difficulties and build a better marital relationship. If you need any further counseling, I’ll always be here to support you. Wishing you well!
What should I do if my sense of self-worth is extremely low, but I’m also way too guarded?

You clearly don’t dare to trust anyone, yet you also feel you need to be around people. You don’t allow yourself to show emotions like complaining or being angry, and you also can’t accept yourself acting like you’re trying to please others. These years must have been really hard for you. Still, I want to ask: do you believe that you can be liked by others?

Actually, my sense of my own worth is really low. I don’t trust anyone, and I’m very guarded. Because I feel like I’ll automatically go into a people-pleasing mode with no boundaries. Every time I show even a little emotion, like complaining or getting angry, there’s this voice in my head that keeps saying I hate myself and blaming myself, and then I start sinking into feeling down. How can I like myself a little more, and feel more at ease when I’m with people?

I understand how you feel. The reason you’re afraid of being around people may be that you’re worried you’ll automatically go into people-pleasing mode. But I want to ask: would you be willing to believe that you can be liked by others? Even though you may please others from time to time, and you may dislike yourself too, if that willingness to believe is there, it can help us step back within relationships and look for relationships that feel more comfortable and more trusting. At the same time, it can also make it easier to accept the parts of yourself that don’t feel good enough right now, and put your energy into things that can help you build your sense of worth.

I’ve never thought about believing that I can be liked by others, because I feel like I’m not worthy of being liked. I always feel like I don’t do things well enough, so how could I possibly be liked by others?

I understand that you have doubts about your sense of worth. But we need to understand that besides the sense of self-worth our family of origin gives us, we can also gain a sense of self-worth from providing value to others. When you subconsciously try to please others, in fact, that’s a way you’re trying to replenish your sense of worth. So, could you try to blame yourself a little less? The truth is, you’ve already been trying hard enough.
But I always feel like I’m not doing well enough, not trying hard enough. How can I change this dissatisfaction with myself?

In the process of building your self-identity, we can try to pay attention to the value and meaning you provide to others. Doing this can not only strengthen your confidence, but also help you find ways that feel satisfying to you. Of course, it’s important to let go of being overly demanding and critical of yourself, gradually accept your imperfections, and give yourself recognition and encouragement for your progress and effort.
Then how should I go about discovering the value and meaning I provide to others?

You can start by looking for opportunities in your relationships with family and friends, colleagues, or other people around you, and try to understand their needs and help them solve problems. When you notice that you’re helpful to others, you’ll gradually discover where your own value and meaning lie. At the same time, you also need to learn to seek help and support from others, and accept their praise and encouragement. This can help you build a more positive sense of self-identity.
It sounds like it might be a bit difficult, but I’m willing to give it a try. Thank you for your advice and support.

I’m glad I could offer you some help and support. Remember to give yourself some time and patience. Gradually developing a positive sense of self-identity is a process. If you have any difficulties or doubts, feel free to come back and talk with me anytime. You’ve already taken the first step. I’m rooting for you!

I'm 30. For nearly a year, I've always felt very tired, and sometimes I suddenly feel like crying. What's going on? I have insomnia. Once it gets to nighttime and I try to sleep, I start overthinking, and I can't control it. My boyfriend and I are long-distance, and we may be breaking up. I feel very lost.

Hi. If it's okay with you, I'd like to first give you a big hug, and I hope it can bring you some warmth and support. I'm not sure whether the tiredness you've been feeling this past year is related to what you mentioned, this relationship that may be about to end. If it is, then that really is something that can make a person feel very "tired." For most people, a relationship, whether it's "passionate" or "warm and tender," is supposed to be a beautiful and enjoyable process.

Thank you for the hug and for understanding. I feel like every time I think about the possibility of breaking up, I feel like I can't bear it. I'm worried that after losing him, I'll be in even more pain and feel even lonelier.

Your worry is very normal. Facing the pressure of a breakup can make someone feel like they can't bear it. In fact, for anyone, losing someone important brings pain and loneliness. But you need to believe that you have enough courage and ability to face this challenge. Maybe things feel very unclear right now, but as long as you can quiet your mind and sort through your thoughts and emotions, you can find a clearer attitude and direction for how to handle this relationship going forward.

I really don't know what to do. I love him a lot, but the distance makes communication difficult, and lately our relationship has been getting worse and worse. I'm worried this situation will make me suffer even more.

I can understand your confusion and pain. A long-distance relationship can indeed bring a lot of difficulties to a relationship. But don't forget that love needs both people to work together to maintain it. Since you still love him, you can try to communicate honestly with him about your worries and struggles. Maybe the two of you can find a way to solve the problem, or consider how to change the situation you're in right now.
I understand. I need to have a good talk with him. But even if we solve the communication problem, I'm still really worried about whether our relationship can get back on track.

I understand your worry. In fact, whether you break up or continue, it will require effort and determination from both you and him. If you can truly express your thoughts and feelings, and both of you are willing to put effort into this relationship, then there will be a greater chance for your relationship to get back on track. But try not to worry too much about the outcome. Whatever happens, you need to take good care of your emotions and mental health.

Thank you for your advice and support. I've decided to communicate with him honestly and see whether we can find a solution or reassess our relationship. At the same time, I'll also pay more attention to my mental health and not let myself become too exhausted and lost.

I'm glad to hear you've made that decision. Remember, communication is the first step toward solving problems, and paying attention to your mental health is just as important. If you need any help or want to talk again, feel free to come to me anytime. You are not alone. I'll always be here to support you.
Thank you for your support and encouragement. I will cherish this relationship, and I'll also take good care of myself. Thank you again for listening and for your advice!

You're very welcome. I'm glad to help you. No matter how things develop in the future, trust your choices and your efforts. I hope you and he can get through this difficult time and find the happiness that belongs to you both.
What should I do if my sense of self-worth is extremely low, and I’m also too guarded?

It seems like you’re only seeing the negative side and feeling that your sense of worth is low. But from another angle, you’re always considerate of others, thoughtful and sensitive, with a more introverted personality, and you’re good at looking inward for energy. This isn’t something that needs to be changed, or something that can be easily changed. What you need to do is go along with your own personality and accept yourself. That’s how you can live better, and truly develop yourself.

But sometimes I feel like my introverted personality keeps me from enjoying being with other people. I’m afraid of social interactions and feel very exhausted. I don’t have the courage to change, and I don’t know how to improve myself.

Being introverted isn’t wrong. Introverted people usually don’t like socializing that much. As you said, being around people makes you feel tired, and you need to be alone to recharge. So with this, I think you can go along with yourself. Since you don’t like being in crowds, don’t force yourself to socialize. Do things you genuinely enjoy, like reading, doing crafts, taking walks, and so on. Of course, sometimes socializing is unavoidable. People are social beings, and we need to interact with those around us to get better resources and survive better. So you can spend most of your time alone, and then give a small part of your time to interacting with others. That way, you can maintain your social relationships while also living in a relatively happy and comfortable way.
I understand. I can balance my time alone and my time socializing based on my own comfort level. That way I can protect myself better and not feel too much pressure.

Yes. You need to find a balance that works for you, one that meets your need for solitude while also taking into account the importance of socializing. Also, you mentioned that you’re worried about falling into a pattern of pleasing others without boundaries. In what kinds of situations does that tend to happen?

Usually when I’m building a close relationship with someone, I automatically think about the other person and keep trying to please them. But that makes me feel very tired, and I also feel like I’m lacking self-fulfillment.

I understand. In close relationships, you don’t want to make yourself feel too wronged, right? Actually, in a close relationship, it doesn’t have to be one person pleasing the other. You can look for a win-win pattern together, so that both of your needs can be met. For example, if your friend asks you to have hot pot, but spicy food doesn’t sit well with you, you can honestly tell your friend your situation and suggest choosing a suitable restaurant or dishes together. If your friend truly cares about you, they will understand your needs and make adjustments accordingly.
Yes, I should have more confidence in my own needs and don’t need to overly accommodate others. If others can’t accept my needs, then maybe they aren’t people who truly care about me.

Good. You’ve already realized this. What’s important is not to forget to have enough understanding and respect for yourself. You need to express your own needs, and also respect other people’s rights and needs. That’s how you can build healthy, balanced close relationships. What do you think is the key to liking yourself a bit more and feeling more at ease with other people?

I think the key is to improve my self-awareness and ability to accept myself, to accept my introverted personality, and to keep expressing my needs honestly when I’m with others. I also need to learn to let down my guard and trust others more.

You’re very right. Self-awareness and self-acceptance are important ways to strengthen your sense of self-worth. At the same time, learning to let down your guard and gradually build trust in others is also very important. This takes some time and effort, but I believe you can do it. Keep working at it and believe in yourself. You will definitely be able to like yourself a bit more and feel more at ease with other people.

How can he pull away so quickly? Is he being heartless or rational? We’re long-distance. Why did my boyfriend not reply to my messages from noon until the whole night, and when I said the next day that I felt sad and unhappy, he just said he felt helpless? (Because he was busy working overtime?) For the next two days, neither of us talked to the other. This has happened many times before over replying to messages, and it’s always like this.

Long-distance relationships can deepen how much you miss each other, but they also make communication harder. I can understand your worry and sadness. Maybe your boyfriend didn’t reply to your messages in time because he was busy with work. That doesn’t mean he’s heartless or rational. A lot of the time, our emotions can lead us to over-interpret the other person’s behavior. Communication and understanding between the two of you are key to resolving this issue.

That night I posted on Moments that I was “letting go,” and then I found he had deleted the QQ status where he said he wanted me to walk with him. I just hoped he would come and comfort me on his own, but in the end he left even faster than I did. Then I posted another Moment, crying my eyes out, with his favorite photo of us together, saying it was the final goodbye. He still didn’t contact me first. Why, when I said I was crying, didn’t he feel bad for me?

I understand that you wanted comfort and care from him, but using Moments is not an effective way to communicate. Everyone expresses emotions and handles problems differently. Maybe he isn’t good at expressing himself, or he isn’t very clear on what kind of response you want from him. This doesn’t mean he doesn’t feel bad for you; he may just not have found a suitable way to express it. I’d suggest that you still communicate directly face to face, so you can both better understand each other’s real thoughts and feelings.

He just keeps not contacting me. How can he stay so calm? It’s not like I’m insisting on anything. Even if we’re separating, doesn’t it deserve him taking a little time to say something? Just because I said I wanted to let go, does he think there’s no relationship between us at all anymore?

Your feelings are understandable. But sometimes, when a person has a problem or is facing some difficulties, they may choose to be alone for a while to deal with their emotions and the issue. This doesn’t mean he doesn’t care about you or is indifferent to your relationship. Everyone handles problems differently, and some people tend to solve things on their own. I think the two of you should sit down and have a good talk, and listen to his thoughts and feelings. That can help you better address the problems between you.

So whatever I do, whether I’m happy or sad, has nothing to do with him anymore? How can he pull away so quickly? Does he not have any feelings at all? Even if we were just ordinary friends, if you found out the other person was crying, you’d at least politely comfort them, right?

Feelings involve both people. Whether as partners or ordinary friends, everyone handles feelings differently. Maybe he hopes you can face your emotions independently, rather than completely relying on his comfort. This doesn’t mean he has no feelings for you; rather, he may hope you can become more independent and mature. He may think you need to handle your emotions yourself instead of relying on him to soothe you. I suggest you try giving each other some space, and also learn to face your own emotions independently. That will make your relationship healthier and more stable.
Last time, we were also on the verge of breaking up because of this. He didn’t contact me for five days, and in the end I was still the one who reached out to him first, and we barely kept it going.

I understand the effort you made before to maintain the relationship. But maintaining a healthy relationship requires effort and communication from both people. If you feel emotionally exhausted, I suggest that the two of you sit down again and have a good conversation, see whether your expectations and needs are aligned, and find a way to solve the problem. At the same time, you also need to learn to take care of your own emotions and needs. This is very important for the development of your relationship too.
Okay, thank you for your advice and for listening so patiently.

You’re welcome. I’m very willing to offer you help and support. Remember, communication and understanding are key to solving problems. I hope the two of you can find the way that suits you best and get through this difficult time together. If you have any other questions, feel free to come back and talk with me anytime.
I'm almost 60, and I really hate my mother's control. How can I break free from it?

You're almost 60, so your elderly mother must be at least in her 80s. Generally speaking, this is the time to care for her and fulfill your filial duty. But you haven't said why you're unwilling to take care of your elderly mother—is it only because she calls you every day asking you to look after her? We won't make moral judgments here. Perhaps you have your own difficulties.

When I was little, I felt my mother didn't treat me well. She was always criticizing me and was very strict. Also, my older brother has always been the one taking care of her, and I feel like I've been ignored.

You were not treated well by your mother when you were young, which led to negative feelings toward her, and that is understandable. And since your older brother has always taken care of your mother, you may feel somewhat neglected. However, throughout a person's life, there are many responsibilities we have to take on, and one of them is supporting our parents. Supporting one's parents is everyone's legal obligation, so we need to understand how difficult it was for your mother to raise her children.
I understand the legal obligation, but inside I really feel very weighed down. My mother feels far too intrusive to me, and I don't know what I should do.

Yes, I understand the sense of heaviness you feel inside. Older adults face many psychological and physical changes and challenges; they experience a sense of loss. Also, as they age, their physical health may decline, which can lead to mental and emotional issues, and their loneliness may increase as well. Although you feel your mother is very bothersome, please try to be a bit more tolerant and understand more of her current situation and needs.
I know my mother is in a difficult situation, but I also have my own life needs, and I'm afraid it will affect my quality of life. I really feel caught in the middle.

I understand your worries. Everyone has their own life needs. Still, in your mother's final days, being with her may be a way to ease the knots inside you. Perhaps through being there for her, you can reach reconciliation with your mother, and also with yourself. Please try to face your mother with understanding and care, and look for a point of balance, while also remembering to take good care of yourself.
Hearing you say that, I feel like I'm starting to see it more clearly. Maybe giving a little more can help my mother and me reconcile, and also make me feel more at ease.
Yes, giving a little more may bring unexpected changes. I hope you can find a way to reconcile with your mother, maintain a good state of mind, and take good care of both yourself and your mother.
Thank you for your advice and support. I'll do my best, and I hope I can find a point of balance.
You're welcome. I believe you will find the balance that works for you. Best of luck! If you have any other questions, feel free to reach out to me anytime.

I feel like mental health problems are all the result of thinking too much and doing too little? People who think less and do more are at most a bit physically tired, and after a good night’s sleep everything is fine. People who think too much have insomnia night after night, and the more they think, the more keyed up they get. Can’t we just do as much as we think about?

Ah—after reading what you wrote, it seems you’ve been having your own thoughts recently about mental health issues. I can really understand the confusion you’re feeling, since I’ve had similar thoughts too. Based on your description, “mental health problems are the result of thinking too much and doing too little,” I have a similar example: in primitive society, there were no mental illnesses; mental illness gradually appeared after social rules formed. Personally, I think this example is very similar to what you’re saying.
Yeah. I’m thinking maybe modern society has too many temptations and pressures, which makes it hard for us to focus on thinking and putting things into practice. Do you have any suggestions?

I can understand your concern. Modern society does bring people more choices and challenges. In response to this, I’d suggest you try some ways to reduce stress, such as setting aside some free time each day to relax. That could be reading, taking a walk, or listening to music. Also, if there are things you feel confused about, you could try talking with friends or family. They may be able to offer some new perspectives and suggestions.
Mm, I’ll try those methods. I also want to know, why is it that the more I think, the more keyed up I get, and I can’t calm down?

That’s a very good question. Sometimes when our thoughts are overly active, it can lead to emotional excitement. When you’re feeling emotionally stirred up, I’d suggest using deep breathing to help yourself relax. You could also try some meditation or relaxation training to help you stay calm. In addition, a regular routine and good sleep can also be very helpful for emotional stability.
Then how do you think I should change the way I think?

Everyone’s way of thinking has its own characteristics, so there isn’t one fixed way of changing that works for everyone. But I’d suggest you try some more positive ways of thinking, such as paying attention to your achievements and strengths, and learning to look at problems and face challenges from a positive perspective. Also, setting clear goals and plans can help you think and act in a more organized way.
I understand. I feel like the suggestions you gave me are very helpful. Thank you for patiently listening to my worries and giving me advice.

You’re welcome. I’m glad I could help. Remember, no matter what problems you run into, you can always come to me to talk and seek help. Don’t feel like you’re alone; we’re all supporting each other on the path of growth.
Thank you for your encouragement and support. I’ll work harder to face my mental health issues and look for the right ways to resolve them.
I’m very glad to hear that. I believe you’ll definitely be able to overcome the difficulties and get through this. Hang in there! I’ll always support you.

The situation may very well change, or stay the same. What should I do as I keep getting older? I want to press a pause button on aging, wait until I finish this exam, wait until I figure out who to choose—the matchmaking date or my classmate. If I keep getting older, I also have to handle things with them properly. Then this situation may very well change, or stay the same.
I’d like to repeat your question once more: as you get older, these issues all stay the same. Do you mean you’re afraid that your age is increasing, while your current life situation hasn’t changed?
Yes. I’m worried that getting older will have a bad impact on my life, but I also don’t know how to handle this situation.

You’ve repeated two issues, both about making choices. Maybe it feels hard to decide, or maybe you’re afraid of choosing wrong and having your efforts go to waste? But what I want to say is that life is made up of countless choices—some with far-reaching meaning, some as simple as the happiness of a cup of milk tea and the pressure of gaining weight, or bigger-seeming events like what major to choose and who to marry. Everyone’s life experiences are different, their choices are different, and their lives can also be very different.
I understand that everyone has different choices and experiences, but I still feel confused and pressured, and I don’t know how to face these choices.

Feeling confused and pressured is a normal emotional response. People often feel this way when facing important decisions. We need to first think about what kind of life you want. It doesn’t necessarily have to be earth-shattering change to count as success. A plain and simple life can also be peaceful, abundant, and calm. Have you ever thought about what it would be like to live a life where you strive, take risks, and have ambition?

I hope my life is full of energy, with achievements and challenges. But at the same time, I’m also worried that if I choose the classmate I’ve known for a long time, it may be more familiar and more comfortable, but would I miss out on other better opportunities?

Choice really is difficult, because we can’t have everything at the same time. But please remember, no matter how many choices the outside world gives us, the most important decision-making power is in your own hands. You can compare the pros and cons of choosing your classmate and choosing the matchmaking date, and see which one fits your expectations and ideals better.
That’s true. Choosing the person who better fits my expectations and ideals is the most important thing, but sometimes uncertainty and thoughts of regret still trouble me.

Uncertainty and regret are common feelings in life. But please remember, making a decision is about moving forward. No matter which direction you choose, it may bring some regret, but that is also part of growth. Even though there are some risks and doubts, only you can understand your own heart best. Trust that you will make the right choice.
Thank you for your encouragement and support. I feel more confident about my choice now. I’ll think it through carefully and make a decision that suits me.

I’m very glad to hear that you’re feeling more confident. Remember, no matter what you choose, you will grow and learn through the process. Trust yourself, trust your ability to make decisions, and I wish you a future life full of good things and success!
I'm 26, and every day I feel mentally tormented. Does this mean something is wrong with me psychologically?
It sounds like you're experiencing a lot of internal strain right now, to the point that you're using “tormented” to describe your state of mind. Is that right?
Yes. I feel like I'm in a painful state, and I don't know what to do.
I can understand how you're feeling right now. Can you tell me how long this has been going on, and what happened that made you start putting yourself down and not accepting yourself like this?
It's been over a year, roughly. Last year I changed jobs and went back to my hometown to work, but something unexpected happened, and now my career and income are both lower than before.

It seems that changing jobs became a turning point in your life. First, let's look at whether this counts as a psychological issue. Anyone can have psychological issues, and they can be part of a sub-healthy state, so don't be too anxious or worried about whether you have a psychological problem. We need to look at the urgency and severity of it. Have you noticed that a lot of your negative emotions come from negative evaluations of yourself?
Yes. I always feel like I'm terrible, that I can't do anything, that my emotional intelligence isn't high, and that I have no value.

This kind of negative evaluation may come from having overly high expectations of yourself and then feeling the gap. In the past, you could say you were the hope of your whole family. Now your expectations for yourself are in conflict with the expectations of people around you, which has led to a sense of loss. But over all these years, what have you gained?
Although I don't have a house or a car, I do have over a hundred thousand in savings. And my current salary is actually pretty good too; it's just a bit less than before.

These are all your gains and achievements—so many people your age would be jealous and envious of them! Maybe you can think about where the breakthrough point is in your career and personality, and whether you have the courage to break through your own limits and create a world of your own.
I really do hope I can have breakthroughs and make progress, but I always feel like I don't have the ability to make it happen, and I don't know how to plan my life or my career.

You can consider combining your life planning and career planning with your personality traits and professional strengths. Of course, we also need to take some practical limitations into account. All of the above is just my analysis, and I hope it can be helpful to you. Hang in there—I’ll always support you!

Why do I always think about pleasing other people? Actually, deep down I really don’t want to. Why do I always think about pleasing others? It feels awful. Actually, deep down I really don’t want to, but because of certain things, I feel like I have to please them.

I can see that you’re feeling troubled and upset because you’ve done things you really didn’t want to do inside. Sending you a big hug 🤗 Based on what you described, I’d like to understand one thing: when you say you please others, is it because you can’t control the urge to please them? Or is it because there are some external reasons that make you want to please them? Is it one of these reasons, or do both exist?
Actually, sometimes I feel like I can’t control myself. I always end up pleasing others without meaning to, wanting to get their approval and praise.

I understand. Your people-pleasing may come from wanting to gain other people’s approval and praise. In psychological terms, people like this are often called “people-pleasing personalities.” They sacrifice their own feelings and blindly try to please others. The distress and discomfort you mentioned before are related to this kind of personality.
So that’s what it is. Then how should I deal with this situation?

First, you can try to notice why you want to please others. Is it because deep down you lack a need for approval and love? Try to feel that little child inside who needs to be loved and recognized, and do some exercises in loving yourself.
Sorry, I accidentally interrupted you just now. What are the self-love exercises you mentioned like?

It’s okay. Self-love exercises can include giving yourself small rewards, paying attention to your own needs, relaxing your body and mind, developing your interests and hobbies, and so on. At the same time, you also need to be clear about your own boundaries and principles. It’s impossible to make everyone like you. You need to accept your abilities and limitations.
I understand. I’ve also realized that I have a problem with being too pleasing toward others. But sometimes I still can’t help pleasing them without meaning to. How can I solve that?

This kind of situation isn’t uncommon. When you notice that you’re starting to please others, first don’t blame yourself. Observe yourself: why do you want to please them like this? What need is behind it? Can these needs be met in other ways? When you learn to love yourself, the urge to please others will decrease. Also, at work, there may be some behaviors that involve pleasing others, but that’s out of the need to achieve a certain goal. So it’s important to distinguish which situation you’re in. Only when we understand the reasons behind it can we better solve the problem.
Thank you for your suggestions. I’ll try hard to love myself and stop sacrificing my own feelings just to please others. I really appreciate your support and understanding.

You’re welcome. I’ll always be here to support you. I hope you can be brave and be yourself, and in that way find true happiness and joy. Remember, you’re not living for other people; you’re living for yourself. You’ve got this!
My son is 14. He has an adolescent fetish and refuses to communicate. How can I help him?

I’ve carefully gone through what you described: your son is 14. When he was 13, you discovered that he was collecting women’s underwear, usually his mother’s. Recently, you found that he has been buying women’s underwear, stockings, and masturbation products online. You also found that he likes watching Japanese anime and likes Hatsune Miku figurines. What you’ve done so far is tell him he needs to overcome it, talk with him, and buy books about adolescent boys. Now you want to talk with him, but he refuses. Your concern is: how can you help your child?
That’s right. I’m very worried about his behavior. I’m worried this will have a negative impact on his growth and his future.

I can understand your worry. You’re a parent who cares very much about your child, and this kind of concern is very natural. First, we should try to understand the underlying causes of fetishism. It’s possible that his psychosexual development during adolescence has been inhibited, which could lead him to shift sexual interest onto objects. We need to understand whether there are other factors also influencing his behavior.

I really agree with your point. I wonder whether he might have witnessed intimate behavior between me and his father when he was a child. I’ve been thinking about whether that could have had a negative impact on him.

I understand your concern. Witnessing parents’ intimate behavior can indeed affect a child. So we can start with science-based sex education for adolescence, making sure he has accurate awareness and understanding of sexuality. This can serve as early preventive education. At the same time, we can also consider seeking help from a professional counselor to avoid this behavior continuing to develop.
Your suggestions sound very reasonable. But I’m not sure how to start a conversation with him. He has always refused to communicate with me.

This is a common issue. Many children close themselves off from their parents during adolescence. We can try using non-blaming language to communicate with him, express our care and support, and emphasize that we want to talk with him because we have his best interests at heart. Also, to help him feel more comfortable, we can choose a quiet, private setting for the conversation.
Okay, I’ll try using your suggestions to talk with him. But I’m still worried he’ll refuse, or that the conversation will become tense.

That’s understandable, but we need to leave him room to express himself and make sure the atmosphere of the conversation stays positive and calm. If he refuses or becomes tense, we can give him some time to calm down, and then express our care and support again. Try to stay calm and patient, and let him feel your love and understanding.
Okay, I’ll do my best to create a comfortable environment for him to talk, and guide the conversation with patience and love. Thank you so much for your suggestions and support!

You’re welcome. I believe you are a wonderful parent, and you’ve put a lot of effort into your child’s growth. Please remember, we’re always here to support you and to offer help and guidance whenever needed. I hope you’re able to resolve this smoothly and help your child get through this difficult situation.

I haven’t even done my own job well yet, and I’m supposed to share my coworkers’ work too? I’ve just started working in society at a private company, and I don’t really understand a lot of things. There are four people in one office now. Besides having to clean the boss’s office, I also have to take on some of the duties that belong to two other coworkers. I don’t know how to refuse, and I haven’t even done my own job well yet. What should I do?

I can really sense your frustration. You’re troubled because you don’t know how to deal with a lack of boundaries at work. Your basic situation is: you’ve just entered the workforce, you’re working at a private company, and you don’t have much experience with work or interpersonal norms. Besides cleaning the boss’s office, you also have to take on some miscellaneous tasks from two other people. You don’t know how to refuse, and this is troubling you. Analysis and suggestions:
Yes, I feel like this situation is really hard to handle. I feel like I don’t have enough ability yet to help them finish these tasks, but I also feel too embarrassed to refuse.

I understand your confusion. As someone who has just entered the workforce, it’s true that you’ll inevitably run into all kinds of challenges. Your coworkers may be asking for your help because they trust your abilities. You could try communicating with them openly and honestly, and express that your own work still needs more time and energy right now. If possible, you hope they can understand your situation.
But I’m afraid that if I say it like that, they’ll get the wrong idea that I’m not willing to help. After all, we’ve only just started working together.

I understand your concern. While expressing that you need more time and energy to complete your own work, you can also emphasize that you’re willing to help them as much as you’re able to. That way, they can feel your sincerity and friendliness, and it can help avoid giving them the wrong impression.
That suggestion sounds good. I’ll try to communicate with them. But I’m still really worried—what if they don’t understand me?

It’s normal to worry. But even if they don’t understand right away, try not to blame yourself too much or feel discouraged. You can explain and communicate patiently, and try to help them understand your situation. If they’re reasonable people, they should understand and respect your thoughts and feelings.
After hearing what you said, I feel much better. Thank you for your support and suggestions. I’ll go communicate with them as soon as I can, and I hope everything can be resolved smoothly.

You’re welcome. I’m very glad I could help. I believe you can handle this issue well and adapt to the work environment better. If you have any other issues, feel free to come back and talk with me anytime. Good luck!
Thank you for your encouragement and good wishes. I’ll work hard! If I have other issues in the future, I’ll come back to you for help. Thank you again for your support!
You’re welcome. I’ll always be here to support you. I wish you all the best, and I look forward to hearing good news from you! Remember, feel free to reach out to me anytime. You’ve got this!
I haven’t even done my own job well yet, and I’m supposed to take on my coworkers’ work too?

I really understand how you feel, and I can sense how troubled you are. In life, we all have times when we feel caught in the middle—our own work isn’t finished yet, but others hand us unrelated tasks. Inside, we really resist it, but we don’t know how to say no.

Yes. I’ve just entered the workforce and I’m at a private company, so I don’t really understand a lot of things yet. There are four people in our office now. Besides cleaning the boss’s office, I also have to share some of the work that belongs to the other two coworkers.

This is indeed a difficult situation. First, you need to clarify the scope of your responsibilities and your job duties. Try communicating with your supervisor to confirm what work you need to do well. That way, you can better distinguish what is your responsibility and what you can appropriately help your coworkers with.
But I still feel like it’s really hard to turn down their requests. I don’t want to offend them, and I don’t want them to have a problem with me.

I understand your concerns. You can choose a tactful way to decline and say directly to them, “I’m really sorry, but I haven’t finished my own work yet, and this is quite urgent, so I can’t help you right now. I can help you after I’m done.” As long as your own work is completed, you can help when you have the capacity. But if doing work that belongs to others delays your own work, then you’re being too unfair to yourself.
Mm, I understand. I’ll try this more tactful way of saying no. But what if my coworkers have a problem with me because I refused?

If your coworkers have a problem with you, you can communicate with your supervisor and explain your situation and difficulties. After all, you’ll still need to get along in the same office in the future, and mutual understanding is very important. I hope you can get out of this worry soon.
Thank you for your advice. I’ll try talking with my supervisor, and I’ll also be more firm about doing my own job well.
You’re welcome. I believe you can handle this issue well. Put your own work first, and I believe your coworkers and supervisor will understand your situation too. Good luck!
Thank you for your support and encouragement. I’ll handle this with a positive attitude. I wish you all the best too!
Thank you for your kind wishes. If you need any help, feel free to come to me and talk anytime. We’ve got this!
Severe depression. It feels like this time is different from before—like it’s actually really serious?

Oh—after reading what you described, it sounds like you’ve been feeling your depression getting worse lately, and you’re also facing difficulties in real life. I can really understand how exhausted you must feel, both physically and emotionally.

Yes, I really feel awful. Before, it was just severe depression and moderate anxiety, but now I’m pregnant, eight months along. But this is definitely not prenatal depression. I’m 19 this year, almost 20. My family is having financial difficulties, and I still have moderate depression myself. I’m overly sensitive, and I feel like I have a bit of social phobia too.

It sounds like you’re facing severe depression, moderate anxiety, and social phobia all at the same time. Having all of these together must be extremely painful for you. And you’re pregnant now, so if your mental state keeps getting worse, it could seriously affect both your health and the baby’s health. So your emotional state really needs to be taken seriously.
Yes, I’m really worried about how this will affect the baby. And I also feel a bit resistant toward the doctors I saw before, maybe because of their irresponsible attitude toward me.

I understand. Maybe you could try changing doctors and find one who has no connection with your family. That might help you feel less disappointed or dissatisfied. Maybe your expectations of the previous doctors were too high, so you were more easily affected by what they said and did.

Maybe. I really did have pretty high expectations of doctors. The stress during pregnancy has also made me more sensitive and anxious, and I’ve become especially concerned about the doctors’ attitudes.

I understand how you feel. Pregnancy itself is already a test of both physical and mental health, and on top of that, you’re feeling really awful right now, so you need extra care and support. Changing doctors may help you feel a bit more relaxed and avoid more anxiety.

Mm, yes. I’ll try changing doctors, and I hope I can find one who gives me a sense of safety. I also know I need to take steps in time to ease this situation, but I really feel so hopeless. What should I do?

It’s very normal to feel hopeless in a difficult situation like this, but it’s also important to believe that there are many ways to help you get through it. Besides finding a professional doctor who can provide appropriate treatment, you could also try talking to family and friends, or try some forms of emotional support, like relaxing your body and mind, doing some soothing activities, or finding ways to guide your emotions, such as listening to music or writing in a journal. These are small steps, but they can help ease the psychological pressure you’re under.
Mm, I’ll try. Thank you for your advice and encouragement. It really makes me feel a little bit of hope.

You’re welcome. I hope my suggestions can be helpful to you. In this process, remember that you’re not alone. You have family and friends supporting you, and there are also professional doctors who can help you get through this difficult situation. I believe you can make it through this hard time.

My child is five. After coming home from school, he just keeps watching TV. How can I talk to him so he’ll listen? When I’ve told him and he doesn’t listen, I really want to yell at him, or scare him by saying I’ll hit him, but I’ve never actually hit him. I always feel that hitting only treats the symptoms, not the root issue, and yelling at him isn’t good for him either. I want to help him become confident and self-disciplined, but sometimes I feel like I just can’t manage it.
Dear parent, I can understand how you’re feeling right now. You’re hoping your child can better control the amount of time he spends watching TV, is that right?
Yes. I don’t want him watching TV for long periods, but he just won’t listen. What should I do?

Your child is still young, so we can’t expect him to listen and be self-disciplined the way an adult would. This needs to be developed step by step. I’d like to ask, after your child comes home from school, does he have any other activities?
Other than eating and sleeping, he just watches TV.

I see. He’s very absorbed in TV, and that’s quite normal. Still, you can try setting a fixed TV-watching time for him, for example, one hour every evening. Then, during the rest of the time, do some fun interactive activities with him, like drawing together, playing games, reading, and so on. This can help him better control his TV time and gradually build his self-control.
That’s a good idea, and I’ve thought about it too, but he just won’t listen. Other kids might listen, but he just doesn’t.

What I want to say is that every child has their own personality and traits. You don’t need to expect your child to be the same as other children. As long as you can respect his individuality and interests, and give him enough understanding and support, gradually helping him develop self-awareness and self-control—that’s what matters most.
I understand. But if I need to take care of some things, I can’t stay with him, and then he’ll watch TV by himself.

I can understand how hard that is for you. But it’s important to maintain a balance—taking care of your child’s needs while also attending to your own responsibilities. You could look for help from relatives or friends and ask them to watch him, or arrange some other activities to fill his time, such as joining an interest class.
Thank you. I’ll try the methods you mentioned. I hope I can become a good parent and bring my child more happiness and growth.

You’re welcome. Being a good parent isn’t easy, and children also need time to grow. As long as you keep putting in the effort and maintain a positive mindset, you’ll definitely be able to help your child grow to be more capable and independent.
The confusion after starting senior year, the fear before the college entrance exam—could you give me some advice?

You’re seeing what the issue is. Don’t worry, we can work through it slowly together. During the college entrance exam period, you must be facing a lot of pressure. How long has it been since you really calmed down and spent time with yourself?

It really has been a long time since I took good care of myself. At this stage, parents, teachers, and classmates around me are all carrying their own anxiety. I really feel so sad, like none of it needs me.
I understand how you feel. At this age, we all sometimes feel denied, ignored, or even like we’re unnecessary. But please believe that you have value to this world and to other people.

Yes, I need to find my sense of self-worth again. Right now I’m always living a really exhausting life, I hardly have any friends, and I can only be alone by myself. I don’t know how to face the college entrance exam.

The college entrance exam is indeed a big challenge, but we can’t let it completely define our worth. We need to learn to adjust our emotions, not be easily affected by others, and not blindly try to prove ourselves. We need to calm down and think carefully about how to improve ourselves better.
You’re right, the college entrance exam is just one stage. But I feel like I don’t know how to study, and every exam hits me hard. I’m really lost.

Studying is a concrete skill. We can learn together how to manage time, how to rest, and even what to do during breaks. Also, we can keep improving our study methods by communicating with classmates and teachers. As long as we keep a positive mindset, I believe there will be progress.
Thank you for your encouragement and advice. I feel like I need more support and understanding, so I don’t feel lonely and helpless anymore. Do you have any other suggestions?

When you feel sad and lost, you can look for some positive, uplifting things to motivate yourself, like reading some inspirational books or watching some encouraging videos. Also, remember not to forget to talk with friends. Their support and encouragement can also help you get through this difficult time.
Mm, I’ll try to find some positive things to give myself some motivation. I’m really grateful for your company and help right now.
It’s okay. I’ll be with you throughout the college entrance exam. Believe in yourself—you can definitely overcome the difficulties and get good results. You’ve got this!
Thank you for your trust and encouragement. I’ll work hard!

Actually, I feel a lot of resistance inside. How can I improve my ability to follow through? There are so many things I want to do, and I keep thinking about them but don’t take action. How can I get myself to start? Actually, I feel a lot of resistance inside, but how can I get moving?

I can see that you have many things you want to do, but you haven’t been able to take action. Inside, you also feel a lot of resistance about not taking action, but you don’t know how to get moving. For internal motivation, you might reflect on and feel into whether the inner drive for these things may not be strong enough.

Yes, I easily fall into inertia. For some things, I don’t have an inner push, so I keep procrastinating. I often feel confused and disappointed, because I know these things are important to me, but I just can’t take the first step.

I understand your confusion and disappointment. When we’re facing many tasks, choosing the first step to take can feel stressful and uncertain. But please think about whether these things you want to do are very urgent and important. If you don’t do them, what consequences might there be?
Some things really are relatively urgent and important. If I don’t do them, I might miss opportunities or there could be negative effects.
I understand. Then aside from these urgent and important things, could you also break down the other things and find the parts of them that feel more appealing to you?
Maybe. Some things might just be things I feel I need to do, but they aren’t actually that important to me. I can try to prioritize these tasks and do the more important ones first.

That’s a very good idea. Prioritizing tasks and putting the most important things first can help you take action in a more focused way. Also, you can start with the things you feel more motivated to do, so you can give yourself some momentum for taking action.

That’s true. If I can start with the things I’m more motivated to do, then once I start taking action, it may be easier to keep going. I can also allow myself to start with small things and gradually build confidence and habits.

Very good! Gradually building confidence and habits really is important. For example, if you want to read a book, you can first ask yourself to read one page a day. That way the task is relatively simple, and you can start reading right away. Completing this small goal every day will gradually strengthen your confidence and help you feel more and more capable.
That sounds good. I should give it a try. I hope that through these methods, I can find motivation and start taking action.

I really hope you can find your inner motivation and get that momentum for action started. When you’re ready, move forward with determination. I believe you can make the changes you want. You’ve got this!
Thank you for your support and encouragement! I’ll do my best!
No matter what I do, I don’t feel confident. It affects me a lot—even when I’m walking, I don’t feel confident?
Deep down, you don’t want to compare yourself, but you can’t control it and keep comparing all the time. You also know that it’s because of the comparing that you’re feeling not confident enough now.
Yes, I know comparing makes me lose confidence, but I just can’t stop. I’m always comparing myself with others.
So do we need to stop comparing? Not necessarily. If you can’t stop, then maybe just keep comparing for now. But we can change the angle we compare from.
Change the angle of comparison—what do you mean?

Dear, have you noticed that when you compare, you’re using your own weaknesses to compare with other people’s strengths? Now try comparing your strengths with other people’s weaknesses instead. Since it’s all comparing anyway, what difference does it make how you compare?
Comparing like that seems a bit unrealistic. I do have some things about myself that aren’t good. If I overemphasize my strengths, can I still improve?

Actually, our focus right now is whether you have confidence. When we build up your self-confidence, you may actually compare less. Because by then, you’ll have more things you want to do for yourself, and they’ll take up most of your time, so the time you spend comparing yourself with others will naturally decrease.
I understand. Accept the part of me that compares, become confident little by little, and believe that I can get better.
Good. I’m glad you understand. Believe in yourself—you will definitely become better. May both of us live as the people we want to be.
Thank you for your encouragement and support. I’ll work on improving my confidence, stop over-comparing, and work toward my own goals.
That’s right. Believe in yourself—you can do it. Hang in there! I’m watching you get better and better!
Thank you for your good wishes. I’ll definitely keep going!

Lately I’ve been getting more and more scared. As long as I have a cut on my hand, I don’t dare go to public places. If I got infected myself, that would be one thing, but what worries me most is, what if I got infected and then passed it on to the children? Their lives would be ruined! Now I’m almost unable to work. As soon as I get ready to work, there’s a voice in my head reminding me to check whether I’ve had any cuts on my hands recently, whether I’ve touched public objects or facilities, whether I could get infected, and what I would do if I did. I’m asking for help: how can I give up the need for absolute safety, so I can still focus on work even with risk?
Hello, I can sense how anxious and frightened you are right now. Have you ever wondered whether you might be experiencing a psychological issue known as AIDS phobia?
Yes, I’ve heard of this issue too. But the fear I’m feeling right now is very real. I’m really afraid of getting infected with HIV and passing it on to the children.

I understand your worry, but no matter what it is, if it’s limiting your life and work, it needs to be addressed. You used to be happy and able to move forward actively, but now you’re unable to work because of fear. I’d like to know, what do you think caused you to suddenly start seeking an absolute sense of safety?
I think maybe it’s because I had paid sexual encounters many times in the past, and that made me lose confidence in my own sense of safety.

I understand. At that time, you may not have realized that your behavior could lead to negative consequences. But now, besides regret, what else can you do? I think you need to hold on to the present and learn to face your fear. Because only then can you move forward.
I understand what you mean, but I don’t know how to face the fear I have now. Can you give me some advice?

Of course. First, you need to recognize that your fear is a psychological issue. You need to become clearly aware of your emotional state and find the root behind those emotions. Second, you can ease your fear by talking with friends and family, seeking help from a mental health professional, and trying some stress-reducing activities, such as yoga and meditation.
Thank you for your advice. I’ll try to take action to ease my fear.

Good. Keep in mind that building an absolute sense of safety is impossible, because there is no absolute safety in the world. We should find ways to adapt to different environments, and learn and grow in that process. Believe in yourself; things will get better.
Thank you for your support and encouragement. I’ll keep working hard to overcome my fear.
You’re welcome. Remember, you’re not alone. When you need support and help, you can reach out at any time and share your feelings with people you trust.
Okay. I need to face my problems bravely. Thank you again for your advice and support.
My boyfriend is a good person, but he just isn’t very motivated and kind of just gets by?
I know you don’t have too many complaints about your boyfriend, but you feel a bit worried about the way he’s living.
Yes, he’s very content with the way things are, but I want him to have higher goals.
Because you hope he can become a “better” version of himself, you feel dissatisfied with the current situation.
Yes. I always feel like he isn’t motivated enough, his life feels a bit muddled, and because of that, our future feels uncertain too.
But everyone has different values. His definition of success may be different from ours.
I know, but I hope he can work hard and strive for our future.
You could talk with him and see what his plans and hopes for the future are.
Sometimes we end up arguing because of this.
When we notice we’re arguing, it means there are some things we haven’t understood, so we can try to find a calmer way to resolve the problem.
If he isn’t willing to make an effort, what should I do?
What you can do is, with love and support, do your best to help him discover his own direction for the future.
Thank you for your encouragement. I’ll try to have a good talk with him.
When my leader criticizes other people, I feel anxious. Why do I always feel a bit fearful and scared inside?
When your leader criticizes someone else, you feel nervous and anxious. At those moments, what thoughts come up for you? You can take a little time to think back carefully.
I think about my own abilities and work performance. I feel like maybe it’s because I’m worried my abilities aren’t good enough and I can’t meet my leader’s expectations.

Yes. If someone’s abilities don’t quite match the demands of their current work, then feeling anxious is normal, and feeling scared is normal too, because problems may come up at any time, and when they do, they need to be handled. Have you considered improving your abilities to deal with these challenges?

I didn’t really pay much attention to improving my abilities before. Maybe it was because I was afraid to face my own shortcomings. I’m aware of this now, but I still don’t know how to start improving myself.

Improving your abilities isn’t an easy thing, but it’s only through continuous learning and practice that you can become stronger. You could try to understand some processes for handling tasks, learn from other people’s successful experiences, and try to apply them to your own work.

That’s true. Right now I need more understanding and experience to deal with different work situations. But I’m also worried that the speed at which I improve won’t keep up with my leader’s demands, and then I won’t meet their expectations.

First, it’s important to understand that at work, you don’t need too much affirmation from others, and you don’t need to imagine too much praise or criticism from them either. Just do your own job well and do your best. Don’t worry too much about other people’s expectations; instead, focus on improving yourself and working toward progress.

You’re right. I should focus on my own growth and progress, rather than paying too much attention to other people’s expectations. But sometimes I’m still afraid of criticism and praise, and I don’t know how to handle them.

It’s very important to accept that there may be moments of criticism and praise. From criticism, you can draw lessons; praise can build confidence. You can try to accept both criticism and praise, and learn to take in the positive effects from them. Also, learn to take responsibility for what you do. Don’t be afraid of making mistakes; what matters is being able to correct them in time and make changes.
Thank you for your advice. I understand now. I’ll work hard to improve my abilities, accept criticism and praise, and be brave about taking responsibility.

I’m glad to hear your determination. I believe that as long as you keep working at it, you’ll be able to overcome the feelings of anxiety and fear, and become a more outstanding professional. You’ve got this!
Thank you for your support and encouragement. I’ll work even harder!
Whenever it’s a reunion holiday like Spring Festival or Mid-Autumn Festival, I feel especially awful and don’t want to go home?

The world has given you a lot of unkindness, but it can also give you many surprises and warmth. When we are always taking in pain and misfortune, we become more and more afraid, and less and less willing to hope for anything, so we may miss the chance to notice the gentleness and beauty in life.
Yes, I feel a kind of fear now when I think about going home. My relationships with my parents and my boyfriend both feel unstable, and that makes me feel very uneasy.

Hearing how painful this sense of instability in your family feels for you, I can really understand how you’re feeling. When you haven’t spent much time with your parents, it’s very normal not to feel a sense of belonging. Your boyfriend also hasn’t made a choice to stay with you all the way to marriage. These objective factors can make us feel more uneasy and anxious when we’re under pressure.
Yes, I’m preparing for the graduate school entrance exam, and the pressure really is intense. Maybe because I’ve been through too many unpleasant things, I feel resistant even about going home.

I understand that preparing for the graduate school entrance exam is putting a lot of pressure on you, and I feel for you. I hope you can keep working hard and become the excellent version of yourself. If your family of origin only brings back painful experiences, then please keep your distance from it.
But I feel very lonely, like I don’t have a place where my heart belongs or a warm harbor. During the New Year, it would feel really empty not to have family around.

I understand that, growing up with loneliness, it’s hard for you to accept this feeling. Lacking your family’s company can make the New Year feel very lonely. But if your family cannot make you feel happy, then keep your distance from them. You can stay in touch with close friends and let them care for you.
Thank you for your suggestions. I’ll try to stay in touch with my friends. Are there any other ways?

You could choose to read some books that bring comfort to the heart, to help soothe yourself inside. Also, you could choose to return to Kunming—the place that gave you so many painful experiences—and see it as a journey for your heart, getting to know the city again. You could find a relaxed job, keep yourself busy, and meet some lovely friends.
That sounds good. I can try going back to Kunming and getting to know the city again. I hope I can have some new understanding and emotional connections.

I’m very glad you’re willing to try going back to Kunming. I believe you will find new understanding and emotional connections. Remember, during the New Year, try to be among people, celebrate with everyone, and interact with others with a positive mindset. I believe everything will get better and better. Wishing you well! If you need to, you can message me privately anytime. I’ll always be here.
Thank you so much for your support and encouragement. I’ll try my best. If I need to, I’ll message you privately. Thank you!
His personality is like a child’s. He doesn’t worry about anything. Can he ever grow up?

Reading your description, it felt like I was seeing my own husband. There really are many immature men in life. What they tend to have in common is: ~~Aside from normal work and daily life, they spend the rest of their time in the virtual world.~~ They don’t take the initiative to face or solve problems in real life; as long as things are barely manageable, they don’t want to make changes. ~~Their ability to handle ordinary day-to-day matters is very low. If things aren’t explained clearly enough, mistakes happen. If you live with a man like this, a woman can become fussy, nagging and complaining every day. So does that mean divorce is the only way to solve the problem? Actually, they can change too, but we need to give him an opportunity.
Then may I ask how to give him an opportunity to change?

First, give him as much acceptance and tolerance as you can. When we first got married, facing such an immature husband, I was also very distressed and even often argued with him, but it had very little effect and at one point affected our relationship as a couple. Later, I changed myself and stopped speaking to him in an accusatory way. Slowly, I found that he was also changing little by little. Now, when he makes a mistake, I talk it over with him while laughing. It solves the problem, makes it lighter for both of us, and most importantly, he can actually take it in.
I’ll try, but sometimes it’s really hard to hold back from blaming him.

Yes, I understand how you feel. Don’t be too hard on yourself; after all, it takes time to build new habits. Also, you can try not to accuse him directly, but instead express your needs and expectations through a suitable way of communicating. That will make it easier for the other person to accept and understand.
Are there any other suggestions?

Don’t take on everything yourself. Give him chances to practice appropriately. Before, I was always afraid my husband would mess things up, so I hardly let him do anything. Later it got to the point where, when I asked him to pick up shoes from the shoe-cleaning shop, he didn’t even know to check whether they had been cleaned properly. And he wouldn’t accept being questioned, saying I had only told him to pick up the shoes and hadn’t told him to check them, which left me not knowing whether to laugh or cry. Later, I would consciously arrange some things for him to do and explain the specific details clearly. Lower your expectations; as long as he does what you’ve asked him to do, that’s enough.
Won’t that make him even lazier?

At the beginning, don’t be overly demanding. Even if he doesn’t do it well, don’t complain directly, because then he may be even less willing to do things in the future. Give appropriate praise and encouragement to increase his sense of accomplishment. You can give him some small goals and gradually guide him to develop good living habits and the ability to handle problems.
Thank you for your advice. I’ll try to change my own mindset and give him chances. I hope things can change.

You’re welcome. I believe your relationship can improve. While helping him change, also pay attention to your own emotions, focus on the positive side, and give each other more understanding and support. I wish you both can grow together and build a happy family.
Thank you for your blessing and encouragement. I’ll really work on it.
I feel like I care too much about what other people think, and I always overthink before I do anything.

I understand how you feel. As we grow up, everyone may go through a stage where they care more about other people’s evaluations. We all long for others’ approval, and we also care about how others see us. Right now, you feel you care too much and think too much. I’d like to share my understanding with you, and I hope it will be helpful.
Thank you for understanding. I want to know how to change this problem of caring so much about other people’s evaluations.

First, it’s important to know yourself clearly and accept yourself, so you won’t focus too much on others. When you really want to leave a good impression on others, have you thought about the deeper reason? Is it to get good evaluations from others, or to make more friends?
I think it’s to get good evaluations from others, and I also hope I can make more friends.

I understand. We can try to change this way of thinking. There are no perfect people in the world. When we are only trying to appear perfect, rather than actually being perfect, we become hesitant and afraid to try. When we care too much about others, we lose our freedom. How can we improve this? When we have a steady understanding of ourselves, clearly know what kind of person we are, and don’t change that understanding of ourselves just because of what others say about us, our emotions and personality become much more stable. When our inner sense of self is very fragile, we start overthinking, wondering whether others dislike us, fearing that we’ll fail, and so on. We can keep encouraging ourselves inside: we are good as we are, we don’t need to rely on others’ approval, and we are already enough. At the same time, we can allow ourselves to have shortcomings, recognize them, and be willing to improve. You’ve already recognized that you focus too much on others, and that means you’ve already taken the first step toward change.
I understand. I need to try to accept myself and not pursue others’ approval so much. Are there other ways to improve this problem?

Of course. There’s another very important point: changing how you think about failure and being afraid to try. You know, life is an experience. Whether you succeed or fail, it only adds to your experience and helps you grow. Imagine if someone tried not to do anything at all. They wouldn’t fail, that’s true, but would you want that kind of life? You surely know that failure is the mother of success, and nothing is guaranteed to succeed. Also, no one is paying that much attention to you, except your family and friends. Everyone is busy. No matter how big your failure or success is, other people won’t keep it in mind forever. So bravely do what you want to do. No matter what others think, as long as you’re clear about what you think, that’s enough.
I understand. I need to change how I see failure and bravely try. But I’m still a little scared, and I don’t know how to start.

Take it slowly, and practice step by step. Start with the smallest and simplest things, and build confidence little by little. For small things, think about how even if you fail, it’s not a big deal. Tell yourself that perfection never exists, and of course there are no flawless people. Also, be willing to take responsibility; this will help you make decisions more bravely. Try more and more, and you will definitely become more decisive. Another good method is to keep a success journal. Whenever you do something decisively, write it down. For the parts you don’t do well, tell yourself: I can’t do it that perfectly for now, and that’s okay. As long as we keep a mindset of continuous growth, we will definitely be better than we were yesterday.
Thank you for your advice and encouragement! I’ll slowly change myself and try bravely.
You’re welcome. I believe you can do it. I hope you can get through what’s troubling you soon. Best of luck!
Thank you for your good wishes. I’ll work hard! Thank you for your support!
I’m a 25-year-old man. I’ve never been in a relationship and I don’t have sexual urges. Am I asexual?

Regarding asexuality, I think this requires a certain process of assessment. We can’t look at the issue only from the surface of the situation. Next, we’ll explore the following aspects together with you, and try as much as possible to clear up your doubts. Is your current lack of interest in dating and sexual urges an ongoing state?
Yes, it’s been several years since I’ve had any urge to be in a relationship.

Okay, then let’s explore this a bit further. You can try to think back: after you entered puberty, did you ever experience sexual arousal? Or at times like waking up in the morning or going to sleep at night, have you had natural erections or other physiological responses?
Let me think... It seems like I haven’t had experiences like that, and I haven’t had any recently either.
In that case, we can consider ruling out some physical causes or abnormalities. I’d suggest you go to the hospital’s reproductive urology department for a physical examination as soon as possible.
Okay, I’ll go to the hospital for a checkup. But if there’s nothing wrong physically, and I’m still asexual, what should I do?

If the examination finds no physical cause, we can consider whether psychological factors may be involved. Try to think back on whether you’ve had any traumatic experiences related to “dating and sexual urges.” These experiences may have led to feelings such as fear or worry, and these emotions are often buried deep in the unconscious, making them hard to notice effectively. They may only show up through certain behaviors, such as resistance to dating and sexual behavior.
Actually, I did have a relationship before, but it ended in a breakup. Maybe it left some shadows.

Thank you for being honest. An experience like that could indeed have had an impact on you. Also, we can consider whether your current state is related to your parents pressuring you to get married. Before your parents started urging you to marry, were you already in this kind of state?
Mm, now that I think about it, before my parents pressured me to get married, I also wasn’t very interested in dating.

This information is all very valuable, and it helps us understand the deeper reasons behind your current state. I’d suggest that you consider seeking help from a professional counselor for counseling and exploration, to help you better uncover what’s going on inside, and understand your own needs and psychological state.
Thank you for your advice. I’ll consider seeking help from a professional counselor. Thank you for your support and encouragement.

You’re welcome. I’m very willing to offer you help and support. Remember, you’re not facing this issue alone. A professional counselor can give you more guidance and support. I hope you find a better solution soon and regain inner balance and confidence.
I'm 26, and every day feels like mental suffering. Does this mean something is wrong with me psychologically?
You're still young—what's the rush? Try not to be so anxious. Tell me, what exactly has been tormenting you?

I'm someone at the bottom of society, a 26-year-old woman. Family issues have been bothering me all along. I don't have a house or a car, only a little over 100,000 in savings. After graduating from junior college, I worked for 3 years, then changed jobs and went back to my hometown to work, but some unexpected things happened. I've been unemployed for two months now.
