Recently I started working at a local company in my hometown, but the work is different from what I did before. My monthly salary is only 7,000 yuan, and the benefits are 1,000 to 2,000 yuan less than before. I feel like I'm stuck in a state where I can't die, but I can't really afford to live either. I used to always imagine when I could make over 10,000 a month, when I could buy a home. But now, I look at the people around me and people on my social media doing better and better, living more and more exciting lives. I feel like I'm terrible, I can't do anything, my emotional intelligence isn't high either, and I feel completely worthless.

First of all, 26 is still young, so you don't need to be too hard on yourself. Secondly, you have over 100,000 in savings, and having worked for 3 years is actually a pretty good achievement. Many people when they're young live under other people's expectations and comparisons, but maybe you could try comparing yourself with your past self. That might lead to more helpful discoveries. A lot of people have lost their jobs this year, so being able to find a job that pays 7,000 yuan a month is actually already pretty good. I think you could consider getting into a relationship, to let your energy have an outlet, hahaha.
Can being in a relationship help me get out of this low mood and confusion?

A relationship is one way to gain a sense of happiness and fulfillment. It can make your mood better and also help you face life more positively. As you build an emotional connection with someone else, you'll have more support and care. A relationship can't solve every problem, but it can bring you new experiences and opportunities to grow, and help you move out of the difficult place you're in right now.
I know a relationship can't solve every problem, but I still haven't met the right person. Sometimes I feel especially lonely and helpless.

Loneliness and helplessness are emotions people often experience, but they don't mean you have to rely on someone else in order to feel happy. You can take part in more social activities, meet new friends, and expand your social circle. At the same time, it's also important to learn to think independently and face difficulties on your own. That way, you'll become stronger and more confident. When you become stronger inside, you'll be more able to handle life's challenges.

I want to get rid of this feeling I've always had, where I only feel my own value when other people need me or approve of me. But it's been troubling me all this time, and I can't pull myself out of it.

What you're feeling is very normal, and many people struggle with similar things. First, it's important to learn self-affirmation and realize that your value doesn't come from other people's approval, but from your inner confidence and efforts. You can take part in more activities you're interested in and do things that help you improve yourself. That way, you'll feel a greater sense of achievement and fulfillment. Also, you could seek counseling or attend some psychological guidance courses. Professional support and guidance can help you sort through your thoughts and find ways to solve the problem.

Yes, I think self-affirmation is very important. I'll try taking part in some activities to improve myself. At the same time, I'm also considering finding a counselor to help me better understand and face the distress inside me.

I'm very glad to hear about your decision. Seeking professional support is a very wise choice. A counselor will provide you with a safe space where you can talk to them about what's troubling you, and they will also give you professional advice and guidance. I believe that with their help, you'll be better able to discover your own potential and value, and move toward a more positive and happy life. Wishing you all the best!
Thank you for your support and encouragement. I'll do my best.
There are problems in my family. I like a girl, but I’m afraid of “repeating” the pain. What should I do?
Could you first tell me what problems you’re currently facing with your family?

I feel like I lacked care and emotional expression in my family environment growing up. Now I’ve met a girl, and I’m worried she might also lack care and emotional expression. I’m afraid this will bring up my past pain.

Your worry is understandable, but not everyone is affected in the same way by their upbringing. Try not to let past experiences make you dismiss future possibilities. We can start with the relationship as it is now, and slowly build trust and communication with each other.

But I’m worried there will be a lot of distance between us. I’ve always had this serious image, and I’m not very good at communicating with people. I don’t know whether we can get along well, and I also doubt whether I’m good enough for her.

Building a healthy relationship takes time and effort. First, you can try taking the initiative to talk with her, share your interests and hobbies, and try to understand her life and thoughts. Try not to doubt yourself too much. Everyone has their own worth, and you are also a unique and attractive person.
I’ve noticed that when I act normal, she seems to have some special reactions to me, more obvious than with other people. I don’t know why that is, and I feel a bit confused.

Communication and interaction between people often have different chemistry. Maybe she has a special liking for you, or feels that you’re different from other people—those are both possible. You can keep observing her reactions and gradually build deeper communication, so you can understand her better.
I want to know how to break through that suffocatingly serious air I have, and make myself more approachable and more able to fit in with the people around me.

Changing your demeanor takes time and effort, but it’s not impossible. You can work on developing a more relaxed and pleasant attitude, starting with small things. Try to become more open and cheerful, take part in more social activities, talk with others, and slowly adapt to and fit into the environment around you.

I’ve already started actively looking for things that make me happy, and I smile more naturally than before. But right now, I still don’t know whether I can build a relationship with her, or how to move this relationship forward.

Building a relationship takes effort from both people. You can express your care and friendliness toward her through small actions, such as taking the initiative to chat with her or inviting her to join activities together. Don’t rush for results. Take it slowly, and let your feelings for each other develop naturally.
Thank you for your advice and encouragement. I’ll try to relax and take the initiative to develop my relationship with her.
I’m glad I could help. Remember, confidence and a positive attitude are key to building a relationship. Good luck!

I always can’t stop thinking about accidents, or death? I feel uneasy and scared, and I keep uncontrollably thinking about frightening things. I can’t make myself not think about them. It feels really awful and scary.

For you right now, I’d like to give you a warm hug. Psychological research shows that extreme emotionality comes from long-term anger and low self-esteem. This anger is not hatred toward the outside world, but dissatisfaction with yourself, and a sense of powerlessness about controlling the world.
I realize that I lack a sense of control over myself and things, but I can’t get away from the anxiety and fear.

This huge inner disorder and loss of control is only one step away from affecting others and hurting yourself. We need to know that in life, things often don’t go as we wish. No one can have a smooth life with nothing they’re dissatisfied with, and everyone has times when they’re in a bad mood.
Yes, I understand that everyone has times when things don’t go their way, but I feel like my emotions being out of control has already affected my daily life.
This is a normal reaction. When we feel our emotions are out of control, we often feel the negative impact on our lives. But we can change this through emotion management.
Emotion management sounds really difficult. I don’t know where to start.

Emotion management does require certain skills and practice, but it isn’t impossible to learn. John Milton once said, “If a person can control their emotions, desires, and fears, then they are stronger than all. Emotions are the demons of the mind; if you don’t control them, they will devour you.”
That makes a lot of sense. So do you have any specific suggestions to help me manage my emotions?

First, we need to learn to recognize our own emotions. When we notice that we’re starting to feel anxious and afraid, we need to become aware of those feelings in time and try to listen to our inner voice. At the same time, we also need to learn to accept our emotions, and not feel ashamed or blame ourselves for having them.
I’ll try to accept my emotions, but I’m still not very clear on how to adjust them.

Everyone may regulate emotions differently, but you can try talking with others. Share your feelings with friends, family, or a counselor; they can offer you support and suggestions. In addition, you can also look for some relaxing activities, such as exercise, listening to music, meditation, and so on, to help you calm your emotions.
I’ll consider talking with others and trying some relaxing activities. Thank you for your suggestions. I feel a little more at ease now.

I’m glad my suggestions were helpful to you. Emotion management is a long-term process, but as long as we consciously take the first step and keep working at it, we can definitely gain better ability to control our emotions. Remember, rather than letting emotions control you, it’s better to adjust your mindset, let go of absolutist ideas, and try to look at people and things with an optimistic attitude, so that you can become the master of your emotions. I hope you can spend every day in happiness.

I have this really uncomfortable feeling that stays with me, and I feel especially irritated? Today I’m feeling a bit down. My mom came back from outside and was busy doing things around the house. Hearing those sounds made me feel really uncomfortable, just inexplicably annoyed! It reminded me of when I was little. Back then my mom and dad were away, and I stayed with my grandma and my aunt. Every time my aunt bought me shoes, or my grandpa bought me shoes, if I didn’t like them, I would rub them hard against the ground. Even if I didn’t, I felt really uncomfortable inside! I never expressed it! Every time I was unhappy, my aunt and grandma would try to help me solve my problems, but I still wasn’t happy, and I felt really irritated. One time I really wanted to ride my bike into a big well. This feeling has often stayed with me, especially during adolescence! There was also a period of time when I was in eighth grade. I just felt empty inside, like I had no support, and it felt especially awful. I was unhappy all day and just wanted to cry, and I didn’t know why. Now I have bipolar disorder, with mood and cognitive difficulties. I feel like it’s related to that time. My grandma and aunt were actually pretty good to me; they never hit me or scolded me. Could any counselor help explain this to me? Thank you.

Hello, I understand how you’re feeling right now. It seems that because your mom came back from outside and was busy around the house, your mood became very low. Is there a kind of loneliness inside? A feeling that you’re quite distant from your parents. I can really understand how you feel. “Every time I was unhappy, my aunt and grandma would try to help me solve my problems, but I still wasn’t happy, and I felt really irritated. One time I really wanted to ride my bike into a big well. This feeling has often stayed with me.” I can see that your family took quite good care of you, but it seems that no matter what they did, it was hard for you to feel happy. It seems like there is a part of your feelings that was missing inside. And you also mentioned above that when your parents came back, your emotions actually became worse. Doesn’t that also say something? Look, there were so many people in your family who were good to you, but they still couldn’t replace your parents.

Yes, my feelings toward my parents have always been complicated. When I was little, they weren’t by my side, and I always had a sense of loss inside. And I wasn’t very satisfied with the care my aunt and grandma gave me, so I feel they couldn’t take my parents’ place.

I understand how you feel now. Maybe you hoped your parents could be by your side and give you more care and companionship. When you were little, your parents weren’t with you, and children really long for their parents to be by their side. But because of real-life circumstances, your parents couldn’t give you that kind of companionship. Maybe in that moment you both loved and hated them. You loved them, but you shifted the hatred you felt toward them onto other family members, and even onto yourself. “Every time my aunt bought me shoes, or my grandpa bought me shoes, if I didn’t like them, I would rub them hard against the ground. Even if I didn’t, I felt really uncomfortable inside.” In that moment, did you long for the shoes to have been bought by your mom? Actually, when they bought you shoes, if they didn’t look good, you could have told them. Then next time they wouldn’t buy something you didn’t like. But you said that every time they bought them, you didn’t like them. Why didn’t you tell them? Or was it that you didn’t want anyone else to buy them, and just wanted your mom to buy them for you?

Yes, I really wished the shoes had been bought by my mom, but I was afraid they would feel disappointed and wouldn’t understand. I know I should have told them honestly, but I always feel like I can’t do it.

I understand. You’re worried about their reaction and afraid of disappointing them. That worry is understandable. But instead of letting yourself stay unhappy all the time, it might be better to try expressing your thoughts. Tell them how you feel and what you think; maybe they will understand you better. After all, they are your family, people who care about you.

I’ll try my best to tell them, but I’m also afraid they’ll think I’m hard to get along with. Maybe that’s also why I felt empty inside during adolescence. I feel like I lacked a kind of belief and warmth that could support me.

Yes, what you’re saying makes a lot of sense. During adolescence, with physical and psychological development, growth-related issues can easily come up. You felt empty inside, felt there wasn’t any belief to support you, and were very unhappy. Do you feel this was caused by a lack of warmth? Or is it that you yourself can’t find the reason either? Everything that happens has a reason. Back in eighth grade, was there something that made you very sad? Would you feel comfortable talking about it? I had a similar experience to yours when I was in middle school. I think we can talk about it more, and maybe it will be helpful to you. When a person feels awful, there is usually a reason. And when you feel awful, it must be because of some event or some person; there is always a background to it. You can think about what you are thinking each time you feel awful. And how do you view that situation? I hope the above can be helpful to you.

Thank you for your care and understanding. Actually, in eighth grade it was because the relationships in the class were quite complicated. I felt like I hadn’t found my place, and I didn’t get enough support. That led me to feel very sad and lonely.

I understand how you feel. Class relationships can indeed bring some challenges sometimes. But we shouldn’t rely completely on others for support and recognition. We can also find our place through our own efforts and a positive attitude. You can try communicating more with your classmates, taking part in some class activities, and making more friends. Maybe that will help you.

Thank you for your suggestions. I’ll try to change my attitude, take more initiative in communicating with my classmates, and work toward getting more support and recognition. If I feel unhappy again, can I still come talk to you?

Of course. I’d be very willing to talk with you. If you have anything that makes you unhappy or confused, you can come to me anytime to talk it through. Remember, you are not alone; we all care about you. I hope our conversation can be helpful to you.
Thank you very much for your support and encouragement. I will work hard to face my difficulties and actively seek help. Thank you for your time and patience!
You’re welcome. I’m truly very willing to help.
I don’t know whether I should give up pursuing an absolute sense of safety, and let myself be able to focus on work when facing risks.
I can understand your confusion. Actually, pursuing an absolute sense of safety isn’t possible, because we can’t completely isolate ourselves from the outside world.

I understand that, but in the past I was always very happy. I felt the world was good, and I was also very proactive at work. But in the past few years, I’ve made many business-related mistakes, and that has left me feeling lost about life.

This is indeed something that’s been troubling you. But everyone makes mistakes. What matters is being able to learn from them and keep looking ahead. You’ve already recognized the mistakes you made in the past, and that’s a positive step.

Yes. I used to be afraid of AIDS, but I had several tests and the results were all negative, so I started not to worry anymore. However, the emergence of the COVID pandemic gave me more time to learn about AIDS, and I found out that the virus can also be transmitted through wounds.

Learning this information may have made you feel fearful and anxious. Although the chance of AIDS being transmitted through wounds is very small, it is theoretically possible. But please remember, fear won’t solve the problem. We should look for the right ways to prevent and control the spread of disease.

I’m getting more and more scared now. As long as I have a wound on my hand, I don’t dare go to public places. What worries me most is that if I get infected with AIDS and then pass it on to my children, their lives would be over.

Your worry is understandable. After all, as parents, we all worry about our children’s future. But please remember that the routes of AIDS transmission are limited. As long as we take the right preventive measures and reduce the risk as much as possible, we can protect ourselves and our families.

I can barely work normally now. Every time I’m about to start working, there’s a voice in my head reminding me to check whether I’ve had any wounds on my hands recently, whether I’ve touched public objects or facilities, and I’m afraid I might get infected. Once I’m infected, I won’t know what to do.

This kind of anxiety can affect both work and life. Please first try to calm down and sort out your thoughts. We can’t let fear dominate our behavior and decisions. We need to learn to face fear and gradually overcome it; otherwise, it will keep interfering with our lives.

I reflected on it, and I feel I may be pursuing an absolute sense of safety too much. The reality is, there is no absolute sense of safety in this world. I want to know how I can give up this pursuit and let myself focus on work when facing risks.

Your understanding is very accurate. Giving up the pursuit of absolute safety is a key step. We can start with some small things and gradually adjust and change your mindset. For example, learning to view risks correctly, increasing personal awareness of prevention, and taking appropriate preventive measures.
I understand what you mean. I’ll also try to adjust my mindset and learn to face risks correctly. Thank you for your support and suggestions. I feel more confident now.

I’m glad I could offer you some help. You’ve already taken the first step, and next you’ll need to keep putting in steady effort. If you need more support and guidance, feel free to come back and talk with me anytime. We’ll work together—hang in there and overcome these difficulties!
Every time I'm with my partner, we don't really have anything to say?

I completely understand how you feel. This kind of situation can really be troubling. First, I want to say that you're not alone; this is a very common issue. Every couple faces this kind of difficulty.
Yes, I know it's a common issue too, but it really bothers me. When we're together, we're always quiet and don't talk much. It feels like we don't know what to say.
First, I'd like to ask: when you're together, does it feel awkward? Or are you hoping to have deeper conversations?
A little awkward. Neither of us knows what to talk about, and it feels really boring.

I understand. Every couple has their own way of being together, and it doesn't have to be the same as other couples. Some couples like things lively, and some like things quiet. Maybe you're the kind of couple who enjoys being silent together.
But I still hope we can communicate more. After all, we're in a relationship.

Of course, communication is very important. You could try finding some topics to guide the conversation, like asking him if anything new has happened recently, or sharing your own thoughts and feelings.
I understand. Maybe I can take the initiative to start conversations, try to find some shared interests, or make some fun plans together.
Right, those are all good approaches. At the same time, it's also important to give each other some space and not force every conversation to have lots of topics.
That's true. I should learn to respect the other person's personality and needs. Thank you for your suggestions. I feel much better.
You're welcome. I'm glad I could help. Remember, every couple has a different way of being together. The key is to find what works for you and enjoy each other's company.
Mm, I'll try. Thank you again for your support and encouragement.
You're welcome. I'm always here to support you. I hope you're happy and well. If you have any other concerns, feel free to come back and talk with me anytime.

I hate him so much, but I can’t help contacting him. Should I get divorced? My husband and I were high school classmates. We’ve known each other for more than ten years. When we were dating as students, I felt like he could tolerate my bad temper without limit. If I hit him or cursed at him, he could accept it, so I mistakenly thought he had a really good temper. In the two years we lived together before getting married, he also hit me twice. One time, he came home late after drinking, and I got angry. I slapped him first, and he got furious and slapped me back. The second time, I was in a bad mood and picked a fight. In front of our friends, he hit me again. But we still got married. During my postpartum confinement, I was annoyed that he didn’t do anything, so I kicked him, and he slapped me in front of my mom. The day before yesterday, because he came home late and keeps lying to me, and my parents were helping me take care of the child, I was afraid of waking them up. I told him not to pull me back to our room to sleep, that I wanted to sleep with the child. He wouldn’t listen, so I called his mother. Then he got furious and kicked the door like crazy. After my parents came out, somehow he got into a fight with my dad. My dad was in the hospital for two months this year and is still recovering. We called the police, but no case was filed. He was detained for one night and then released, and he didn’t come home either. I hate him so much, but I can’t help contacting him. I really need someone to comfort me and hold me.

After reading what you described, I can sense the hurt between you and your husband caused by your conflicts, as well as the conflict inside you. First, I want to give you a warm hug, and I hope it can bring you some comfort and support. I want to tell you that right now, you are not facing all of this alone.
Thank you for your hug and understanding. I really feel so helpless, and I don’t know how to deal with this.

I understand that you feel helpless and confused. These feelings are very normal when facing complicated marital issues. First, I think you should consider your own safety and health. Violence absolutely cannot be tolerated. Being hit and hurt in a marriage is unacceptable, no matter the reason. You have the right to protect yourself and to cut ties with violence.
I know what you’re saying is right, but sometimes I feel like he still has good sides. I don’t know whether he can change.

I understand your mixed feelings about him. When you’re with someone who has violent tendencies, there can indeed be feelings that are hard to let go of. But please remember, people can change, but only if they are willing to and take action. However, this issue is beyond what you can handle alone. If you’re willing, I suggest you seek professional counseling support and explore with a professional whether you should continue this relationship and how to protect yourself.
Hearing you say that, I do think it makes sense. I’ll consider seeking help from professional counseling. But I’m still afraid of the difficulties and pain I might face after divorce.

Divorce is a major decision, and it may bring some difficulties and pain. But your happiness and safety come first. A professional counselor can help you work through the emotions and challenges during the divorce process, and provide practical advice and support. Remember, you are not alone in this fight. You have family and friends you can rely on, and they will continue to support you.
Thank you for your encouragement and advice. I will seriously consider seeking professional help. But I’m still torn, and I’m worried about the impact divorce would have on the child.

When it comes to the child, I understand your worries. Divorce may have some negative effects on children, but what matters is creating a healthy, stable, and balanced environment for them to grow up in. If you can protect yourself and talk with child professionals about how to help your child adapt to this change and reduce their stress and hurt, they will have a better chance to develop well. At the same time, remember that you are your child’s role model. It is very important to show them positive and healthy relationships.
You’re right. I can’t ignore my child’s needs and interests. What I need to do is create a stable and safe environment for them, even if that means I have to face the uncertainty of divorce.

You really are an amazing mother. Your determination and the care you have for your child truly make me admire you. As your child grows, your perseverance and selfless love will be their support and strength. At the same time, please remember that you don’t need to face the uncertainty of divorce alone. A professional counselor can help you work through problems during this process and provide support and guidance.
Thank you for all your encouragement and support. I feel more determined now and more confident about facing the future.

I’m very glad I could help you and see you becoming stronger. Please remember, no matter what difficulties and challenges you encounter in this process, you will never be alone. You have the support of professionals and the people around you. You deserve a happy, safe, and healthy life. Hang in there!
When it comes to pornography, how can I firmly say no?
The fact that you’re facing this issue means you’ve become aware of the negative impact this behavior has on you, and that’s a very good start. You can refuse pornography in the following ways.

I was young and didn’t know any better. I got addicted to the online world, and in the face of all kinds of temptations, I neglected the rest of my life. I fell into this sticky state every day and couldn’t pull myself out.

I understand the difficulty you’re in. The online world does have many temptations, especially for young people. You can try some methods to help yourself get out of this state. For example, set up website filters to limit your access to pornographic content.
But even if I want to leave the internet, it’s hard, because when my mother was working away from home, the internet was what kept me company.

I understand that because of your family situation, it’s hard for you to get free from the pull of the internet. But you can try to actively find other interests or hobbies to fill your time, such as reading, writing, or exercising. This can shift your dependence on the internet and also enrich your life.
Sometimes I impulsively satisfy my sexual urges, but afterward I feel very painful regret.

This kind of impulsive behavior may be a sign that some suppressed emotion inside you is seeking release. You can try to find other, more positive ways to regulate your emotions, such as exercise, meditation, or seeking social support. This can reduce the likelihood of these urges arising.
I feel like my soul is very dirty, and I often regret what I’ve done.

It’s understandable to feel like something inside you is dirty, but try not to blame yourself too much. We all make mistakes. What matters is learning from them and seeking change. The fact that you can recognize that you need to change is a very good start. If you feel it’s hard to handle these emotions and behaviors on your own, professional counseling may bring you more help.
I want to change myself, but I don’t know where to start.

Change is a gradual process. First, you need to recognize your problem and have the determination to change, and you’ve already done that. Next, you can consider seeking professional counseling. A counselor can help you analyze the root of the problem and offer practical solutions. At the same time, you can also share your struggles with friends or family around you and seek their support and understanding.
Thank you for your support and advice. I feel like I now have some direction and confidence to change myself.

You’re welcome. I’m very glad I could help you. Please remember that on the path of change, you are not alone. There are people who are willing to support you, including me. Keep going, and I believe you can definitely get through this and find a healthier, more positive way of life. I wish you well!
Why is it that when I encounter attacks or hurt, my first reaction is to act like nothing happened?
Having this awareness is already a really good start, I think. The next step is to see whether you want to make some adjustments.
But I feel like I have no backbone. Why can’t I get angry and fight back?

It may be because something inside you is afraid of conflict or unexpected situations, so you suppress your emotions. Past experiences may be affecting your attitude now. Did elders ever teach you that conflict is bad, and that being good-tempered, tolerant, and kind to others is what’s good... things like that?
Yes, I was taught that way when I was little.
Then it’s very possible that this is what has made it hard for you to protect yourself, and has left you feeling unsafe.
Then what should I do?

If you want to change the current situation, you can try learning to express yourself. For example, you could write a mood journal, or try quiet meditation, going back to the moment of the event and feeling what the real emotions are behind your numbness. If something similar happens next time, what could you do?
These methods seem like they could help me.
Yes. Because you now have this awareness and understanding, you can slowly begin to change.
But I feel like it’s really difficult.

That’s very normal. You can find people close to you to practice with, such as talking loudly with friends or letting out your feelings with family. You can also find a professional for counseling and treatment.
Thank you for your suggestions. I’ll try them.
You’re welcome. This is my responsibility. Remember not to give up on the path of change. Slowly, you’ll find yourself becoming braver and more confident.
I'm 28, and I have severe depression and moderate anxiety. What should I do?
It sounds like a setback in your relationship has triggered your anxiety, and because of that you're in a lot of pain. Is that right?
Yes. I feel extremely hurt and hopeless, and I don't know how to cope.

I'm wondering how you determined that you have depression and anxiety. Was it diagnosed by an authoritative institution? Or was it a conclusion you came to yourself after looking up your symptoms online?
I did go to the hospital to see a doctor, and the doctor diagnosed me with depression and anxiety.
Then you've already taken the right step by seeking professional input, and that's a very important step. Could you tell me what happened in your relationship?

I feel like I didn't do anything wrong. He promised me things, but my boyfriend didn't follow through. Now he's avoiding me and doesn't take the initiative to message me. If I message him, he still replies, but when I ask him, he says he doesn't want to move forward and wants to keep things the way they are now. It makes me feel really awful.
It sounds like your boyfriend's behavior has brought you a lot of psychological pressure. Could the way you two interact be related to your current anxiety and depression?
Maybe it is. I've become very sensitive and easily anxious. Every time he doesn't reply to my messages, I start to worry.

I understand that your emotions are fluctuating a lot right now. But it's important to know that those emotional ups and downs don't depend entirely on his behavior. A large part of your state and emotions depends on your own thoughts and the way you handle things.
Yes, I've realized that too, but it's still really hard for me to control my emotions. I feel very confused and don't know how to solve it.

Yes, learning to manage emotions takes some time and practice. I suggest you try some ways to relax and regulate your emotions, such as breathing exercises, meditation, or finding some hobbies to help shift your attention. These can help you regain a sense of inner calm. Also, if you feel it's hard to deal with your emotional struggles on your own, you could consider seeking help from a professional counselor. They can help you build suitable strategies for managing your emotions.
Thank you for your suggestions. I'll try these methods and hope they can ease my depression and anxiety. I feel this counseling session has been very helpful. Thank you for your support.

You're welcome. I'm glad I could help. Remember, you're not alone, and there are many people willing to support you. If you have any other questions or need further help, feel free to come back and talk with me anytime. I hope you can get through this difficult time soon and find joy in life again.

If I just study hard in this honest, rigid way, can studying really bring me the life I want? I’m a junior in college now. My grades were always really good in high school, but I messed up the college entrance exam. Now I’m at a non-Double First Class university, though it’s actually quite strong. My grades in college are also okay, and I’m planning to apply for a master’s program in the UK. But recently I’ve started feeling lost. I’m in science and engineering, and honestly, if you really take university studies seriously, it’s exhausting, and it’s also really boring. Lately I’ve started envying the lives of a few friends from my hometown. Their grades weren’t good; some are even at vocational colleges, and some are at first-tier universities but the kind that are Chinese-foreign joint programs, you know what I mean. But their lives feel so rich... At night, if there’s nothing to do, they go to bars; in the afternoon they play mahjong. But it’s not like they’re just drifting through life. They actually get to meet a lot of people, their social circles are really broad, their parents have decent financial conditions, and they all have pretty high emotional intelligence. So I feel like their future development probably won’t be too bad. And I’m the kind of person who just studies obediently, exhausted every day. My life isn’t that colorful, and I don’t meet that many people. I feel like my current life state is pretty unsatisfactory. Actually, I had this feeling back in high school too, but at the time I had the belief that I could get into my ideal university, so I was still very motivated. But now when I think about it, even if I go study in the UK and come back, if my life is still this boring, then it feels meaningless...

#Honestly, if you really take university studies seriously, it’s exhausting, and it’s also really boring. Lately I’ve started envying the lives of a few friends from my hometown. Their grades weren’t good; some are even at vocational colleges, and some are at first-tier universities but the kind that are Chinese-foreign joint programs, you know what I mean. But their lives feel so rich... At night, if there’s nothing to do, they go to bars; in the afternoon they play mahjong. But it’s not like they’re just drifting through life. They actually get to meet a lot of people, their social circles are really broad, their parents have decent financial conditions, and they all have pretty high emotional intelligence. So I feel like their future development probably won’t be too bad.#
Actually, I’m a junior now, and I’ve already drawn some conclusions from the facts I’ve seen. Maybe the way I’m looking at things is too one-sided.
Can studying really bring me the life I want?
Yes, I want to know whether studying can help me achieve the life I want, but can I be sure now that my thoughts won’t change?
You’re a junior now, and some of the conclusions you’ve reached based on what you’ve seen are a bit too hasty. From the conclusions you’ve analyzed, your perspective is too narrow.
Lately I’ve started envying the lives of a few friends from my hometown.

I can understand your mindset. Let’s add some more dimensions to what you’ve described and look at parts you may not have seen. You envy their lives, so when you’re on break, do you have a chance to experience their way of life?
When I go home, I can indeed experience their lives a bit, but I don’t know much about their lives.

The “countryside” and the “university” environment you’re in now are completely different worlds. When you described it, it seems like you overlooked the fact that these two “environments” are completely different. When the environment is different, the “people” it shapes are also different. That includes their thinking, behavior, values, and way of life—there can be big differences. Have you experienced these differences?
To be honest, I don’t spend much time at home. It’s mainly gatherings and meals, so I haven’t experienced it very deeply.

You may go back during Chinese New Year, but you probably don’t stay for very long, right? The main activities also tend to be eating, drinking, and getting together, so you probably don’t have much deep experience of what daily life is actually like. For example, you can start by comparing the job situation in the city where your university is with that in the countryside. For example, when you interact with “people,” pay attention to what they talk about. And also their daily lives.
You’re right. I really haven’t tried to understand their lives more, and I also haven’t paid attention to comparisons in these areas.

For example, with these friends you envy, take a look at where their way of life comes from. When you go back, you can talk with them about it. For example, compare the differences in education resources, medical resources, and eldercare resources between the city you’re in and the countryside. For example, if you want to find a “partner,” compare what differences there would be in the “partners” available in those two places. When you compare the two places across more dimensions, then look at the “opportunities” you currently have—if they wanted to get those opportunities, you could try helping them find the “paths.” If they wanted to obtain the “opportunities” you have now, where would the road be? Conversely, if you wanted to live their “life,” what would you need to do in order to have it? Of course, the premise is that after understanding it, you still want to live in the countryside. By comparing things from these more multidimensional perspectives, you may be able to find the answer to your question. Through this comparison, you can also see where the “real gap” between China’s cities and villages shows up. These comparisons also don’t yet take into account that after you graduate in your senior year and come back from studying in the UK, you may have more “opportunities” and choices. If you have any thoughts after making a more multidimensional comparison, you can leave a comment or message me privately.
What should a left-behind child in my neighborhood do if they’re being bullied at school?
First, you need to know that you’re not alone. Many people have faced problems like this. You shouldn’t feel ashamed or helpless because of the bullying.
But my parents aren’t home, and I don’t dare tell the teacher. I’m worried that if I tell the teacher, the people bullying me will bully me even more.

I can understand your worry, but telling a teacher is necessary. Teachers need to know that something like this is happening at school so they can take steps to protect you and other students. You can choose a teacher you trust, or the principal, and tell them what you’ve been going through.
But I feel so helpless. I’m afraid more people will bully me. I’m afraid this problem won’t get solved.

I understand your worry and fear. In this process, it’s important to be patient and keep going, and to believe that the problem will eventually be resolved. At the same time, you’re not alone. You can find people who support you, like teachers, family members, or friends. Talk to them about what’s troubling you; they can help you.
But I feel like I’m being bullied because I don’t have the ability to protect myself. I feel very helpless and inferior.

Don’t blame yourself. Being bullied is not your fault. Everyone faces challenges as they grow up; it’s part of growing. What’s important is rebuilding your confidence and self-esteem, and believing that you can overcome difficulties.
But I don’t know how to rebuild my confidence.

Rebuilding confidence is a gradual process. You can try taking some positive steps, like joining activities you’re good at and showing your strengths. You can also seek counseling; a professional counselor can help you find ways to rebuild your confidence.
If I tell the teacher and the people bullying me stop, how should I face them?

If the people bullying you stop, that’s a good development. But remember, you don’t have to accept their apology because of that, and don’t easily forgive people who have hurt you. You should stay alert, and if they bully you again, be brave and seek help from your teachers and parents.
Thank you for your advice. I’ll do my best to face this problem.
I believe you can get through this difficult time. Remember, you’re not alone. We’ll be with you and support you. Hang in there!
I feel really inferior, like I’m not good enough. I always feel like I’ve let my parents down. What should I do?

Don’t worry, okay? Let’s think through some ways together. I noticed you said you always feel like you’re not good enough, and you also feel very inferior in front of your husband. When you say you feel you’re not good enough, what part of yourself are you looking at?

I feel I’m not good enough because my family’s financial situation is poor, and I haven’t been able to give my parents a better life. And they have very high expectations of me. I feel like no matter how well I do, I can’t meet their expectations.

Hearing you say that, the pressure from your parents’ expectations really does seem to make you feel very inferior. But please believe that you’ve already done very well. Your grades used to be pretty good, and you were also pretty good at drawing. These are all your strengths, and they show that you’ve worked hard and that you have talent. Even if your family’s financial situation isn’t good, you can keep working hard in the future and improve your life.

But I’ve always felt my parents are unfair to me. They never came to see me when I got married, and they didn’t come when my child was born either, but they often ask me to buy things for my natal family. I feel really useless and inferior.

You don’t just “feel” that way—be more confident and take out the word “feel.” At the very least, they haven’t shown basic understanding and respect for what you’ve given. They’ve gotten used to your giving. My suggestion: have you ever talked to your parents about this? After all, the child who cries gets the candy, and parents are also being parents for the first time in their lives. They can make mistakes too. What you need to do is first try to make them realize their mistakes. You can try refusing a few times when they ask you to buy things for your natal family, to show your stance. Then, at the right time, when they’re angry or dissatisfied, say out all of your dissatisfaction too.
Maybe I’ve never expressed it clearly, and I haven’t given them a chance to know how I feel. I’ll try talking with them and help them understand what I’ve given and what I hope for.
Good. I want to emphasize again: manage your emotions well, and express your thoughts and feelings calmly. If you hope to receive their understanding and respect, you need to express it clearly.
I understand. I’ll try to communicate with them and let them know how I feel. But I’m still worried about my feelings of inferiority. What should I do?

It’s okay; this takes time. When you long for care, you need to express it. Maybe your parents also haven’t realized this. You need to let them know. As for what to do when you feel inferior, even if you’ve become aware of these strengths, you may still not be able to get rid of the feeling of inferiority right away. This takes time. Become stronger, read more, and improve your inner qualities. I recommend the book Little Women. It covers girls’ experiences in love, family relationships, marriage, and other areas, and it may give you some insight.
Thank you for your suggestions. I’ll read this book. Also, I have another question: how can I overcome my inferiority and become a bit more confident?

Overcoming inferiority needs to start with accepting yourself. Accept both your flaws and your strengths, and don’t be too hard on yourself. At the same time, learn to make changes in yourself, such as changing a bad temper or changing unhelpful ways of communicating. Start with some of your own attitudes and work on improving yourself. Learning to accept yourself is a process, so be patient. We can take it slowly. As long as you put in the effort, things will definitely get better and better.
Thank you for your encouragement and support. I’ll work on accepting myself and try to start by changing myself. I believe I can do better.
Great! Believe in yourself—you can definitely do it. You’ve got this! If you need any help or want to talk again, feel free to come to me anytime. I’ll always support you.
Whenever it’s a reunion holiday like Spring Festival or Mid-Autumn Festival, I feel especially awful. I don’t want to go home?
I really understand how you feel. These reunion holidays can bring back unpleasant memories for you. Could you tell me more about your situation?

I’m 24 this year. I worked for three years, and now I’m preparing for the graduate school entrance exam. I have a boyfriend I’ve been with for four years, but he’s preparing for a PhD exam and doesn’t plan to marry me.

It sounds like you’re facing quite a lot of pressure—work, the graduate school exam, your relationship. These are all things you have to deal with. Are you feeling somewhat uncertain about your boyfriend’s choice?

Yes. I’m not sure where our future is, or where I belong. I was a left-behind child growing up. My dad left home to work away when I was in my second year of high school, then came back to Kunming when I was a junior in college and divorced my mom. Both of them said the other had cheated. I’m not sure which one it was, because I spent very little time with them and don’t really know them.

Your family background has had an impact on your growth, and your parents’ divorce has left you facing a sense of uncertainty. All of that is understandable. Have you had experiences of going home for the New Year before?

The day before Spring Festival in 2017, after I had an argument with my mom, I stopped going back to Kunming for the New Year or other holidays. The few times I did go back weren’t very pleasant either. The days I spent with my mom were almost all arguments.

It sounds like you have some resistance to going home for the New Year, because your past experiences have left you with not very good feelings about family. This kind of psychological pressure can lead to feeling down and unsettled. So what do you feel is the reason for going home?

Maybe it’s because when I go back, I don’t feel like I belong anywhere. My family is relatively poor, and I grew up with my grandmother. But now my grandmother is old and lives with my uncle because my dad cheated, and I don’t want to go find her. My dad doesn’t have a house either. As soon as I think of my mom, my mind fills with scenes of her insulting me. It’s really painful, and I don’t know what to do.

Hearing about what you’ve been through, I can understand your pain and confusion. First, I suggest you look within yourself for a home that belongs to you. Your family of origin is not perfect, and you didn’t receive your parents’ care and love growing up. Their divorce has made you feel even less of a sense of belonging in a family. Now that you’re grown up, you can learn to take care of yourself and make up for those missing parts. Although this is very hard, we have to accept reality and think about what we ourselves can do to face a painful reality. If going back to Kunming makes you feel bad, you can choose not to go back for now and keep yourself away from those triggers. As you slowly become stronger inside, you may find a way to get along with your parents.

What you said makes a lot of sense. I should learn to care for myself, and at the same time get to know my family of origin again. But right now, all I remember are the scenes of my mom insulting me, and I don’t know how to look at these experiences from another perspective.

You can try to interpret the scenes of your mother insulting you from a different angle. I’m not sure if you’ve heard of the program Hear Her? There’s a character in it who grew up in a single-parent family, and her mother is very controlling. She also went through a lot of pain, and even went very far away to study in order to stay away from her mother. When we don’t get the love we want, we can learn to care for ourselves. Many people say they care about themselves, but actually it isn’t easy. We can try to treat ourselves with kindness, care for ourselves the way we would care for our best friend, listen to our inner feelings, understand what needs of ours have not been met, and at the same time not be too demanding of ourselves. With our parents, although they also have their bad sides, we can try to understand things from their perspective—for example, understanding the hurt divorce caused your mother, and recognizing that as a mother, she also has her limitations. She hasn’t yet learned how to love you. When we let go inside, we also grow.

I understand. I can try to learn to let go of the pain from the past, and get to know and care for myself again. At the same time, I also need to understand my parents’ mistakes and accept their humanity. I’ll work on becoming psychologically stronger.

Very good. Letting go of past pain, learning to move toward healing again, and caring for yourself—this process takes time. As you gradually grow and become stronger, you will also have a better life. I hope you can heal your trauma little by little and have the happy life you hope for. Wishing you well!
I care too much about what other people think, and I always overthink things before I do them.
I see what you’re struggling with, and I understand that you want to make a change. Let’s think together about how you might change this.

I’ll give you a few examples first. For example, when competing for some important positions, I can actually clearly see that the people running for them are going in with a very strong sense of purpose, or you could say a very utilitarian mindset. I feel pretty turned off by that, so I’m also afraid that if I do it that way, other people will see me like that too, so I don’t want to go for it.

I understand. You’re worried that your image might be affected. Actually, a lot of the time, the decisions we make because we care about our image don’t really mean much to other people. Unless something is extremely unusual, draws attention, is worth becoming something they talk about, or affects their interests, people won’t keep paying attention to it or caring about it.
But I’m really worried that other people will see me fail. I guess I have this mindset that if I don’t try, I won’t fail.

This is a kind of self-protective mindset, because failure may make you feel embarrassed or not accepted. But it’s important to know that everyone experiences failure. It’s part of growing. By accepting failure, we can understand ourselves better, improve ourselves, and achieve greater success.
I understand. But I’m like this when I interact with people too. I’m afraid they’ll feel like I’m approaching them with an agenda. A lot of the time I’m especially passive, and I think way too much.

You’re afraid of being misunderstood or rejected by others, and that’s very normal. But it’s important to know that interacting with others doesn’t require thinking too much about what they think. We need to learn to relax, express our thoughts and feelings honestly, and build sincere connections with others, without worrying too much about their judgments and reactions.
My girlfriend says that sometimes I’m like a girl, indecisive when I do things and overthinking too much. Now I’m gradually starting to feel that way too.

Everyone has their own unique personality and way of doing things. There’s no such thing as a specifically male or female way of acting. What’s important is that you believe in yourself, and believe in your ability to do things and make sound decisions. Don’t worry too much about other people’s judgments. Do what you believe is right.
I really want to change my personality and become the kind of guy who seems more outgoing, confident, direct, and decisive.

Changing your personality takes time and effort, but that doesn’t mean there’s something wrong with your personality now. Everyone has their own traits and strengths. If you feel your personality doesn’t fit certain situations, you can slowly adjust and improve it. Try participating in more social activities, build your confidence, and believe that you can adapt to different situations and make the right decisions.
Thank you for your suggestions. I understand. I’ll try to start from my own perspective, notice what I truly want, and work hard to make it happen.

I’m glad to hear that you’re willing to try to change and accept yourself. Remember, everyone has their own unique qualities, and you don’t need to care too much about other people’s judgments. Trust your own choices and decisions, and be brave in doing what you believe is right. I wish you success!
Why do I always think about pleasing other people? Deep down, I really don’t want to.
Why do you always think about pleasing other people? Can you tell me what feels confusing about it?
I feel like every time I meet other people, I can sense that reluctance inside me, but because of certain things, I have to go and please them.
I understand how you feel. Can you tell me about some of the things that make you feel you have to please others?
For example, some promotion opportunities at work, or in social situations where I need to cooperate with people. I’m afraid that if I don’t please others, it will affect me.
Are you worried that your relationships with others will be affected? Sometimes this kind of worry makes sense, but we can also explore how to handle this situation.
Yes, I’m afraid of disrupting the harmony in my relationships, but deep down I really, really don’t want to.

I understand. Pleasing others can have a few reasons. First, you may care about other people’s feelings, and that comes from goodwill. Second, you may be afraid of the other person’s disapproval, which could lead to an awkward atmosphere. Third, you may believe that only by pleasing others can you maintain harmony in your relationships. Fourth, you may feel that you need something from others and are afraid of being rejected. These are all understandable.
You’re very right. I really am worried about these things.

If deep down you really don’t want to please others, then being yourself is still the most important thing. Sometimes, your true self can earn more respect. If there is more sincerity, genuineness, and wholeheartedness between friends, then others can feel your warmth. Maybe that is the most harmonious and most relaxed kind of relationship. What do you think?
I think what you said makes a lot of sense. Maybe I should express myself more authentically, instead of catering to other people’s expectations.
Yes, that’s a good way to think about it. Try to let go of expectations about others and show your true self. At the same time, learn to respect your own feelings, and don’t always cater to others.
Thank you for your support and suggestions. I’ll try my best to do that.
I’m glad I could help you. If you have any difficulties in this process or need further support, you can always come talk to me. Let’s get through this process of growth together.
I feel like I’m suffering mentally every day. Does that mean there’s something wrong with me psychologically?
I can feel the anxiety and suffering inside you. Sending you a big hug 🤗

Thank you. Over the past two months of being unemployed at home, I keep feeling like I’m terrible, like I don’t know how to do anything, my emotional intelligence isn’t high either, and I feel like I have no value.

The feelings you’re describing are very normal. Many people feel this way when they’re unemployed or going through things that haven’t gone well. You can first spend some time getting to know yourself, finding your strengths and what you’re good at. That can help you look at yourself again and feel more confident about facing the future.
But I’m always comparing myself with others. Seeing the people around me living better and better makes me feel worse and worse about myself.

Human beings naturally tend to compare themselves with others, but comparing yourself to others can be a negative behavior, because it can make you feel even more incapable and discouraged. Actually, what people post on WeChat Moments isn’t necessarily real. So reducing comparison and finding your own value and strengths can help you feel more confident and have more strength to face the future. This is also one approach and method we use in counseling.
But my life feels like it has hit a low point, and it’s really hard for me to accept this gap.

On the journey of life, ups and downs and changes are very normal. Sometimes there may be only a fine line between success and failure. The most important thing isn’t other people, but how you think about it. While reducing comparison, you can also learn to accept yourself, keep improving your professional skills and broaden your perspective on development, and do better in pursuing and achieving your goals. These are all ways we can support mental health, build confidence, and increase a sense of self-worth.
Something unexpected happened to me a while ago. Now the pay at my job is 1,000 to 2,000 yuan less than before, and I feel like the halo I used to have has completely disappeared.

You may need to give yourself a little time first and allow yourself to transition. You can also think about your career development plan and look at what advantages and strengths you have, then apply those strengths to your work and life. This can help you feel a stronger sense of value. At the same time, you might also consider consulting some professional career development experts. They can provide more detailed and professional guidance and suggestions.
I’ve been trying so hard to get rid of this feeling that “I can only feel my own value when I’m needed or recognized by others,” but I’ve been struggling with it the whole time.

This is a very common feeling, and we need to give ourselves some time to slowly accept it and learn from it. You can think about this: where do you feel your value and meaning lie? What gives you the greatest sense of achievement? The answers to these questions may not be easy to find, but as long as we keep trying and learning, we can better understand and know ourselves, and find our sense of belonging and where our value lies.
Thank you for your help and suggestions. I think I need some time to digest this information, and I’ll also actively take action to improve myself.

I’m very glad I could help you, and thank you for your trust and courage. I believe you will be able to get through this psychological difficulty and find inner balance and confidence. If you have any needs or worries, please feel free to contact me anytime. I wish you happiness and joy.
I'm 26, and every day I feel like I'm suffering mentally. Does this mean there's something wrong with me psychologically?

People at the bottom of society, no house, no car, with over a hundred thousand in savings. It sounds like you have hopes for yourself to be more secure and fulfilled. You've been struggling with this for a long time. You don't want to live just waiting for other people's approval, and at the same time, you've also held on for a long time because of this.

Yes, I'm really confused. Slowly watching the people around me, people on my social media, living better and better, more and more exciting lives. I feel like I'm terrible, like I can't do anything, my emotional intelligence isn't high, and I have no value.

Are all the people around you really living such exciting lives, or is it that what they show on social media looks good? Do you really know nothing at all, not even a little? I believe the answer is no. In our interactions, I can see the hopes behind your anxiety, the things you care about behind your discouragement, and the wish to be understood and the sharp eye behind your envy and jealousy. You are also someone who shines in other people's eyes. Hang in there.

Thank you for your encouragement, but I feel like the glory I had before is already gone. I used to be the hope of the whole family, but now I've become the worst one. Every day is suffering. I don't know what I'm doing. I have no desire for life. The person who used to be so full of ambition has now become useless. I want to escape this life, but I can't get away.

How did you achieve that past glory? Who was there supporting you at that time? Even though every day has been painful, you've still held on for a year. It seems like you're bravely trying to live alongside these negative emotions. Everyone has low points, but you are not useless. Maybe you just need to find your inner motivation and direction again.

I used to be the pride of my whole family, and back then my relatives all thought highly of me too. But now I feel like I've lost my goals and motivation to strive, and I feel like I have no value in this society. I'm really lost right now, and I don't know what I should do.

Losing goals and motivation is a normal stage of life. Whether someone is at the bottom of society or in another social class, they may experience this feeling. You are not alone. Many people are like you, on the road to exploring new goals and meaning. You could try talking and communicating more with others, listening to their stories and experiences. Maybe that can spark the passion and motivation inside you.
What has always troubled me is that I can only feel my own value when I am needed or recognized by others. I feel really bothered by this, because these emotions have been tormenting me all along.

You've been caught in these emotions for a long time, and it may be time to try changing the way you think. Your value does not depend on other people's recognition of you; it should come from your own acceptance of yourself and affirmation of your worth. Everyone has their own uniqueness and potential. As long as you can believe in yourself and recognize your own achievements and value, you can free yourself from the distress of these emotions.
I really hope I can change the way I think, but I still haven't found a way to do it. I feel like I'm in a dead end and can't get out.

Changing the way you think doesn't happen overnight; it takes time and effort. You've already been bravely trying for a long time, which shows that you have a strong desire to change. Maybe you can try some ways to build yourself up psychologically and regulate your emotions, such as seeking professional psychological support, or helping yourself better understand and adjust your emotions through reading, writing, exercise, and so on.

Thank you for your advice and encouragement. I'll try some methods to change the way I think and adjust my emotions. I hope I can get out of this difficult situation and find my inner peace and confidence again.

I'm very glad I could help you. Believe in yourself, and believe that you can get through this difficult situation. If you ever need help or want to talk, remember you can reach out to me anytime. I believe you can find inner peace and confidence. Wishing you the best of luck!

Obsessive-compulsive disorder—I always feel like I can’t do anything right. How can I regulate my emotions? I’m 23. After graduating, I came to Beijing by myself for work. I’ve been working as a flight attendant for over two years. Ever since I can remember, I’ve lived with my parents arguing every day. Every time they argue, I feel especially panicked inside.

Hearing your story, I can sense your loneliness, hurt, and helplessness, and how you’ve had to quietly carry those feelings on your own. As someone living and working in Beijing away from home, that inner strength may also make it hard to allow yourself to show vulnerability. That kind of state is really understandable.
Yes, I’ve always felt like I need to play the role of being strong, but inside it’s actually really hard.

I completely understand how you feel. Living for a long time in an environment where your parents argued can bring a lot of psychological pressure, and it may also make you place very high demands on yourself. In this situation, we can look for some ways to regulate your emotions and help you.
Do you have any specific suggestions?

First, I’d suggest finding some time to be alone, quieting down, and thinking about your emotions and needs. Understanding your emotions can help you regulate them better. Also, try some relaxing activities, like listening to music, reading, taking walks, and so on, to let yourself step away from sources of stress and relax your body and mind.
I’ll give it a try. Thank you for your suggestions. Are there any other methods?

Of course. You can also try talking with others and seeking support. Find a friend you can trust, or a professional counselor, and share your struggles and feelings with them. They can offer you support and help. Sharing with others can lighten the burden inside and help you feel supported and understood.
I’ll consider looking for help from a counselor. Thank you for encouraging me. Are there any other suggestions?

In addition, you can try some mind-body relaxation practices, such as deep breathing, meditation, and yoga. These practices can help calm your emotions and reduce anxiety and stress. Also, building a good daily routine and making sure you get enough sleep are very important for emotional regulation.
Okay, I’ll try these methods. Thank you for your suggestions and care.

You’re welcome. I’m glad I can offer you some help. Please remember, you’re not facing these problems alone; many people have gone through similar situations. As long as you keep looking for methods that suit you and give yourself some time, you will be able to regulate your emotions and regain your confidence. Hang in there!
Thank you for your encouragement and support! I’ll work on it. I believe I can get through this difficult time.

Very good. Believe in yourself—you can definitely overcome these difficulties. If you run into any difficulty while regulating your emotions, don’t hesitate to reach out to me anytime for help. I’ll continue to be here to support you. Wishing you a soon return to your bright, confident self!

My boyfriend had a messy past and lies a lot. I’ve become very controlling, and being with him feels so exhausting. We met through a matchmaking date. At first glance, I felt we weren’t a match, but later, as we slowly spent more time together, I got used to it. Our family backgrounds, education, and jobs are all very different. We’re two different kinds of people.
Anyone who encounters a man like this would need to become more controlling. That’s very normal, because his behavior doesn’t give people a sense of security.
You’re right. I always feel like his behavior can’t be trusted, and that’s why I’ve become so controlling.

Yes. You have the right to ask him to make changes for the sake of your own feelings. But you also need to understand that even if he does change, will you still be able to keep tolerating this feeling of distrust?
I’m really conflicted, because I really cherish the time we have together, but at the same time I don’t believe his behavior will change.

You already know that, mentally and emotionally, the two of you are not in the same world. When you make yourself fit into his world, you become more “controlling,” and you have to spend a lot of time every day “monitoring” where he goes. That drains a lot of your energy.
Yes, what you said is very true. Every day is really hard for me, but I don’t know what to do, or whether I should leave him.

Do you really have no other choice? Or is it just because he was your first, so you feel he will “change”? But from what you’ve described, he just has a relatively strong sexual drive, and in his free time he looks for different women to get sex. He doesn’t value the “person”; what he values is his own sexual needs.
You’re very right. I do feel he really isn’t someone worth relying on or trusting.

Then you can continue maintaining the current situation, but take good “contraceptive” measures to avoid an unplanned pregnancy increasing the “cost” of leaving. When you’re so exhausted that you can’t keep going, you can also choose to break up and end this relationship.
But I feel like I’ll be very lonely after leaving him, and I don’t know whether I’ll be able to find someone better.
Getting to know someone takes time. You’ve already spent quite a lot of time. Sometimes, only by leaving him do you have the chance to meet a better “person,” right?
What you said makes sense. I need to think it through carefully. After all, this kind of relationship has already become too exhausting for me.
Yes. You need to think about your own happiness. If you feel you can’t keep tolerating this kind of relationship, then breaking up may be one way to solve the problem.
Thank you for your advice. I’ll think about it seriously.
The interview exam is coming up soon, and I’m a little nervous. The pressure feels a little high?

Let’s first look at what’s going on for you: facing the teacher qualification interview and final exams, you’re feeling a bit under pressure. Actually, this is something we come across quite often. There are always periods when we’re really busy, and life, study, and work all pile up together. It really makes you wish you could split time in half. So what can we do?
That’s true. It’s really hard to deal with both of these challenges at the same time. I feel a bit lost and don’t know where to start preparing.

Making a good plan is very important. You can make a list of the subjects for your final exams and the things you need to prepare for the teacher qualification interview. Then, based on that list, plan your time and make your goals specific to what you need to do each week and each day. That can help you feel less lost.
That sounds like a good approach. I can list out the knowledge points I need to master, and then assign study tasks for each day. That would make things more organized.

Yes, studying in an organized way can make the pressure feel much lighter. Also, you can prioritize based on the timing. If you have enough energy, you can work on both at the same time, preparing for the finals and the interview. If you don’t have enough energy, you can prioritize your review and interview preparation based on which one comes first.
I understand. I’ll arrange my time and energy reasonably based on my actual situation.

Good. Another important method is to release stress. You can choose some things you enjoy to help release stress, like exercising, listening to music, taking walks, and so on. Stress shouldn’t be allowed to build up—the more it builds up, the more weighed down you feel. It’s important to release it in time.
That’s true. I usually really like listening to music, and I also like taking walks. I’ll pay more attention to giving myself some time to relax and release stress.

Very good. One more important thing is to maintain enough energy. The busier and more anxious you are, the more you need to keep your energy up. When you have good energy, you’ll be more efficient and get better results with less effort. The best way to maintain your energy is to get enough sleep.
I realize that during this period I should pay more attention to sleep. I’ll try to make sure I get enough rest each day, so I can stay energized.
Very good. I believe these methods will be very helpful for you. Don’t be too nervous. Trust that you can handle the challenges of these exams and the interview well. You’ve got this!
Thank you for your support and encouragement. I’ll feel more confident facing these challenges. Thank you for your suggestions and help!
You’re welcome. I’m always willing to help you. If you need anything, feel free to come back and talk with me anytime. I wish you all the best with your exams and interview. You’ve got this!
Thank you for your good wishes. I’ll work hard. Thanks again for your help!
Whenever it’s Spring Festival, Mid-Autumn Festival, or other holidays for family reunions, I feel especially awful. I don’t want to go home?

Reading your story, I can see that your relationship with your mom is so-so, and I also know you were a left-behind child. The fact that you were able to get into a master’s program in that kind of environment is truly impressive. Still, there are some things weighing on your mind. Let’s take a look at them together.
Ever since I left that time, I haven’t gone back.
It may be time to go back and take a look. But what has kept you from taking action all this time?
It’s my mom’s attitude. In my memory, “someone who loves to insult people” is the image I have of her. Because things like that happened, the intense emotions became very deep memories for me.

Yes, that kind of experience can feel very painful. Home is always where a person’s roots are, and part of you longs to go back and see it. You could try reaching out in a tentative way—calling her or messaging her on WeChat—to get a sense of how she is now and observe how she communicates. You can also tell her what kind of relationship you hope to have with each other, and what kind of family atmosphere you would like. At least then you would have something to base your judgment on.
Mm, you’re right. I can try communicating with my mom and see whether she has changed at all.

If your mom’s attitude has changed, and it’s fairly in line with the relationship you’re hoping for, then you could try going back, and work on repairing the relationship while also getting to know her better. But if your mom still has the same attitude and doesn’t care about your needs, then you can decide for yourself whether you want to go back again.
I understand. If my mom doesn’t change, I can also choose to forgive her and let go of the knot in my heart, right?

Yes. Forgiveness doesn’t mean agreeing with the other person’s unreasonable behavior; it means making peace within yourself. You can write a forgiveness letter to yourself, expressing your forgiveness and sense of release. If there is anyone else in your heart you haven’t forgiven, you can keep writing from there.
Forgiveness is a kind of release. Even if I don’t go back, I can still forgive my mom and let go of the knot in my heart.

Exactly. In addition, you can learn about what kind of atmosphere and communication a healthy family needs, as preparation for building a more complete and healthy family in the future. Through understanding your family of origin, you can also feel warmth even when you are living on your own.
Mm, I understand. I’ll try to learn from my experiences in my family of origin and prepare myself for family life in the future.

Very good. Whether or not you plan to go back in the future, your family of origin gave you the most basic thing—life itself—and that is a gift worth being grateful for. I hope you can let go of the knot in your heart and keep moving forward happily. Wishing you well.
Thank you for your support and encouragement. I’ll work on letting go of the knot in my heart and keep moving forward!
I keep complaining, and people around me feel like I’m doing things as if I’m being forced?

After reading your question, I can feel that you’re very troubled and upset because you seem to habitually complain, and because of how that complaining affects the way people around you see you. You’re not sure how to resolve it. The main issue is: “I keep complaining. Even when I’m doing something I may actually like, I’ll still make a symbolic little complaint, which makes people around me feel like I’m doing it as if I’m being forced. It leaves me not really knowing what to do.” Actually, it seems the root of the problem may be your habitual complaining behavior. Whether something good or bad happens, you habitually make a complaint. On the surface, this looks like a habitual behavior, but there is likely an inner reason behind it. Generally speaking, there are many main reasons complaints arise: 1) A negative psychological state leads to complaining. Someone who is often in a negative psychological state can easily develop a tendency to complain. And because of this, they may express dissatisfaction with the people or things around them. This is because too much unhappiness or negative emotion has been stored inside. These unhappy or negative emotions can all “cultivate” a complaining mindset.
You’re right. I really am often in a negative psychological state, and that makes me realize my own problem.
Good. Becoming aware of your own problem is the first step toward change. Next, let’s explore some ways to address it together.
Okay. I want to change this habit as soon as possible, but I don’t know where to start.
