First, you need to look for what the reason is behind your habitual complaining. Only by finding the root of the problem can you address it more directly and better find a solution.
I’ll try to think about the reasons why I complain, and I hope I can find the answer.

Second, self-awareness is very important. You can try to consciously control this complaining behavior, say more positive things, and stop yourself in time once you are about to say, or have started to say, something complaining. You can also ask friends for help and have them remind you, so that you can become more aware of your behavior. Awareness is the beginning of change.
I understand. I’ll pay attention to self-awareness and try to change my habit of complaining through more positive words and actions.
Good. You’ve already become aware of your problem and are seeking change, and that’s a very good start.
Thank you for your encouragement. I’ll keep working on it.

Finally, action is even more important. Change is difficult for a person; it takes time and persistence. So after you become aware that the problem exists and can notice it in time, long-term persistence becomes especially important. If everything only stays at the level of imagination, the current situation can’t change. Only by taking action is it possible to change it completely. I hope my answer can be helpful, and I wish you success in changing this habit.
Thank you for your advice and encouragement. I’ll work on taking action. I hope I can overcome this habit and become more positive and upward-looking.
Believe in yourself. You can definitely do it. If you have other concerns or need further support, you can reach out to me for help anytime.
Okay, thank you for your support. I will.
I'm too soft-hearted and always end up losing out or getting fooled. I feel too embarrassed to refuse. How can I change?

You are a very kind person. When things come up, you’re always soft-hearted, thinking of others in everything, and you don’t know how to refuse—or feel too embarrassed to. But in our lives, there are times when we really need to set boundaries for ourselves and for others. Otherwise, other people won’t know what matters to us.
Yes, I really do want to think of others, but every time I refuse someone, I feel embarrassed.
That way of thinking is very normal. Refusing someone is not easy, especially for someone kind-hearted. But we also need to understand that if we don’t refuse, we may end up paying a greater price.
So how should I change this problem of being too soft-hearted?

First, you can practice using clear language to express your feelings and needs. Don’t use vague wording; say your position and wishes directly. For example, when you feel uncomfortable, you can say, “I’m not comfortable. Please wait a moment.” That way, others can understand your needs and give you the respect that goes with them.
That method sounds good. I’ll try it.

Also, you can learn to use the XYZ method. When you encounter a situation where you need to refuse, you can try saying something like, “I strongly feel that, given how much I’ve contributed to the company, I should receive more recognition.” Or, “Yesterday at dinner, when you made fun of me, I felt very hurt.” This way of expressing yourself can help you communicate your feelings and needs effectively without hurting others.
Okay, I’ll try using these methods to express myself.

Very good! Remember, change takes time and practice. Don’t demand too much of yourself. Every attempt is a step forward. Believe in yourself—you can definitely change this pattern of being too soft-hearted.
Thank you for your encouragement and support. I’ll work on it!
You’re welcome. I’ve always believed in your ability. If you run into any difficulties during the process of changing, feel free to come talk to me anytime. I’ll always support you.
With your support, I feel like I have more courage to change. I’ll keep your words in mind and face refusal bravely.
I believe you can succeed. By bravely facing refusal and setting boundaries for yourself and others, you’ll be better able to protect yourself and experience more respect and happiness.
Thank you for your patience and encouragement. I’m really grateful!
You’re very welcome. I’m always willing to help you. Remember, you’re not fighting this alone—you have family, friends, and me by your side supporting you. You’ve got this!
What should I do? Is it that there’s no chance for us anymore?

Please don’t keep saying things like you can’t be together. Maybe you’re just saying it casually, and the other person may take it casually once or twice, but over time, the way it feels to hear it can change.
Maybe I’ve said it too much. I’ll try not to say these things anymore.
Good. Since you’ve become aware of this issue, it’s important to work on changing it. Why do you think the two of you argue?
I think there are communication problems between us, and I’m always expecting him to apologize to me.

When two people have been together for a long time, they need to learn to find a way of getting along that works for both of them. You can start by looking back at some past situations and learning from them.
Do you have any suggestions? I feel like the way we handled things before doesn’t work anymore.
Try a different approach. Each time he apologizes to you, you can also learn to apologize to him first, or take the initiative to communicate with him, instead of getting stuck in a cold war.
Next time we have an argument, I’ll try to take the initiative to talk with him instead of giving him the cold shoulder.
Good. One more thing: when both of your emotions have settled down, then talk about where the problem lies. That can help you solve the issue better.
Okay. I’ll go talk things over with him after my emotions have calmed down.
In the process of getting along, you don’t necessarily have to wait for him to apologize. You can also take the initiative yourself. After all, the two of you are going to build a life together.
I understand. I’ll take the initiative to change myself and stop being so fixed on getting an apology from him.
Good. No matter how you argue, the ultimate goal is to live well together. Don’t push the other person out into the outside world.
Thank you for your advice. I’ll try my best to do it well.
You’re welcome. I hope the two of you can resolve the issues and live a happy life. If you need any more help, feel free to come back and talk with me anytime.

Why does seeing someone I don’t like seriously affect my mood? Whatever I see her doing affects my emotions. For example, when she takes a shower, I feel like she’s using my electricity. When she uses the bathroom, I feel like I’m the one who keeps the bathroom clean, so why does she get to use it like it’s only natural? Anything that has to do with me, I just can’t stand it.

From what you’re describing, it seems this person really does have a big impact on your emotions. It may be that your relationship with her is relatively close, but you don’t want that kind of closeness, so without realizing it, you’ve become more critical and dissatisfied with her. I’m wondering if you have certain expectations of her, but she isn’t able to meet them, and that has led you to feel dissatisfied with and unable to accept many things about her. In psychology, we often say that being critical of and dissatisfied with others is actually connected to not accepting and being dissatisfied with ourselves. You might think about whether you’re also being a bit too harsh on yourself and dissatisfied with yourself.

Maybe. I do have very high expectations for myself. I always feel like I’m not good enough, so when I see other people doing things, I unconsciously criticize and blame them. But I don’t want to be like this either. I can’t control these emotions.

I understand. Your expectations for yourself are indeed very high, and that may be bringing you a lot of pressure and negative emotions. But emotions can be regulated through some methods. Have you tried any ways to regulate your emotions?
Actually, I’ve tried meditation and breathing exercises before, but they didn’t work especially well. Whenever I see that person, my emotions just become uncontrollable.

Meditation and breathing exercises are very good ways to regulate emotions, but everyone’s experience may be different. When you see that person and find your emotions hard to control, there may be other reasons as well. Maybe we can look together for other emotion regulation methods that suit you. Would you be willing to try?
Okay, I’m willing to try other methods. Do you have any suggestions?

First, I suggest you try to identify what triggers your negative emotions toward that person—for example, whether it’s her behavior, her words, or certain specific situations. Then you can try practicing emotional anticipation and cognitive restructuring, which means when you face that trigger, you imagine it in advance and work on changing your emotional response and way of thinking. In addition, you can also shift your attention and reduce stress by taking some relaxation training classes or talking with friends. Do you think these methods would be workable for you?

Mm, I understand. I’ll try to find the triggers and try to change my emotional reactions and way of thinking. I’ll also consider taking relaxation training classes or talking with friends to reduce stress. Thank you for your suggestions.

You’re welcome. I’m very glad to be able to help. Remember, if you run into difficulties while trying these methods, or if there’s anything you need help with, you can talk with me anytime. You don’t have to keep carrying these emotions on your own. We can look for solutions together.
Okay, I will. Thank you again for your support and encouragement.
You’re welcome. I believe you can overcome this issue that’s been troubling you. Believe in yourself—you’ve got this. If you need anything, feel free to talk with me anytime.
Thank you, I will. If I run into problems, I’ll come to you. Thank you for your support and for being here with me.
You’ve already taken the first step, so do your best to keep going. I’ll always be here to support you. Wishing you all the best.
Thank you for your encouragement and good wishes. I’ll work hard. I hope I can readjust my emotions. Thank you again for your help.
You’re very welcome. I believe you can do it. I hope you soon find an emotion regulation method that works for you. Remember to contact me anytime. I’ll always be here to support you.
I feel like I care too much about what other people think of me, and I always overthink before I do anything. What do you think I should do?

Hi, being able to consider things from other people’s perspectives is a good quality. But don’t forget to also take care of your own rights and needs in communication. Next, I’d like to help you find some ways to get out of this kind of tangled thinking. What do you think?
Sure, I really appreciate it!

First, we need to recognize that not paying attention to others at all can have a big negative impact on us. But we also shouldn’t give too much weight to what other people think, because we live in a collective environment, and communicating with and evaluating each other is hard to avoid. You need to build your own way of understanding things, be clear about your relationship with others, and look at yourself, other people, and the broader social environment objectively. Do you think this approach is workable?
Mm, I think that makes a lot of sense. But I always feel like other people will see me that way. What should I do?

We can’t avoid other people’s opinions, but we also shouldn’t let them alone control our behavior. Everyone’s views are different, and we can’t care about every single person’s opinion. So we need to strengthen our inner stability and not be disrupted by what others say. We should stay firm in our own direction and not let other people sway our thinking. Do you think this approach could help you deal with this situation?
Mm, I think that’s good. But I’m always afraid of failing, and it’s the same when I face competition.

Everyone has times when they fail, and that’s normal. So we should learn from failure, keep improving our abilities, and make progress. Again, we need to be clear about our goals and direction, and not be swayed by other people’s opinions. Do you feel this approach applies to you?
Mm, I think it really applies. But sometimes I’m still very passive. I don’t dare to be too proactive, because I’m afraid others will think I have impure motives.

You don’t need to worry about what other people think. Everyone has their own thoughts, and sometimes there can be misunderstandings. The key is that you yourself are clear about your original intention and goals. We should develop a healthy view of interpersonal relationships, not focus too much on other people’s thoughts, and pay more attention to our own behavior and attitude. Do you think this suggestion is helpful for you?
Mm, I think it’s very useful. But I also want to ask, how should I become more outgoing and decisive?

First, it’s important to understand your own personality. We need to recognize our strengths and shortcomings, and then start making improvements. Take the initiative to communicate with others; this can help you understand yourself better. At the same time, participate more in social activities and actively make new friends, which can strengthen your social skills. Have you thought about your strengths in this area, or about what abilities you’d like to strengthen?
Mm, I want to strengthen my abilities in the social area.

Good. If you want to build better relationships with others, you can take the initiative to invite them to do activities you’re interested in together. This can help you feel more confident. At the same time, you can also try more new things, which can help you keep learning and growing. Do you think suggestions like these could help you?
Mm, thank you for your suggestions. I feel like I’ve already found some ways to overcome my limitations.

I’m glad to hear you say that. Practice is the only criterion for testing truth; only through practice can you know which methods are truly effective. Share with me how your practice goes and how you feel about it.
How can he pull away so quickly? Is it being heartless, or is it being rational?
Reading what you described, I can really understand how you’re feeling right now. Do you feel like he pulled away so quickly because he was being heartless, or because he was being rational?

We’re long-distance. Why would my boyfriend not reply to my messages from noon all the way through the night, and then the next day when I said I was upset and unhappy, he acted helpless? (Because he was busy with work and working overtime?)
I see. Why do you think your boyfriend didn’t reply to you in that situation? Was it because he was busy with work?
For the next two days, neither of us paid attention to the other, because this thing about replying to messages has happened many times before too. It’s always like this.
I see. Then, since this kind of situation has happened many times before, why do you think neither of you reached out to the other over those two days?

That night I posted a Moments saying “let go,” and then I found that he had deleted the QQ status where I said I would walk with him. I just hoped he would come and coax me a little on his own, but in the end he left even faster than I did. Then I posted another Moments, crying my eyes out, with his favorite photo of us together, saying it was the final goodbye. He still didn’t contact me on his own.
I understand your disappointment. You hoped he would take the initiative to comfort you, but instead he chose to leave, right? You posted that Moments, and he still didn’t respond.
Why, when I said I cried, didn’t he feel bad for me? He still hasn’t contacted me. Is he really that calm?
You feel very disappointed. You cried, but he didn’t show that he felt bad for you, right? He still hasn’t contacted you, which makes you wonder whether he really can stay that calm.

It’s not like I’m insisting on something. Even if we’re separating, am I not worth him taking a moment to say one sentence? Just because I said I wanted to let go, does he think there’s nothing between us anymore?

You’re not asking him to do anything special. Even if it’s a separation, couldn’t he take a little time to say something? Do you feel like he might think that because you said you wanted to let go, it means there’s no relationship between you anymore?

So whatever I do, whether I’m happy or sad, has nothing to do with him anymore? How can he pull away so quickly? Is there not even a bit of feeling left? Even if it were just an ordinary friend, if they knew the other person had cried, they would at least politely comfort them, right?

You feel like whatever you do has nothing to do with him anymore? You’re wondering how he could pull away so quickly. You mentioned that maybe the feelings are already gone—even if he were just an ordinary friend, he should still politely comfort you a little, right?

Last time, we were also on the verge of breaking up because of this. He didn’t contact me for five days, and in the end I was still the one who took the initiative to contact him, and we barely kept it going.

You mentioned that last time, you were also on the verge of breaking up because of this issue. That time, he didn’t contact you for five days, and in the end you were still the one who reached out first and kept the relationship going.

Just studying hard and doing what I’m supposed to—can studying really bring me the life I want? I’m a junior in college. My grades were always really good in high school, but I messed up on the college entrance exam. The university I’m at now isn’t a “Double First-Class” school, but it’s actually quite strong. My grades in college are also okay, and I’m planning to apply for a master’s program in the UK. But recently I’ve started feeling lost. I’m in a science and engineering major too, and honestly, if you really try to study seriously in college, it’s really exhausting, and it’s also very boring. Lately I’ve started envying the lives of a few friends back in my hometown. Their grades weren’t good; some are even in vocational colleges, and some are at first-tier universities but the kind that are Chinese-foreign joint programs—you know what I mean. But their lives seem so rich… going to bars at night when there’s nothing to do, playing mahjong in the afternoon. But they’re not just wasting their days either. They actually get to meet a lot of people, they have a wide social circle, their parents are fairly well-off, and they all have pretty high emotional intelligence. So I feel like their future development probably won’t be too bad. And I’m the kind of person who just studies honestly, exhausting myself every day. My life isn’t that colorful, and I don’t meet that many people. I feel like my current life situation is pretty unsatisfying. Actually, I already felt this way in high school, but back then I had this belief in getting into my ideal university, so I was still very motivated. But now when I think about it, even if I go study in the UK and come back, if my life is still this boring, then what’s the point…

First, let’s clarify the issues you brought up. They can be divided into three smaller questions. First, is studying hard and doing things the proper way useful? Second, what is the life you want? Third, can studying hard bring you the life you want?
Then let me start with this question: is studying hard and doing things the proper way actually useful?

Studying hard is definitely useful. That’s beyond doubt. Just imagine—if you hadn’t studied, you wouldn’t be at a school that, while not a “Double First-Class” university, is still very strong. If you hadn’t studied, even if you had completed the nine years of compulsory education, chances are you’d be working on some assembly line right now.
I understand. Studying hard has indeed given me some opportunities. Then the second question is, what kind of life do I actually want now?

I think this question is really where your confusion lies. You mentioned that in high school, you had this belief in getting into your ideal university, and it supported you through a boring life. Now in college, the courses are hard, and studying feels exhausting. I understand that very well. I also studied science and engineering, and all those mechanics courses made me doubt my life and wonder whether my IQ had just gone offline. Even if you study abroad and come back, life still may not necessarily feel satisfying.
Yes, I really have started envying the lives of my friends back home. It feels like their lives are very rich and colorful.

You envy the lives of your friends who stayed in your hometown: ordinary schools, time to socialize, going to bars, playing mahjong, high emotional intelligence, good family circumstances. Their futures may very well be colorful too. Comparing the two, a feeling of “what’s the point” starts to grow in you. But have you carefully thought about what kind of interesting life you actually want? Is it the life your classmates have now? You’re a junior in college now—can you guarantee that ten years from now, you’ll still want the life your classmates have now? Right now, your idea of a possible future life is built on imagination and comparison. If you saw your other classmates who got into 985 or 211 universities, busy every day with classes, internships, exams for certificates, and club activities, what would you think? Would you think that kind of life is too exhausting? Or would you also think that kind of life is interesting? So the first issue to work on is: what is an interesting life for you? What is a meaningful life now, and what will be a meaningful life after you enter society in the future?
That’s true. I haven’t really thought deeply about what kind of life I want. A lot of the time I’m just judging it by comparing myself with others.

Exactly. We all judge our lives by comparing them with others. But that kind of judgment is very subjective, and it can easily lead to dissatisfaction and confusion. To find the life you want, you need to think and explore. You can try asking yourself: what kind of life would feel meaningful to me? Also, the studying and effort you’re putting in now are laying a foundation for your future development.
I understand. I need to think about the life I want and work toward it. But I’m still worried about whether studying hard can bring me the life I want.

Whether studying hard can bring you the life you want—I don’t think that’s absolute. But studying hard can bring you a little closer to the good life you want. Even if what you want is the life your classmates have now, that also requires a lot of financial support. Yes, it’s that realistic. And studying can increase your income, which means you’re more likely to live the life you want. Whether studying can bring you the life you want depends entirely on your attitude toward studying and the effort you put into it. I don’t know if you’ve seen that famous photo of the Wuzhen dinner gathering—a table surrounded by CEOs, all graduates of top, prestigious universities. What your future life will be like depends on what you do now.
I understand. I need to adjust my attitude and effort, and put more energy into studying.

Good. When a goal is set too far away, it’s easy to feel powerless. I suggest you start by setting some small goals, such as attending every class seriously this semester, not letting your ranking drop in the final exams, taking part in some volunteer activities or club activities, preparing for studying abroad—specific and measurable goals like these. At the same time, read more books in the humanities and social sciences to refresh your understanding and improve your thinking skills. I hope that through reflection, you can find the life you want and work toward it.
Thank you for your suggestions. I’ll think about them seriously and put them into action.

You’re welcome. I’ll always support you. If you have any other questions or concerns, you can talk with me anytime. This occasionally motivated and hardworking counselor will always be here waiting for you.
Every time it’s a family reunion holiday like Spring Festival or Mid-Autumn Festival, I feel especially awful and don’t want to go home?

Are you from Kunming? I’m from Kunming too. I feel like meeting you here is a kind of fate. From what you described, you’re living in another province now, is that right? You wrote that you worked for three years and now you’re preparing for the graduate school entrance exam, so are you not working right now? These things are important, so I can understand whether you have a source of income now and whether you can live independently away from home.
Yes, I’m in another province preparing for the graduate school entrance exam. I haven’t found a job yet, and I don’t have a source of income.

From what you’ve shared about what you’ve been through, it seems like you no longer want to return to your hometown. You give me the sense that you have a home in Kunming, but you can’t go back to it. I feel a kind of rootless drifting and loneliness in that.
Yes, I feel lonely when I’m away, and when I go home I don’t feel like I belong there either.

Let’s first talk about your relationship with your dad. It seems like you feel a little less resentment toward him, and more that you don’t understand him. It’s as if his divorce from your mom happened too suddenly, and you weren’t mentally prepared to accept it. But from the timeline, we can infer that from when he left home during your second year of high school to when he came back and asked for a divorce during your junior year of college, something must have happened during those four to five years. Maybe your father had already started another family outside, and it became impossible to maintain both sides, so he decided to let go of you and your mom’s side.

Yes, my dad and my mom’s divorce really felt impossible for me to accept, and I don’t know what happened. They both said the other person cheated. I’m not sure which one it was, because I spent very little time with them and don’t really understand either of them.

As an outside observer, his cheating was out in the open. As for him saying your mom cheated, whether that was to make public opinion more favorable to him, or whether he had some evidence, we can’t know. But from this, I can see your attitude toward him and your mom: you’re willing to believe that their separation wasn’t only because of him, and you feel your mom also bears part of the responsibility.
Yes, I feel my mom also bears part of the responsibility for the divorce.

Next, let’s talk about your relationship with your mom. You and your mom could be described as being in a love-hate kind of state. You’re willing to be good to her. From your description, I can see that you’re a filial daughter. You usually do a lot of housework, you’re very hardworking, and you’ve taken on a lot of the burdens at home. But after you did all these thoughtful things, your mom still insulted you like that. If it were me, I wouldn’t be able to accept it either. I can feel your pain.
Yes, it’s very hard for me to accept my mom’s insults.

Maybe a lot of the time your mom is someone who lives in her own world. That is, when she says those things, it’s completely out of habit and without thinking. Of course, it may not be directed at you personally. The divorce may also have been a big shock to her, so much so that for now she can’t get out of that painful emotional state. So besides keeping your mom company, maybe you could find a reliable counselor to help your mom work through her issues.
I think finding a counselor might be helpful for my mom.

Next, let’s talk about other influential people in your life. I saw that you grew up by your grandmother’s side, so your grandmother must have been the person who gave you the most love and the best memories. But now she lives with your uncle, and your uncle also cheated. About your uncle’s cheating, I think it may be a coincidence. If we dug deeper, we might also find some family dynamics on your mom’s side, but that isn’t the main issue. The main issue may be that if you go back to your grandmother’s home, you’ll have to face your uncle who cheated. And your grandmother’s side of the family will probably talk about your uncle and, along with that, bring up your parents’ divorce. You clearly find that kind of situation too much to face, so you don’t really want to go back to your grandmother’s home either. So could it be like this: during Spring Festival, you still go home and stay at your own home. Then, if your uncle’s home isn’t far from yours, during the day you can take your grandmother out to relax, just you and your grandmother together, staying a little farther away from your uncle and your mom. Then once you get through the hardest few days of the New Year, you can go back to another place to work and study. I wonder whether this way of spending the New Year would feel a little easier for you to accept.
That suggestion sounds good. I can try using this way to get through the New Year.

And during all this time after your mom divorced your dad, there must have been certain moments when she was in a good mood and was close to you. Think about what was happening then. The more details you can remember, the better. Then you may be able to find ways to help your mom feel happier, and when she’s in a better mood, she won’t be so harsh and disrespectful to you.
Why do I always feel like I’m the one being bullied? Am I easy to push around?
I understand that you’re feeling bullied. Can you tell me what happened?
I live in an old residential compound. Every time the water fee is collected, we take turns doing it, but every time it’s my turn, something goes wrong.
I see. What problems do you feel come up when collecting the water fee?
Everyone knows someone’s home has a leak, but no one admits it, and no one is willing to split the extra water fee.
That sounds really upsetting. Have you tried talking with your neighbors about this?
But I’ve already paid all the water fees upfront, and not a single person has paid me their share.
That’s really frustrating. Have you told them that you’d like them to pay you back?
Did I make them feel like I’m easy to push around?
It’s not that you made others feel they can bully you; it’s that you’re feeling frustrated in trying to protect your own rights and interests. It’s very normal to want fair treatment.
But I feel like they’re just selectively ignoring me.
I can understand how you feel. In this situation, you could try to keep communicating with them and express what’s bothering you. Maybe you can find a way to solve the problem.
How should I start this conversation?
Try talking with them honestly and openly in a comfortable setting. Please remember, understanding and mutual respect are key to solving the problem.
I’ll try to communicate with them properly, and I hope we can resolve this.
Good. I believe your efforts will pay off. If you need help, remember you can reach out to me for support anytime.
How can he pull away so quickly? Is he being heartless, or rational?

Actually, when we enter a relationship, we think about what we get from it, and we can become concerned with gains and losses. If we can see ourselves as already whole, then meeting a partner is just sharing our wholeness with them, rather than only becoming whole after meeting a partner.

We’re long-distance. Why would my boyfriend not reply to my messages from noon through the whole night, and then the next day when I said I was sad and unhappy, he acted helpless? (Because he was busy with work and working overtime?) For the next two days, neither of us talked to the other, because this has happened many times before with replying to messages, and it’s always like this.

I can sense how anxious you feel, and how much you’re hoping he can come back to you. But maybe your boyfriend isn’t deliberately ignoring you; he may simply not have replied because he was busy with work or working overtime. Since neither of you has communicated these past two days, perhaps you could try sitting down and having a proper talk.

That night I posted on Moments about “letting go,” and then I noticed he had deleted the QQ status where he said he wanted me to walk with him. I only hoped he would take the initiative to comfort me a little, but instead he left even faster than I did. Then I posted another Moment where I was crying my eyes out, with his favorite photo of us together, saying it was the final goodbye. He still didn’t contact me first.

I know you’re feeling very sad and disappointed right now. But venting your emotions through Moments may not be a good way to resolve this. Perhaps you could reach out to him directly, honestly express how you feel, and see whether you can rebuild communication and understanding.

Why doesn’t he feel bad for me when I say I cried? He keeps not contacting me—is he really that calm? It’s not like I’m insisting on anything. Even if we’re separating, am I not worth him taking a moment to say one sentence? Just because I said I wanted to let go, does he think there’s no relationship between us anymore? Whatever I do, whether I’m happy or sad, has nothing to do with him anymore? How can he pull away so quickly? Does he have no feelings at all? Even if we were just ordinary friends, if you found out the other person had cried, you’d at least politely comfort them, right?

I understand the pain and helplessness you feel from being ignored. But everyone handles emotions and expresses care differently. Maybe your boyfriend isn’t being cold to you on purpose; he may have his own way of dealing with problems. You can try to speak with him honestly about your feelings, and let him understand your needs and expectations.
Last time, we were also on the verge of breaking up because of this. He didn’t contact me for five days, and in the end I was still the one who reached out first, and we barely kept it going.

It seems the communication issue between you has been a long-standing source of distress. Communication is an important foundation for maintaining a relationship. You could try finding a more effective way to communicate, such as regularly sitting down to share each other’s thoughts and feelings, and listening to each other’s needs and concerns.
I understand that communication is important, but why does he always make me be the one to contact him first? Why can’t he take the initiative to comfort me a little?

Everyone has different ways of handling things and expressing love. Maybe there is a mismatch between the two of you in communication styles and needs. But that doesn’t mean he doesn’t love you or doesn’t care about you. You can communicate your needs and expectations with him honestly, and explore together how to better meet each other’s emotional needs.
I’m really lost right now. I don’t know what I should do.

When you’re facing confusion and feeling lost, you can try returning to your inner voice, and listen to your own feelings and needs. At the same time, you can also seek help from a professional counselor, who can offer you more specific guidance and support.
Thank you for your advice. I’ll try to listen to my own heart, and also consider finding a counselor to help me work through this problem.

You’re doing well. Listening to yourself and seeking professional help are important steps in addressing the problem. I hope you can find a way that suits you to handle this relationship distress. I wish you the best of luck!
How can he pull away so quickly? Is he being heartless, or is he being rational?

Maybe he’s been too busy with work and didn’t reply to your messages in time. It may not necessarily be heartlessness or rationality. Sometimes people can’t take care of the other person’s feelings for all kinds of reasons.

We’re long-distance. Why would my boyfriend not reply to me from noon all the way through the whole night, and then when I told him the next day that I felt hurt and unhappy, he acted helpless? (Because he was busy working overtime?)

Maybe he really was working overtime, and being busy with work can leave someone with little time to take care of other things. But I understand that you feel hurt and unhappy. You can tell him how you feel so he can better understand what you need.
For the next two days, neither of us talked to the other. Because the issue of replying to messages has happened many times before, and it’s always like this.
In this situation, have you thought about having a proper conversation with him? Tell him about your confusion and dissatisfaction, and see if you can find a way to work it out together.

That night I posted a WeChat Moments post saying “letting go,” and then I found out he had deleted the QQ status where he said he wanted me to walk with him. I just hoped he would take the initiative to come comfort me, but in the end he left even faster than I did. Then I posted another Moments post saying I was crying my eyes out, with his favorite photo of us together, saying it was the final goodbye. He still didn’t contact me on his own.

Your feelings are very understandable, but expressing your emotions doesn’t necessarily lead to a response from the other person. Maybe he doesn’t really know what’s going on inside you. You could try communicating with him directly and letting him know your needs and feelings.
Why is it that when I say I cried, he doesn’t feel sorry for me? He just keeps not contacting me. Is he really that calm and able to hold back?

Everyone expresses love and care differently. He may not be very good at expressing emotions. But that doesn’t mean he doesn’t care about you. Sometimes it takes giving each other some understanding and space.

It’s not like I’m insisting he has to do something. Even if we’re separating, isn’t it worth him taking a little time to say something? Just because I said I wanted to let go, does he think there’s nothing between us anymore?

Maybe his thoughts are different from yours, and he wants to put things down and not keep getting entangled. But that doesn’t mean there is nothing between you. You could try communicating with him from a calmer place and see if you can find a solution that both of you can accept.
So whatever I do, whether I’m happy or sad, it has nothing to do with him anymore? How can he pull away so quickly? Does he not have any feelings at all?

Maybe he is dealing with his own emotions and temporarily doesn’t have much energy to handle yours. But feelings are complicated. It may not be that he has no feelings at all; he may just not be able to face it right now.

Even if we were just ordinary friends, if you found out the other person was crying, you’d at least politely comfort them, right? Last time we were also on the verge of breaking up because of this. He didn’t contact me for five days, and in the end I was the one who reached out to him first, barely keeping things going.

Yes, as friends, caring for and comforting each other is very important. But if you hope to continue maintaining a relationship with him, perhaps you can try taking the initiative to communicate in a more direct way, so he can understand your needs and feelings. When it comes to handling a relationship, sometimes it takes effort and communication from both sides to resolve things.
This man’s personality is like a child’s. He doesn’t worry about anything. Can he still grow up?

A person’s self has three states: the Parent ego state, the Adult ego state, and the Child ego state. A person with a well-developed personality can use all three ego states flexibly. The man you described may rely too much on the Child ego state in certain situations, which makes him unable to handle some important matters. But as long as he becomes aware of this and is determined to make changes, it is still possible for him to grow.

He’s a man in his 40s, but his personality is still like a little kid’s. He likes to play, doesn’t worry about anything, and just waits for others to provide and take care of things. Can he still change at this age?

Age is not something that limits a person’s growth or change. No matter how old he is, as long as he has the awareness and determination, he can change. The key is to help him realize the negative impact this behavior has, and to spark his motivation to change.
So does that mean he’ll be like this for the rest of his life?

Not necessarily. Everyone has the potential to change, as long as they are willing to recognize their own issues and make an effort. Although change may take some time, with appropriate guidance and support, they can grow and gradually shift. What matters is maintaining a positive attitude and making consistent effort.
Then how should he change?

First, he needs to realize that he is overly dependent on the Child ego state, and recognize the negative impact this behavior has on his life and on others. Only when he becomes aware of this and is determined to adjust and change will change become possible. At the same time, he can seek help from professional counseling, and through conversations with a counselor, explore healthier ways of behaving and thinking.
But right now he may not be aware of his own problem. How should I guide him?

You can gradually help him reflect on his own behavior. Through communicating with him, guide him to pay attention to the ways he relies too much on the Child ego state, and remind him of the problems and difficulties this behavior may bring. At the same time, you can share some related information and examples to help him see the necessity and possibility of change.
If he starts to realize the problem and wants to change, how should I support him?

You can encourage him and let him know that change is a gradual process that requires consistent effort. Offer support and understanding, so he can feel your support and encouragement. You can also help him look for learning and growth resources that suit him, such as books, courses, or professional counseling.
If he runs into difficulties or setbacks on the path of change, what should I do?

When he faces difficulties or setbacks, you can offer him comfort and encouragement. Help him analyze the reasons behind the problem and look for ways to solve it. What’s important is to give him enough support and understanding, and let him know you will always be by his side supporting him on his path of change.
Thank you for your advice. I’ll do my best to support his change.

You’re welcome. I hope my suggestions are helpful to you. I believe that with your support and his own efforts, he can gradually grow and change. If you need any further help, remember you can come to me for support anytime.

Lately, I’ve turned 26, and every day I feel mentally tormented. Is there something wrong with me psychologically? I’m a woman, 26, from the bottom of society. I have issues from my family of origin. No house, no car, and a little over a hundred thousand in savings. I graduated from a junior college and worked for three years. A while ago I changed jobs and came back to my hometown to work, but something unexpected happened. I was unemployed at home for two months. Now I’m working at a local company in my hometown, doing a different kind of position than before, with a monthly salary of 7,000. The benefits are 1,000 to 2,000 yuan less than before. It feels like I’m not dying, but I can’t really afford to live either. Before, I was always thinking about when I’d make over 10,000 a month, when I’d buy a house. Slowly, watching the people around me, people on my social media, living better and better, more and more exciting lives. I feel like I’m terrible, I don’t know how to do anything, my emotional intelligence isn’t high, and I have no value. Actually, I really want to get rid of this feeling that I can only feel my own value when I’m needed or recognized by others, but I’ve been struggling painfully with it. I used to have a glorious past too; you could say I was the hope of the whole family, but I fell. Among my relatives, I’m probably doing the worst. Now every day feels like torture, and I don’t know what I’m doing. I have no desire for life. The person who used to be so spirited has now become useless. I want to escape this kind of life but can’t get away. My biggest wish is to go live in seclusion deep in the mountains, hahaha. In the past, when things were bad, I would always try to adjust on my own, but now this negative mood has lasted for more than a year and is still going on.

Hello, let’s talk about what’s been troubling you lately. From what you described, you’re feeling a lot of anxiety and low self-esteem. I really understand how you feel. These are very common emotions, and you don’t need to be too hard on yourself. Would you like to talk with me about how you’re feeling?
Yes. Actually, I just feel like life has no meaning at all. I don’t know what I’m doing, and my thoughts have been in a negative state all the time.

Hearing you say this, actually, meaning is something each person defines for themselves. You can start by sorting out your thoughts and emotions, and try to avoid emotional ups and downs as much as possible. You could find some things you’re interested in doing, or set small goals for yourself to complete. In this way, little by little, you may find meaning in life and feel a sense of achievement.
But I don’t know what I’m interested in. Every day feels very plain and ordinary.

You can look for things in life that are worth trying. How about going for a walk in a nearby park every weekend, taking photos, or picking up some kind of handicraft? These are all ways to help you relax, and they can help you find beauty in life. You could also sign up for some hobby classes you’re interested in, and try out more new areas. You may gain something from that too.
I feel like I’m a failure. Everyone around me is better than me.

Actually, everyone’s path of development is different, so you can’t compare yourself with others. Maybe you’re in a low point right now, but this period can be part of the process before you rise again. You can find ways that suit you to learn and build up your experience, and then you’ll have more chances to meet a better version of yourself.
But I always feel like I’m good for nothing, and I don’t know what strengths I still have.

From the experiences you shared when you introduced yourself earlier, we can see that you have a junior college education, work experience, and stable, independent financial ability. These are all real strengths. You can also try writing down your strengths. This can help you see that there are things about you that are valuable.
I want to escape this kind of life and go live in seclusion deep in the mountains.

This idea may look like escape, and I wouldn’t recommend it. Avoiding the current problems will only make them more complicated and difficult. We need to face problems in order to solve them. You can improve your emotional state through exercise, listening to music, reading, traveling, and other ways. These are relatively healthy ways to relax and can give you some positive energy. At the same time, actively talking with friends and family, sharing your emotions and thoughts, can also help you receive support and understanding.
I feel like all of that is really hard to do.

Yes, everyone has their own difficulties and challenges. But you must have confidence and hold on to your beliefs. You can slowly change your thoughts and behaviors bit by bit, and gradually achieve some small goals. That’s how you can become more positive and upward-looking.
Thank you for your suggestions. I’ll try to make some adjustments and changes.
Okay. I’m very glad I could help you. If you need anything, you can contact me anytime.

The person I like is being bullied in class, and it feels so awful. What should I do? There’s this boy I like, and he’s really, really gentle with me. I really like him, but in class he’s the kind of person who looks a bit silly, and he’s always getting picked on. A lot of people don’t like him, a lot of people leave him out, and when he talks to others, it seems like hardly anyone wants to respond. I feel really awful. Now whenever I think of him, I feel so bad. What should I do?

You’re a kind-hearted girl. It makes sense that you’d feel sad because he’s being treated unfairly. From what you’ve described, he’s very important to you. You care a lot about him, and you’re very worried about him.
Yes, I really care about him, because he’s really good to me, and he makes me feel warm.

Your description reminds me of Eileen Chang’s short story “Jasmine Tea.” The boy you described is a little like the male protagonist in it, and the female protagonist is a very lovely girl—kind-hearted like you, and drawn to the male protagonist who seems not to be accepted by others.
Yes, I’m a little like that female protagonist. I feel like a boy like this deserves attention and care.

It’s just that in the story, the female protagonist likes him but isn’t aware of it, while the male protagonist is jealous that she has a father. In the end, when the male protagonist asks her to be with him, she says she’s willing to see him as a man rather than as a sister-like friend as before. The male protagonist feels he didn’t get a satisfactory answer and beats her up. The novel ends abruptly there.
Wow, that male protagonist’s reaction was really terrible. I hope our story won’t end like that.

It won’t. In real life, we can find better ways to handle this. Here are some suggestions for what you asked about—what to do. I hope they’re helpful to you. If you feel these suggestions aren’t appropriate, that’s okay too; you can take them or leave them.
Okay, thank you for understanding and for your suggestions. Please tell me what you suggest.
Since you feel so bad for him, you might try talking with him and see what he himself thinks about those things.
Mm, I can try communicating with him and listen to his thoughts.
Or you could ask indirectly—ask your close friends or classmates you’re on good terms with whether they know what’s going on.
I have a few good friends. I can talk with them first and see whether they know anything about the situation.

If you have concerns, you don’t have to tell them at first that it’s about him. You could just say it’s about a story or some news, and then say, “Someone in our class seems to be in a similar situation. Do you know why?”
That’s a good idea! I’ll try to feel them out first, and then talk about the specific situation. Thank you for your advice and support.
You’re welcome. I believe you’ll be able to find a suitable way to help that boy, and I also hope your story can have a beautiful ending.
Thank you for your blessing and encouragement. I’ll do my best!

Hello, teachers. I want to find the people from my memories to talk to, but I can’t accept Gestalt therapy—what should I do? After a period of counseling, I feel that the people in my memories are so precious, but most of them have already gone their separate ways from me, or moved on with their own lives. I can no longer find them and say the things I want to say in my heart. But I’m not really able to accept Gestalt therapy. My understanding of Gestalt therapy is talking to myself about my feelings? What can I do?

When, because of various limitations, we can’t get in touch with certain people or express our feelings to them, those feelings can feel stuck inside. Human emotions need to be expressed, so that our energy can feel like it is flowing.
I understand. But I don’t know how to express these feelings. Are there other ways in counseling that could help me?

In counseling, there is one way that can help you express your feelings, and that is “writing a letter to the other person.” This is a form of healing through writing. By writing down your feelings, your past experiences, and the things you want to express, it can have a healing effect.
Writing a letter sounds like a good idea. Can I write down everything I want to say to the other person, and all of my feelings?

Yes. There are no limits on the content of the letter. You can write down what you want to say to the other person, as well as your feelings. After you finish writing it, you can read the letter out loud, and then notice how you feel before and after writing it.
This method sounds very simple. Can I do it on my own?

Yes. This method is very simple and doesn’t require much in terms of time or setting, so you can do it on your own. One characteristic of words is that they can be seen. By seeing the words you have written down, you can better understand your inner feelings. This is also a process of deepening self-understanding.
Hearing you say that, words really do seem to have a lot of power. I’ll try it. Besides writing letters, are there other ways that can help me express my emotions?

Besides writing letters, there is also a technique called “empty-chair dialogue” that can help you. In emotion-focused therapy, the empty-chair dialogue technique is also an important intervention. It can help you ease inner conflict and better express and release emotions.
What is the empty-chair dialogue technique about? Can I do it on my own?

Yes, you can. You can prepare two chairs. Sit in one chair yourself, and imagine that the important person is sitting in the empty chair across from you. Then express your thoughts and feelings to them. After that, you can sit in the chair across from you, imagine that you are that important person, and then respond to what you just expressed.
This method sounds interesting. I’ll give it a try. If I do this process on my own, what limitations might there be?

There may be some limitations to doing this process on your own, because you may only be able to see part of the issue and may be limited to your own perspective. But practicing on your own can still be helpful to some extent. If you can find someone you trust to accompany you through this process, it may be even more helpful, because they can help you open up more perspectives.
Besides these ways, are there any other methods that can help me express my emotions?

In addition, I think analyzing your own dreams is also a relatively valuable approach. Dreams can reflect some of your inner complexes and changes. By recording and analyzing your dreams, you can deepen your understanding of yourself. Dream interpretation itself is one of the core techniques of the psychoanalytic school.
Thank you for your suggestions and support. I’ll try these methods to help myself.
I was sexually assaulted when I was five. I want to get better. Can you help analyze and correct my thoughts?

I understand your pain, and I really appreciate that you bravely came forward. We can explore this together from a few angles, and I hope it can offer some insight for you now and some help for the you from the past.
Okay, please tell me.

First, I want to help you let go of the sense of responsibility you feel about what happened. In your story, the part you feel guilty about is that you nodded and agreed at the time, but you need to understand that they forced you to do that. This was not your fault.
I’m very grateful that you said these things. I came for help because, deep down, I’ve always felt that I was at fault.

That is a very normal feeling, but I hope you understand that the responsibility for this does not lie with you. They did something unforgivable to you. Also, you were a five-year-old child at the time and weren’t aware of those dangers.
That makes me feel a lot better. But I still feel a lot of pain right now.
I can understand that. You went through something very frightening, and it takes time to recover. But I hope you know that bravely coming forward is a very positive step.
Thank you for saying that. I feel much better now.

Also, some thoughts may make you feel even more confused. For example, thoughts like feeling so dirty after it happened, enduring it until you reached your limit and couldn’t keep going anymore, or suddenly rushing out halfway through like you had lost control, without thinking about the consequences.
Yes. I’ve always thought that if I hadn’t run away, then things wouldn’t have been so bad.

That is a self-blaming thought, and it may make you feel even more pain. In fact, running away was the right thing to do. When facing danger, protecting your own life and safety is the most important thing. Running away was the best decision you could make at that time.
So does that mean I don’t need to blame myself anymore?
Yes. You need to always believe that everything you did was to protect yourself. In such a terrifying situation, you did very well at the time.
Hearing it this way, I feel much better. I feel like I can finally let it go.
Lastly, I want to remind you to learn to protect yourself. If you need anything, you can seek help from your parents, teachers, or anyone you trust. Most importantly, you need to believe in yourself.
Okay, I will. Thank you for your patient guidance. Your support and encouragement are what motivate me to get through this.
You can come to me anytime. I’m willing to help and to listen to your story.
Every Spring Festival, Mid-Autumn Festival, and other family reunion holidays, I feel especially awful and don’t want to go home?
Why do you feel this way? Could you tell me more about it?

I’m 24 this year. I worked for three years, and now I’m preparing for the graduate school entrance exam. I do have a boyfriend I’ve been with for four years, but he’s preparing for a PhD entrance exam and doesn’t plan to marry me. Also, ever since I was little, I was a left-behind child. My dad left home to work elsewhere when I was in my second year of high school. When I was a junior in college, he came back to Kunming and divorced my mom. Both of them said the other person had cheated. I’m not sure which one it was, because I spent very little time with them and don’t really know them.

From what you’re describing, you spent very little time with your parents, so it was hard to develop a deep bond with them. On top of that, your mother’s scolding made an already not very warm family feel even worse. When you go back to that place, it triggers bad memories, and that stress response further reinforces the negative impression home has left on you. Your mother once verbally abused you, and that left a deep shadow over you. Would you feel comfortable trying to communicate with your mom, telling her about the pain inside you, and giving your emotions an outlet? Saying it out loud may also be a moment of letting go.
I do want to talk with my mom, but every time I think of her, scenes of her verbally abusing me come up in my mind. It’s really troubling.

Go back to the scene where the trauma happened, and think about why your mom verbally abused you. Which stress response of hers was triggered? When you can understand the reasons behind her behavior, perhaps things may improve. When you communicate with your mom, you can tell her about the pain inside you. You don’t necessarily need her apology, but let her know that her behavior hurt you.
I understand what you mean. I’ll try to communicate with my mom and express my true feelings. Thank you for your advice.

You’re welcome. I hope you can overcome what’s been troubling you and heal the shadow your family has left on you. Home is supposed to be a place where we feel love and warmth, but sometimes it can bring us trauma. I once read a book by Wu Zhihong, Why Does Home Hurt, which records many cases like this. The book mentions three patterns of separation: mature separation, refusal to separate, and simple separation. Would you be willing to learn about these patterns?
Of course I’d like to learn about them. What does mature separation mean?

Mature separation means loving your family while also enjoying independence. In other words, you can try to develop your ability to be independent while still keeping your feelings for your family. This can help you gain more freedom and a sense of safety.
Then what is refusal to separate like?

Refusal to separate means being attached to home and unable to be independent. Some people may be overly dependent on their family, and when they face living independently, they may find it hard to adapt or may feel anxious.
I feel like sometimes I’m like that, refusing to separate. I’m especially attached to home, but I also don’t want to face the shadow my family has brought me.

I understand how you feel, but only mature separation can truly help you heal yourself. Healing from trauma is a long-term process. Think about whether, deep down, you’d be willing to try mature separation from your family, so you can gain freedom and a sense of safety that belong to you.
I’m willing to try mature separation. I want to heal my pain and build a home of my own.

Good. I believe you can move through this difficult place and build a home where you feel happy and at ease. Please remember, in the end, people do need to become independent. We need to build a home that truly belongs to us. This home can be built in the way you imagine it, and what supports the home is your inner self. Try to give yourself a home, so you can become truly independent and no longer feel homeless.
Thank you for your support and encouragement. I’ll do my best to change and build a home of my own.
Why is it that when I face attacks or hurt, my first reaction is to act like nothing happened?
When you’re attacked or hurt, it may bring up certain past experiences or memories. That can feel painful and leave you feeling at a loss.
Yes, I feel like every time, it’s as if I’m back in some painful experience from the past. It makes me feel very helpless.

This is a psychological self-defense mechanism. Something inside you is protecting you, trying to keep you from going through that pain again. But this kind of avoidance isn’t always an effective solution.
Yes, I’ve realized that. But right now I feel a lot of regret that I didn’t express my anger or have the ability to fight back.
When you can face your emotions openly and recognize that anger and fighting back are normal responses, you can gradually build more positive coping strategies.
I hope I can protect myself better, but I always feel like I don’t have enough courage to face these attacks and hurt.
Remember, courage can be developed. Take it step by step—start by accepting your own emotions, and then gradually find ways that fit you to protect yourself.
But I don’t know how to accept my emotions. Whenever I face attacks or hurt, I always feel like I can’t control my emotions.

Accepting your emotions takes time and practice. You can try some ways to calm yourself down, like deep breathing or relaxing your muscles, to help yourself settle, and then observe and accept your emotions.
Thank you for your suggestions. I’ll try these methods. But I’m still really worried that when I face attacks and hurt, I’ll become helpless.
It’s normal to worry, but you can seek help through counseling to learn how to better face attacks and hurt. A professional counselor can help you build confidence and coping strategies.
Mm, I think seeking counseling really is a good idea. I’ll consider giving it a try.

That’s good. You’ve already taken the first step. Remember, you’re not alone; there are people who are willing to support and help you. As long as you open up and accept help, you can definitely get through this difficult place.
Thank you for your encouragement and support. I feel much better now.
I’m glad I could help. If you have any other questions or need further support, you can talk to me anytime.
Okay, I will. Thank you again for your support!
You’re welcome. I hope you can find your own balance and sense of safety. Wishing you all the best!

There are always so many things I have to think about. I feel like there’s no meaning to me being alive in this world. I feel like the road of making friends has always been really difficult for me. In seventh and eighth grade, when I competed with others, I could never win. I don’t know why, but I always put myself in a very low position. As soon as she got angry, I would humbly beg her to forgive me. No matter what she said, I agreed. I always felt that if I refused even once, she would leave me. Then in ninth grade, my parents suddenly made me change classes, saying it was for my studies. I would cry in class for no reason. I was really suffering. In tenth grade, I met a girl, and we got along especially well. I saw hope. I thought everything would change. But later I found that she was very popular. All the girls in the class liked her, and I could only watch silently. Two months later, she would be very nice to me one day, but the next day she would inexplicably give me the cold shoulder, and this cold treatment would last for a long time. I cried so many times because of this, I can’t even count anymore. For her, I gave up all the friends around me, but I found that she was always hurting me. I saw a psychiatrist, and he prescribed me medication. After I took it, I still didn’t feel better. This makes me feel like there’s no meaning to being alive in this world. I’ve had depression for two years already. Why am I still alive?
Reading what happened to you feels like seeing the past happen all over again. Please allow me to speak to you like an older sister and tell you my story.
Okay. Thank you for being willing to share your story.

When I first went away to university, I met a girl I really admired. She was independent and capable, had high emotional and intellectual intelligence, was cheerful, and very brave. She was a good roommate and also a close friend. When we first started school, we agreed we would take the postgraduate entrance exam together, and from then on we were inseparable.
That time must have been really happy, having such a good friend.

Yes, that time was very happy, and it feels warm when I think back on it. I always thought it would keep going that way. Even when I had a boyfriend, I chose a long-distance relationship, so it wouldn’t take away from the time I had with my close friend. But when I found out she had a boyfriend, and he was even on campus, I was actually very angry. So angry that I cut ties with her.
I can understand how you felt, because you felt like you had become unimportant in her life. I’ve had similar experiences too, feeling disappointed and helpless.

Exactly. For a while I was so disappointed that I shut myself off. I thought, why is it that I can accommodate everything for you, but once you have a boyfriend, you forget about me? I didn’t know how I had changed like that. I became more and more lonely. Everyone else interacted with her normally, but I became more and more of a loner.
Yes, sometimes we feel like we’ve been put in a secondary position and aren’t valued. That feeling is really painful.

I understand how you feel. At that time, I also automatically distanced myself from everything related to her. If someone mentioned her, I would walk away. I became very fragile and really didn’t dare to face it. It just so happened that I changed dorm rooms, and I temporarily adapted to the new environment, made new friends, and my mood improved somewhat.
Changing environments really can help us get to know ourselves again, and making new friends can also bring different feelings.

Exactly. But it seemed like my focus also changed. I turned it toward studying, doing well in my major courses, and preparing for the postgraduate entrance exam. On the surface, I seemed to have returned to normal, but I knew in my heart that I was even lonelier. It was just that I had returned to the path of moving forward.
Yes, sometimes we need to force ourselves to change, but at the same time we may feel even lonelier. Still, through your efforts, you found new goals and motivation.

Yes. When I went back to my hometown and heard the news that my grandmother had passed away, it felt like the sky had collapsed. Truly, nothing will stop and stay for you, not even your closest family. When I was having a hard time, my old good friend also reached out to help me. Only then did I slowly understand that I had been selfish. I had exaggerated my dependence on others and overlooked the care others had for me.
You were very lucky to receive support during a difficult time, and to be able to understand your own value and others’ care for you in a new way. That is very inspiring for me.

I took feelings too seriously and neglected the promise we were supposed to fulfill together. When you have the same goal, you’re never alone on the road of striving for it. I’m very grateful that my close friend still remembered me, even though I endured the pain of that friendship’s separation on my own. I talked about it, and I got through it. Looking back at it now, I really have let it go more. Try changing to a different comrade-in-arms, try changing to a different goal, try changing into a different version of yourself. What’s not possible? If you don’t live in someone else’s shadow, you won’t care so much. First learn to care for yourself, take good care of yourself, and don’t lose yourself.
Thank you so much for sharing your story and experience with me. I’ll try to take things a little more lightly, and also start paying more attention to my own needs and value.
I care too much about other people’s opinions, and I always overthink before I do anything.
Yes. Do you feel this issue has been troubling you a lot?
Yes. I feel like I care a bit too much about other people’s opinions, and I always want to leave a good impression on everyone.
What kind of impact has this worry had on your life and your emotions?
So before I do anything, I always think too much. I’ll imagine, if someone else did this, how would I see them? If I feel like it’s even a little bit not good, then I don’t want to do it.
I understand. You’re worried that how you act might make others have a negative opinion of you.

Yes. I’m worried about leaving a bad impression on others. For example, when competing for some important positions, I feel like a lot of people go into it with a strong sense of purpose and ambition, and I feel a bit put off by that.
Do you feel this attitude toward competition might affect your career development?
I’m worried that if I do the same thing, others will have a negative impression of me.
Everyone has different values, and you have the right to hold on to your own. At the same time, it’s also important to respect other people’s choices and goals.
I understand. Maybe I’m afraid that if I fail, other people will see it, so I have this mindset that if I don’t try, I won’t fail.
Being afraid of failure is very normal, but not trying may limit your growth and development. Trying is also an opportunity to learn and make progress.

You’re right. I’ve realized that too. I also have a lot of concerns when interacting with people. I’m afraid they’ll feel like I’m approaching them with an agenda, so I often don’t take the initiative.

When interacting with people, try to relax a little and not worry too much about what others think. You can focus more on the other person’s needs and feelings, and actively build connections with others.
I’ll try to change my attitude and become a more outgoing, open, direct, and decisive guy.
That’s good. But also remember to stay genuine and open. Life isn’t about living for other people; it’s about living in a way that feels happy and fulfilling to you.
Thank you for your advice and support. I’ll work hard to change myself and live as my true self.
I hope you can find your own balance and happiness soon. If you have any other concerns, feel free to message me anytime.

What should I do if my sense of self-worth is extremely low, and I’m also way too guarded? I’m afraid of being around people. When I’m with others, I put my own feelings last. Spending time with people makes me really tired, and I have to be alone for a while to recharge. I realize my sense of my own value is too low, but I don’t know how to improve it. I don’t trust anyone, and I’m very defensive. Because I feel like I’ll automatically switch into a people-pleasing mode with no boundaries. Every time I show even a little emotion, like complaining or getting angry, voices keep coming up inside, hating myself and blaming myself, and then I start sinking into self-defeat. How can I like myself a little more, and feel more at ease being with people?
Sweetie, maybe what you’re describing is a people-pleasing personality. I’d like to talk with you about it from a few angles.
I’m listening.

First, we can start with the reasons and process behind how a people-pleasing personality develops. All of this comes from childhood trauma. A lack of unconditional love can make us feel deep down that we’re bad and not worthy of being loved. In order to get our parents’ attention and approval, we become willing to go along with other people’s needs, even against our own wishes. We treat meeting other people’s needs as if it were meeting our own needs, but other people’s needs are always endless, so we have to strive for perfection. In this process, we place extremely high demands on ourselves, keeping our brains in a constant state of tension. This also leads us to often feel exhausted, and we can only recharge by being alone.
Yes, every time I go along with other people’s needs, I feel really tired, but I’m also afraid of not being approved of or accepted by others.

That’s right. Because we’re afraid of losing other people’s approval and acceptance, we feel fear, so we always choose to please others, even when it goes against what we truly want inside. So how can we change this situation?
Please tell me what I should do.

First, you can use mindfulness meditation to strengthen your self-awareness and self-compassion. When people-pleasing behavior or inner self-criticism shows up, take a few deep breaths and bring your attention back to the present moment. At the same time, say some affirming and forgiving words to yourself, such as, “I can say ‘no.’ I don’t have to sacrifice myself to meet other people’s needs.” Gradually cultivate love and compassion for yourself.
That sounds like a good method. I’ll try it.

Also, you can try loving touch. When the people-pleasing voice appears, you can go to a quiet place and build a closer connection with your body, for example, by placing your hand on your heart or gently stroking your face. At the same time, say some warm blessings to yourself, such as, “May I not have to suffer fear and pain. May I be healthy. May I be happy and have true freedom.” This will help cultivate love and compassion for yourself.
That method sounds very warm. I’ll give it a try.

In addition, we can also bring kindness into daily life. Observe your own behavior, and try to complete everyday tasks slowly and gently, such as brushing your teeth, walking, or noticing how much pressure you use when drying your hair. This kind of practice helps bring love into your life. At the same time, you can also observe whether there are times when you feel happy and satisfied without needing other people’s approval. Through these observations, you’ll gradually understand that everyone has imperfections, including you.
I understand. Everyone has imperfections, including me. I’m going to start paying attention to my own kindness and changes.

Another method is to build better connections with the people around you. We often feel frustrated after pleasing others, because we can’t receive unconditional love from everyone. At times like this, you can take a deep breath and remind yourself that we all have pain and human weaknesses. Everyone experiences pain, or feels disappointed, and so on. Learning to feel and understand your own pain can also help you view and handle other people’s pain better.
I’ll try to build better connections with the people around me, and also understand and have more compassion for their pain.
Finally, remember to write down every bit of progress and put it somewhere you often see. When we see our own changes, it also strengthens our sense of self-recognition and liking for ourselves.
Thank you for your advice and support! I’ll work hard to change myself, like myself more, and feel more at ease with other people.
You are a brave person, and I believe you can succeed! If you have any other questions or feel confused, you can always reach out to me for help.
I'm 26, and every day I feel like I'm suffering mentally. Does this mean there's something wrong with me psychologically?
Hello, I understand what you're struggling with right now. Could you tell me a bit more specifically why you're feeling this kind of mental suffering?

I'm at the bottom of society, female, 26. I have issues from my family of origin. No house, no car, and I have over a hundred thousand in savings. I graduated from a junior college and worked for three years. A while ago, I changed jobs and went back to my hometown to work, but something unexpected happened.

It sounds like you've been through some setbacks. Although you don't have a house or a car right now, you do have some savings, and that's a positive aspect. Finding a suitable place to settle down takes time, so there's no need to be too anxious.

I was unemployed at home for two months. Right now I'm working at a local company in my hometown, doing a different role from before. My monthly salary is 7,000, which is 1,000 to 2,000 yuan less than before.

A change in work can bring some adjustment, but choosing to work in your hometown also has some benefits. Even though your monthly salary has decreased, you may be able to enjoy a better quality of life, such as more time and less competitive pressure.
I always feel like I'm terrible, that I don't know how to do anything, that my emotional intelligence isn't high, and that I have no value.

Everyone has their own value and strengths, so you don't need to be too harsh on yourself. Emotional intelligence can be improved through learning and practice. You could try some emotion management methods, such as reading related books or seeking counseling.
Actually, I really want to get rid of this feeling that I can only feel my own value when I'm needed or recognized by others, but I've been struggling with it so much.

Many people have this kind of emotional need, and you're not alone. But you can also try to build your own inner sense of values, and not rely only on other people's recognition to measure your worth. Believe that you have unique abilities and contributions, keep exploring and developing your interests, and build your confidence.

I used to have a glorious past too. You could say I was the hope of the whole family, but then I fell. Among my relatives, I'm probably doing the worst now. Every day I'm suffering, and I don't know what I'm even doing.

Past achievements don't represent everything about the present and future. Life always has ups and downs, and that's very normal. What's important is how to find your direction and goals again, and not let the past hold your present and future hostage. You could try focusing on things you're interested in, and look for new opportunities and room to grow.

I have no desire for life. I used to be so full of ambition, and now I've become useless. I want to escape this life but can't. My biggest wish is to go live in seclusion deep in the mountains hahaha.
